The Cardinals are banking on a first time head coach, a young defensive coordinator who has struggled, an offensive coordinator who doesn’t have very much respect around the league and a veteran quarterback sitting at 20-45 in his career as a starter. It is training camp. One thing that has been interesting to watch, and get text about is the quarterback… Jacoby Brissett. Brissett has been understandably up and down, but there are some issues that we have to hope get ironed out before September 13th, which seems really far away, but is in fact right around the corner. title: Cardinals roster: Training Camp ST Outlook
summary: There is a segment of every NFL team that most fans don’t take any time to absorb and discuss. Until something goes wrong. The Arizona Cardinals have players in this group as well, commonly called the special teams group. The small group is all considered “specialists.” The reason is that the majority of players in […]
full_text: There is a segment of every NFL team that most fans don’t take any time to absorb and discuss. Until something goes wrong. The Arizona Cardinals have players in this group as well, commonly called the special teams group. The small group is all considered “specialists.” The reason is that the majority of players in this group only perform one area of expertise, and that’s it. RELATED: RYLAND RETURNS In days past, the punter was usually your quarterback. The kicker was one of the biggest guys on the offensive line. The second-string quarterback was the holder. The starting or backup center, and sometimes a tight end, was the long snapper. The kickoff return man was a guy with some size but had moves and could run, usually your second-or third-string running back. The punt returner was either a cornerback or a receiver, because this had to be somebody speedy who had great hands and had no issue sprinting 30 yards. Of course, rosters back then were 33 guys. Now, with the addition of 20 extra athletes, every NFL club can hire a handful of players that have a single job. There is another job with special teams, called a gunner. There are a pair on every punt. And yes, they are identified as specialists. But these two guys can have other jobs either on offense or defense, like the backup running back or safety man. Now that training camp is in full swing, let’s look at the special teams room. Another #AZCardinals re-signing: K Chad Ryland is returning on a one-year deal, sources say. pic.twitter.com/PVKPAMKHZL — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) March 8, 2026 This year’s group has only a few changes from the 2025 version. This can be good, or simply the fact that new coaches have reached out to bring in guys they are familiar with. When Bill Belichick was head coach, he only hired left-footed punters. His first NFL gig was the ST coach of the New York Football Giants, and the punter at that time was left-footed. They claim that the ball spins the opposite direction and isn’t familiar to most returners. Cardinals’ ST depth chart Punter: Blake Gillikin, backup (none) Kicker: Chad Ryland, backup (none) Long snapper: Casey Kreiter, backup (none) Holder: Blake Gillikin, backup TBD with backup QB Kickoff returner: Devin Duvernay, backup Jalen Brooks, Xavier Weaver Punt returner: Devin Duvernay, backup Xavier Weaver, Michael Wilson Gunners: Joey Blount, TBD Best expectations? The majority of the roster will see action on special teams. On the punt team, usually most of the starting offensive line will go and sit down to rest, which gives the backups time to go onto the field and block. Some linebackers and/or defensive line may also line up to block, especially along the edges. Gillikin has returned this year with a one-year deal after season-ending back surgery last season. The team has not signed a second punter for training camp, which is very odd since each position every camp has competition involved. He kicked extremely well last year with a 51.7 average. Ryland is also the only guy at his position in camp after the team released Joshua Karty. Which means, barring any injuries, both of these guys are guaranteed a roster spot for 2026. Year 11 in a new biome! pic.twitter.com/LptrUGM8w2 — Casey Kreiter (@caseykreiter) March 13, 2026 A new long snapper? New Cardinals head coach hired Michael Ghobrial as his new special teams coach this year. He came from the New York Football Giants. The two were on the staff of the New York Jets under Robert Saleh from 2021-2023. Ghobrial brought over his long snapper, Casey Kreiter, who has been in the league since 2014 and has one Pro Bowl appearance. Worst case? What is the status of Gillikin’s back issues? A person with any back problems doesn’t just have a procedure, and then that is that. These things linger. Did he rehab his problems without any other issues? The Cardinals found out last year that finding another punter isn’t a problem; it is finding a capable punter who can produce that is the roadblock. Ryland is not considered one of the league’s best field goal kickers, although it has been quite a while since he missed an extra point. The franchise had the opportunity to sign one of the UFL kickers who were seen nailing 60-yard field goals yet didn’t invite any to the complex for a workout, much less a training camp contract. 2026 version? Gillikin can change field position in every game this year if he can remain healthy, and has been fortunate to have him on the roster for the past three seasons. Gillikin’s average yards per punt have been 50.6 (2023), 49.7 (2024), and 51.7 (2025). That is complete consistency. Ryland after what had been a season with the occasional miss. He was a perfect 36-36 on PATs, but made just 25 of 33 on field goal attempts. The completion ratio will need to improve, as last year he hit on 75.8% of field goals. He was 0-1 in kicks of 60+ and went 6-9 on field goals that are in the 50+ range. Without another kick in camp, Ryland will trot out every kick. The biggest change for 2026 will be at return man. Last year, Bam Knight and Greg Dortch handled the kickoff duties along with Jalen Brooks and Andre Baccellia. Dortch handled the majority of punt returns, but both Baccellia and Steven Sims filled in. Dortch did have an electric 40-yard punt return last year against the San Francisco 49ers. But other than that, the return game had few highlights. The Arizona Cardinals have signed return specialist Devin Duvernay to a 1-year deal. pic.twitter.com/Reh1xQ6kNp — PHNX Cardinals (@PHNX_Cardinals) March 15, 2026 Last year, it was lots of guys taking kickoffs and punts. This year, it appears Devin Duvernay will handle return duties for both kickoffs and punts. He is a very good returner. While with the Chicago Bears, he was a key weapon who was able to flip the field, being a former track star. His return stats were pretty dad gum good. He was returning both punts and kickoffs with averages of 13.8 in punt returns and 27.5 in kickoffs. He made the Pro Bowl in 2021 and 2022 as an AFC specialist. By bringing in Duvernay, this is one less problem box that doesn’t need to be checked. He will handle it. Hopefully, backup safety Joey Blount makes the final roster again this season for the fourth consecutive year. He is an excellent gunner and a sure tackler.

title: Falcons training camp Day 3 news, standouts, interviews, injuries
summary: Day 3 was the first training camp practice open to fans, who packed the hill and brought the energy on Friday. Perhaps the most interesting note to come out of Friday is that Kevin Stefanski does plan on playing starters in the first and third preseason games. He said there will be limits on how […]
full_text: Jul 30, 2026; Atlanta, Falcons, USA; Atlanta Falcons quarterback Tua Tagovailoa (1) shown on the field during training camp at IBM Performance Field. Mandatory Credit: Dale Zanine-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Day 3 was the first training camp practice open to fans, who packed the hill and brought the energy on Friday. Perhaps the most interesting note to come out of Friday is that Kevin Stefanski does plan on playing starters in the first and third preseason games . He said there will be limits on how long they play depending on a variety of factors, but it is good for them to get some contact before the season starts. Prior to the second game will be the joint practices with Indianapolis, and Stefanski said starters will get most of the run against the Colts in those practices, and guys farther down the depth chart will be featured in that second preseason game. Tua Tagovailoa wasn’t a full go on Friday, but he was able to get some work in team drills and looked pretty comfortable moving around out there. Stefanski said after practice that the back issue that’s flared up is not going to be a long-term issue for Tagovailoa, and Tagovailoa confirmed that himself. Penix, unsurprisingly, was even less of a full go, but did get in some 7-on-7 work. After practice, Kevin Stefanski explained that the team works with the medical staff to determine the practice plan for Penix to make sure they’re protecting his recovery while letting him get some reps and work on his timing, anticipation and connection with his receivers. Our own Kevin Knight is also here for the next few days, and he’ll have plenty of takes and analysis and clips from practice for y’all, and may be adding some thoughts to this story later as well. If you’re free Friday night, we are heading to Fun Spot America Atlanta to ride the Arieforce One coaster before it’s gone forever. You are more than welcome to join us, and what better place for a Falcoholic meetup than a shady amusement park? Being a #Falcons fan is like riding a roller coaster with a terrible safety record. — The Falcoholic (@TheFalcoholic) September 27, 2015 As always, my full reporting from Friday’s activities can be found right here in the Falcoholic’s Feed. Here are the rest of my (Jeanna’s) observations from Day 3 of camp. Jack Strand was running with the 1s in 11-on-11s quite a bit on Friday. The caliber of talent he’s going up against at this level compared to his NAIA college career is vastly different, but Stefanski said he’s coming along nicely. On one play, it looked like a handoff to Brian Robinson, who got caught up in the backfield, but Strand adjusted and completed a catch to a receiver (couldn’t see the number). Cooper Rush also got plenty of run in 11-on-11s, with mixed results. He did toss a beautiful ball to Austin Hooper, which I’m calling a Coop-to-Hoop. Cash Jones stood out to me on Friday. He caught an absolute duck of a ball from Rush in 11-on-11s, and recovered well enough for some yards after the catch, and he caught another nice one from Strand on a short out-route, where he hit a spin move to break loose for some YAC again. Stefanski said after practice that Jones’ abilities as a receiver out of the backfield are a big part of the reason they thought he’d be a good fit, and that Jones is also working hard on special teams, which is obviously important for a young player making a case for a roster spot. Penix’s 7-on-7s were … not great. I did some sloppy, quick charting, and it’s possible I missed a throw or two, but according to my count, he completed just one pass the entire time he was in there. There are caveats, as there always are in training camp. We know he’s not medically cleared for full practice or contact. He wasn’t dropping back with full weight on his recovering leg or at anything close to full speed, and that does impact pass velocity and accuracy. I’m not worried about the performance because of those caveats, and because Tua appears to be making progress physically. We already know it’s very unlikely Penix will be ready to start the season, and there’s no question Tua’s the best option of the other three, no shade to Cooper Rush or Jack Strand. One thing I found interesting was the coaching staff’s use of a fitness/exercise ball for those Penix 7-on-7s. Since they can’t take a risk of any other player falling into Penix’s recovering leg and setting his recovery back, they rolled the exercise ball toward Penix to simulate pressure and create some urgency so he could work on his timing. Tyler Goodson broke loose for a really nice gain in Penix’s 7-on-7s. Penix did have a nice-looking pass intended for Drake London, but AJ Terrell got there quicker for the PBU. Not to be outdone by his big brother, Aveion Terrell picked off Cooper Rush toward the end of practice. Bijan Robinson is still holding in, but he’s extremely engaged with his coaches and teammates during practice, encouraging teammates to keep the energy up on Friday. My preference would be to pay the man whatever he wants. Tua Tagovailoa has been very impressed with Zachariah Branch! “You can put him anywhere (in the formation,” he said of the rookie out of UGA. Kyle Pitts said basically the same thing about Branch, and that he’s not a typical rookie. Kirby’s players always come into the league with more of a pro mindset. Kevin and Adnan Ikic will be here to cover every aspect of camp on Saturday, so ya girl is staying home to catch up on some season prep and not get up at 5:30 a.m. on a weekend. Gotta stay fresh; training camp is a marathon, not a sprint. I’ll be back at it Monday, and look for the fellas’ takes on Saturday!

full_text: FLOWERY BRANCH, GEORGIA - JULY 29: A.J. Terrell Jr. #24 and Avieon Terrell #12 of the Atlanta Falcons warm up during training camp at IBM Performance Field on July 29, 2026 in Flowery Branch, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images Training camp is in full swing, and the battles have begun. While some have been derailed already—Jawaan Taylor can’t compete for right tackle right now because he’s out, and Michael Penix Jr. may not be fully cleared for a month—others are just getting going and offer plenty of intrigue. Here are three that we’ll be monitoring throughout August. Please check out our roundtable and then let us know which positions and players you’re particularly keen to see in camp and preseason. Nose Tackle Since we don’t see many man-for-man trades in the NFL, sending off Ruke Orhorhoro for Maason Smith got a bit more traction than it may have if, say, it happened now. The nose tackle position is not a done deal; LaCale London showed last season that he can make plays in limited snaps, logging five sacks, four QB hits, a pass deflection and a forced fumble with only 270 snaps. Not saying that London is anything particularly special; the nose tackle position is still likely in dire straits and will probably be addressed early in next year’s draft, but I do wonder if we may be able to get a bit of a surprise performance out of London or Smith as we head into training camp. — Saivion Mixson Inside linebacker With the quarterback battle on very uncertain footing, given the injuries piling up, this is the one that intrigues me most. There are plenty of other worthy ones, but I’m most looking forward to seeing Christian Harris and Kendal Daniels duke it out for the starting job next to Divine Deablo. Harris has always had intriguing ability but hasn’t been consistent enough to make the most of it, while Daniels is fresh off a college career where he showed worthwhile potential. Both players fit the rough mold of what Jeff Ulbrich wants in terms of length, athleticism, and physicality, and if Daniels is healthy, it should be a fun one to watch. The only problem is the if with Daniels. –Dave Choate Tight End Is Kyle Pitts’ job security still in doubt after his polarizing new deal? No. However, the return of Austin Hooper has put some pressure on Charlie Woerner. The assumption with the hire of Keven Stefanski is that a 12-personnel (two tight ends, 2 wide receivers, and 1 running back) approach is going to be a staple of the offense, but who will be the tight end featured opposite Kyle Pitts the most? Hooper is the most well-rounded tight end in the room, while Woerner has always functioned as a 6th lineman. If the team wants more versatility out of their anticipated 12-personnel look, it seems that it would be Hooper’s job to lose, but Woerner has a cap hit nearly three times Hooper’s and is the superior blocker. It may not be the most highly anticipated battle, but it will give some insights about how this offense wants to attack defenses down to down. –Tre’shon Diaz

full_text: BIRMINGHAM, ALABAMA - MAY 17: D.J. Miller Jr. #21 of the Columbus Aviators interceptis a pass intended for Jaydon Mickens #12 of the Birmingham Stallions* of the Birmingham Stallions during the first quarter at Protective Stadium on May 17, 2026 in Birmingham, Alabama. (Photo by Butch Dill/UFL/Butch Dill/UFL) The Buffalo Bills continue managing their 91-man training camp roster, with WGR550’s Sal Capaccio first reporting the Bills have signed cornerback D.J Miller Jr., releasing safety Wande Owens in a corresponding move. Prior to signing with Buffalo, Miller spent the previous two seasons playing in the UFL with the Michigan Panthers (2025 UFL season), and Columbus Aviators (2026 UFL season). With the UFL’s Panthers, the 5’10”, 193-pound Miller made 29 tackles (17 solo), two interceptions, and eight pass defenses in 10 regular-season games; adding nine tackles (8 solo) and three pass defenses in two postseason games during the 2025 UFL season. As a member of the Aviators, Miller totaled 24 tackles (20 solo), one tackle for loss, nine pass defenses, and three interceptions for 39 yards in nine games played. Before joining the UFL, Miller played college football at Kent State during the 2022 and 2022 NCAA football seasons. In two campaigns, Miller started 19 of 23 total games played, claiming 109 tackles (68 solo), one tackle for loss, seven pass defenses, and two fumble recoveries. In parting ways with Wande Owens, the Bills close this chapter with a player who Buffalo Rumblings’ own Chris Trapasso tabbed as his favorite under-the-radar story — someone who he thought had a real shot to push for playing time in 2026 . A talented defender with plus athletic traits, Owens was battling to be part of the team’s roster this season. A former UDFA, Owens a productive rookie preseason in 2025 , totaling five tackles in 45 exhibition snaps. However, a then-undisclosed injury saw the Bills wave him at the end of the preseason. He then went unclaimed and reverted to Buffalo’s Injured Reserve for the entirety of the 2025 NFL season. Physical Therapist and Doctor of Physical Therapy Kyle Trimble ( @BangedUpBills ) shared additional information on Owens this past January. His findings, based on photographic evidence, suggested Owens underwent an “ACL reconstruction.” Got another injury update on #Bills S Wande Owens, rookie UDFA. He was put on IR ahead of roster cut downs on 8/23 after leaving practice on 8/21. His IG post shows him in a hospital bed with steristrips on his L knee with the placement suggesting an ACL reconstruction. pic.twitter.com/8aZL1kEuDU — Banged Up Bills (@BangedUpBills) January 23, 2026 In the photo below from Bills mandatory minicamp on June 9, you can see Owens (No. 30) wearing a heavy knee brace while performing drills. It remains unknown what Owens’ status is as of July 31, but there were no reports of him missing time during the first few days of 2026 training camp.

title: Buffalo Bills superfans: Painting Beskar tassets for Mandalorian armor
summary: You got a tease of the paint on the armor last time, and if you’re like I was, once you saw the first color coat go on, you were eager to see the final result. If you were anxious to see it, hopefully there wasn’t a huge delay between publishing that one and this one. […]
full_text: You got a tease of the paint on the armor last time, and if you’re like I was, once you saw the first color coat go on, you were eager to see the final result. If you were anxious to see it, hopefully there wasn’t a huge delay between publishing that one and this one. Anyway, I have the tassets painted (but not fully assembled or made wearable). So let’s take a look. Right tasset – In memory of Sachio Ashida We’ll start things off a little bit heavy. I said each piece was going to tell a story, and this is one I’ve wanted to be told for quite some time. My real name isn’t too hard to find, and neither would be some personal history, so it’s no harm in sharing that I attended SUNY Brockport some years ago. While there, I finally found a martial arts instructor that was a good match for how I wanted to learn. I’ll let you read his biography here , but I must comment that this does have one inaccuracy I need to correct for the record. I can’t correct it on the site directly, because apparently there’s a region block on editing. Anyway, Dr. Ashida would openly speak about his military service and he made it clear that he was not a kamikaze pilot. That was the term for Navy pilots and he was in the Army. I forget the term he used exactly, but the overall term is “ Shinpū Tokubetsu Kōgekitai .” Here’s my design to honor him, then I’ll go into how I made it and why I made the choices I did. I call it “Lunar Eclipse on a Partially Cloudy Night.” Now let’s discuss what I did and why. This is a closeup of the tasset with the metallic blue. First off, why a piece of armor to honor Dr. Ashida? He was quick to praise correct technique, but very rarely gave global compliments. Put differently, he often said “You did this well” but would rarely say “You are good because…” if that makes sense. I was lucky enough to receive one such global compliment from him. When describing something to the class he pointed me out and said I had “very good natural defense.” This armor piece is layered in inspiration of the bamboo armor that a samurai might wear, something his family could trace itself to. I’ve created angles I think convey the look of “space” for the Star Wars look, but he loved the notion of invention. He taught a class on understanding creativity, and once told me how many sushi recipes he invented. To Dr. Ashida, every new iteration of something was worthy of the designation of “invention.” Something to celebrate. I hope he would have liked this. I wanted to get it right, and that meant practice. The first pic here was my first attempt while the paint was still wet. The second picture was after curing, which was a big help. But something was still missing. The next pic is my second attempt, where I decided that craters were necessary to make it look more moon-y. The last pictures are showing that I made a stencil from Frog Tape and how i got the crater look on the final piece. A layer of white then a layer of blue. Smudge to bring out the dark spots. Then another coat of white, then the red to get the eclipse look. You might have noticed that the final piece has some extra blasts of white that give it a cloudy feel, and I also spackled some white spots that look like stars. I’m not a painter, but I know what I like, and I like this. I wanted to pay tribute to Japan, notably known as the land of the rising sun. I didn’t, however, feel that it was right for me to straight up use the flag of Japan on my armor. This is a tribute. I’m a night person so I paid tribute with contrast. This armor piece is from the land of the eclipsing moon. I bet I don’t need to explain this one… I wanted to do an article with the two tassets together, and it works well because it shifts the mood away from somber. I’m going to reveal this one with the process, but I imagine you’ll figure it out before the big reveal. As for story on this one, we all tend to pull from the various families, tribes, clans, or other groups that make us who we are. I think you’ll know which group this represents right away. If you remember from the last article, the tasset for my left leg was painted a base color of white. My first step in getting the “mystery” paint scheme on it, was to tear strips of frog tape. Notice how there are no clean edges of tape facing what you can see of the white tape. The torn edges are critical for this look. If you’re thinking ahead, what you see here covered in tape is what I want to be white when the piece is done. That’s critical to planning. After I applied this tape… I painted the whole thing red. Then it was time for taping round two. It’s hard to see here, but again, the tape is protecting the layer where you want to keep the color (on this picture, the red). The tape here is half on the old tape (that protects the white paint) and half on the new paint. What that means is the white stripes I planned originally, will now be bordered by thin strips of red on either side. I’m confident you know the next steps are to paint over this in blue, then peel the paint to reveal it. With frog tape, they recommend immediately peeling (or very soon after spraying) which means you have to be very careful. Essentially, the only dry color at this stage is the white undercoat which luckily had a corner or two I could use to hold on while peeling paint. And here’s the final “mystery” design revealed. It’s not perfect, but pretty good for my first try. For whatever reason I didn’t think I needed to practice this. Last but not least, I was worried the two pieces would clash side-by-side. I might be biased here, but I really like the two together. As a side note, if you think I screwed up the first piece, I can still claim authenticity to the project by prompting people to point at me and say “That’s no moon!”

title: Buffalo Bills training camp: How rookies fare vs veterans early matters
summary: The classic sci-fi television series “Star Trek” introduced the world to “The Worf Effect.” The trope refers to the phenomenon where a new character is pitted against a character with a high amount of known ability in order to establish the relative power level of the new character, usually a villain. The blockbuster Marvel Studios […]
full_text: Bills defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard visits with players during day two of Buffalo Bills training camp at St. John Fisher University Thursday, July 30, 2026 in Pittsford. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The classic sci-fi television series “Star Trek” introduced the world to “The Worf Effect.” The trope refers to the phenomenon where a new character is pitted against a character with a high amount of known ability in order to establish the relative power level of the new character, usually a villain. The blockbuster Marvel Studios film “Avengers: Infinity War” famously opened with the Hulk (he of super strength and durability unmatched to that point in the running storyline) getting absolutely dog-walked by movie villain Thanos. It was a moment that immediately raised the bar, allowing audiences to note how incredibly dangerous the new antagonist was. It’s like that with rookies too. When the 2025 Return of the Blue & Red practice finished up, Bills veterans had seen then-rookie defensive tackle Deone Walker starting to get positive buzz in large part because his teammates had begun to see the 6’6”, 331-pound lineman against players they knew. They isolated the variable, which isn’t possible to the same degree at rookie minicamps (where first-year unknowns are competing against other first-year unknowns or tryout players) and even mandatory minicamp (where contact is extremely limited and certain positions have distinct advantages that could be used to dismiss or minimize strong performances). Coaches and general managers have told stories of watching a rookie take reps against another player early in the training camp and immediately worrying that the first-year player simply wasn’t going to cut it in the league. Who does this phenomenon apply to on the 2026 version of the Buffalo Bills? Technically, any rookie could pop early and look like a steal. In addition to the aforementioned Walker, former 2022 sixth-round pick Christian Benford popped early in his rookie camp, leading to the early season platoon at CB2 between Benford and a first-round pick from the same draft named Kaiir Elam. This situation mimicked the defensive tackle scenario in 2006, where rookie fifth-round pick Kyle Williams was a standout even compared to first-rounder John McCargo. By the middle of October that year, Williams had been named a starter. But for this camp, rookies like edge rusher T.J. Parker (competing against offensive tackles like Spencer Brown and Dion Dawkins, when he gets “ones vs. ones” reps), cornerback Davison Igbinosun (competing against wide receivers like DJ Moore, Khalil Shakir, and Joshua Palmer) have an opportunity to immediately establish what type of players they are. It’s not as important that the players they’re competing against are All-Pro-level players; it’s simply a matter of establishing an initial bar for new players by having them compete with players we feel we have a handle on. Does linebacker Kaleb Elarms-Orr show ease of disengagement when taking on the blocks of offensive guard O’Cyrus Torrence? Will safety Jalon Kilgore win at the catch point against wide receiver Keon Coleman? Nothing in American football occurs in a vacuum; it’s ultimately one of the most complex team sports in the world because an individual’s performance is always relative to the play they’re running against and potentially multiple different opposing players on that same play. Seeing a new player perform on their college field is excellent. Seeing players perform on tape is great. Seeing them perform in simulated drills is all fine and dandy. But seeing them perform against established NFL veterans can help the team (and fans, in the little live practice time they get) feel better about their investment pretty quickly. …and that’s the way the cookie crumbles. I’m Bruce Nolan with Buffalo Rumblings. You can find me on Twitter and Instagram @BruceExclusive and look for new episodes of “The Bruce Exclusive” every Thursday on the Rumblings Cast Network — see more in my LinkTree!

title: Buffalo Bills training camp: DJ Moore & Josh Allen off to special start
summary: The Buffalo Bills didn’t trade for wide receiver DJ Moore so that he could be just another piece of the offense. They acquired Moore in the hopes of landing a bona fide difference maker, a receiver capable of changing the complexion of games. They were looking for someone to perform as a true number-one target […]
full_text: Jul 29, 2026; Rochester, NY, USA; Buffalo Bills wide receiver DJ Moore (2) catches a pass during training camp at St. John Fisher University. Mandatory Credit: Mark Konezny-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Buffalo Bills didn’t trade for wide receiver DJ Moore so that he could be just another piece of the offense. They acquired Moore in the hopes of landing a bona fide difference maker, a receiver capable of changing the complexion of games. They were looking for someone to perform as a true number-one target for quarterback Josh Allen, something he hasn’t had since the departure of Stefon Diggs. It’s true that there’s only been two days of training camp at St. John Fisher University so far this summer, but the early signs are hard to ignore. If there’s been one storyline that stands out above the rest through Buffalo’s first two practices, it’s the rapidly developing connection between Allen and Moore. Wednesday’s session offered the first glimpse. The timing wasn’t perfect early, which is hardly surprising considering the two are still learning one another’s on-field rhythm. A couple of throws missed their mark, but instead of forcing things, the chemistry seemed to improve with every miscue. By the end of practice, Allen dropped a perfectly placed sideline pass into Moore’s hands, allowing the veteran receiver to drag both feet in bounds despite the rain. It quickly became one of the highlights of Day 1. Then came Thursday. Any questions about how quickly this relationship might develop were answered in a hurry. Allen and Moore connected on multiple explosive plays throughout practice. During Thursday’s 7-on-7 drills, Allen found Moore behind the defense for a long touchdown after recognizing a breakdown in coverage. Later, during 11-on-11 work, Moore created separation on a post route against rookie cornerback Davison Igbinosun before hauling in another deep completion. Two days. Multiple explosive plays. Two deep touchdowns. That’s exactly what One Bills Drive envisioned when president of football operations/general manager Brandon Beane acquired Moore from the Chicago Bears this offseason. Perhaps the most encouraging takeaway isn’t simply the catches. Instead, it’s how both players are talking about everything happening between them. Following Thursday’s practice, Moore credited constant communication as the biggest reason their chemistry is developing so quickly. Rather than waiting, he said the conversations are happening continuously, before reps, after reps, and throughout practice as they work through timing, routes, and adjustments. That approach has clearly made an impression on Allen as well. Allen admitted he initially found himself trying to be too perfect when throwing to Moore. Instead of simply trusting what he saw, he was aiming the football. Once he got back to just letting it rip, everything started to click. Training camp always comes with the usual disclaimer that defenders aren’t game planning. Everyone looks good in shorts. Big plays in July don’t automatically become touchdowns in September. But some things translate regardless of the calendar. Timing. Trust. Communication. Those are exactly the traits beginning to emerge between Allen and Moore. Bills fans have spent the offseason wondering how quickly Buffalo’s newest offensive weapon would fit into the offense. Through two days of camp, the answer appears to be much faster than anyone expected.

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 training camp position battle primer: DB
summary: In the fourth installment of this series, I covered linebackers — Kaleb Elarms-Orr’s dual audition next to Terrel Bernard, and T.J. Parker’s real path to snaps behind Bradley Chubb. Now I move to the back end of Jim Leonhard’s defense, where the outside cornerback room has more talent than settled jobs, and where a rookie […]
full_text: In the fourth installment of this series, I covered linebackers — Kaleb Elarms-Orr’s dual audition next to Terrel Bernard, and T.J. Parker’s real path to snaps behind Bradley Chubb. Now I move to the back end of Jim Leonhard’s defense, where the outside cornerback room has more talent than settled jobs, and where a rookie safety with a fallen draft stock might be closer to playing time than his draft slot suggests. Bills’ DB d epth chart entering camp Outside Cornerback: Christian Benford, Maxwell Hairston, Davison Igbinosun, Toriano Pride, Kani Walker, Jordan Dunbar Slot Cornerback (Nickel): Dee Alford, Jordan Hancock, Te’Cory Couch Safety: Cole Bishop, CJ Gardner-Johnson, Jalon Kilgore, Geno Stone, Damar Hamlin, Sam Franklin, Wande Owens Outside Cornerback: Maxwell Hairston’s 2nd-year leap Hairston enters Year 2 as a first-round pick with a real shot to lock down a starter job — and to become one of the actual standouts of this defense, not just a rotational name. The talent isn’t the debate here. The debate is whether he can stay on the field. If Hairston opens the door with any kind of injury during the preseason or camp, Davison Igbinosun is right there to take advantage. Igbinosun fits what Jim Leonhard wants to do in his first year as coordinator, and I think he’s a real threat to win a starting job outright opposite Christian Benford if he gets the opportunity. That’s what makes this room worth watching closely: If Hairston and Igbinosun both show their ceiling at full health, Benford himself becomes a name worth questioning in this defense — not because of a decline, but because the room around him has simply gotten better, cheaper, and younger. All three of these guys will handle the bulk of the outside cornerback snaps regardless of how the starting battle shakes out. Toriano Pride is the name I’d watch behind that trio. He’s undersized for the outside, but he has real ability to play there anyway, and I believe he makes the 53-man roster. Cuts here: Kani Walker and Jordan Dunbar are competing for whatever’s left at the bottom of this group — practice squad territory more than realistic roster locks. Positional battle interest level: High Slot Cornerback: Dee Alford’s job, for now Alford was brought in to start at nickel, and the job is his to keep for now — he should do enough with it over the course of the season to hold onto it. But this room has real long-term options behind him. Jordan Hancock, who played mostly safety last season, should start seeing more nickel reps, and it could end up being the position that fits him best in Year 2. Pride, mentioned above at outside corner, could also see some nickel snaps if the Bills want that versatility. Rookie Jalon Kilgore, who played safety at South Carolina, looks like the guy stepping into the role Hancock occupied last year while Hancock makes his own transition to nickel — but I wouldn’t rule out Kilgore getting real nickel looks himself either. C.J. Gardner-Johnson also has nickel experience, and if Jalon Kilgore or Geno Stone show enough to be legitimate options next to Cole Bishop at safety, it wouldn’t be surprising to see Gardner-Johnson kick inside to nickel as well. Positional battle interest level: Medium Safety: Cole Bishop and C.J. Gardner-Johnson Bishop and Gardner-Johnson should be the starters here, and I don’t see that changing. What I’m genuinely interested in watching through camp and preseason is everything behind them. Jalon Kilgore is the name I care about most. He’s a rookie who fell in the draft and landed with Buffalo, and I think he’s a real candidate to be Bishop’s long-term partner at safety. How ready he looks right out of the gate says a lot about where this room is headed past 2026. Geno Stone is the experienced, opportunistic veteran of the group — the kind of player who can carve out a bigger role on this team just by generating turnovers. Damar Hamlin is fighting for his roster spot, and I don’t think he makes the 53. Sam Franklin is a special-teams ace, and the rest of this group is mostly fighting for a practice-squad look rather than a real shot at the final roster. Cuts here: I’d expect Hamlin and most of the depth beyond Kilgore and Stone to miss the 53, with practice squad as the realistic ceiling for that group. Positional battle interest level: Medium Final Thoughts This secondary has more talent than it has settled jobs, and that’s a good problem to have. Hairston’s ceiling is obvious if he stays healthy, but Igbinosun waiting behind him means Buffalo doesn’t have to hope — they should have a real answer if something goes wrong. Nickel is Alford’s to lose with depth developing behind him. And at safety, the starters are set, and CJGJ, Stone and Kilgore all offer different reasons to be excited about the group in 2026. Overall, there’s reliability, there’s young star potential, and there are experienced vets trying to show everybody they still belong as starters on a winning team in this league. Things have to go real bad not to have, at least, solid starters all across the board in this secondary. Catch up on the series: Part 1: QB, RB and OL Part 2: WR and TE Part 3: Defensive Line Part 4: Linebacker Catch up on all this and more with the latest edition of Leading the Charge!

title: AFC East 2026 training camp roundup: First-week headlines
summary: Training camps are in full affect around the NFL with fans able to see their favorite players take the field ahead of the upcoming season. full_text: Training camps are in full affect around the NFL with fans able to see their favorite players take the field ahead of the upcoming season. Camp is a time for social media to go crazy with their quarterbacks throwing dimes in 7-on-7 action, or ripping apart one of their receivers for dropping the first football thrown their way. With a couple of days of practice in the books, let’s look at some of the buzz coming out of the AFC East. For the Buffalo Bills one of the questions was how the team would look without Sean McDermott as head coach of the team. Perhaps guard Alec Anderson said it best about the vibes with new head coach Joe Brady by stating “(i)t’s kind of like having your uncle come over… …do stuff that your parents wouldn’t really allow you to do.” Wondering what the vibe is with Joe Brady as Bills head coach? Just ask Alec Anderson "It's kind of like having your uncle come over … do stuff that your parents wouldn't really allow you to do" #BillsMafia pic.twitter.com/Us5xvU4oOU — Rachel Libert (@Rachel_Libert) July 29, 2026 When it comes to the players on the field, fans were waiting to see all offseason if wide receiver DJ Moore would be worth the price of the trade — and so far there’s hope that he could be the answer. He made some nice catches that went for touchdowns in Thursday’s practice and the chemistry is slowly building between quarterback Josh Allen and Moore. On the defensive side of the football C.J. Gardner-Johnson is showing that he’s worth the price of admission. He’s been flying all over the football field in practice and bringing a swagger on defense that’s been missing in the recent past. The reigning AFC East Champion New England Patriots enter training camp this season with a bona fide number-one wide receiver option after a much-publicized and finally realized trade for A.J. Brown. Brown got off to a slow start in camp adjusting to quarterback Drake Maye, but the two have been making strides and had a great practice on Thursday. AJ doesn't know what it's like to have a QB put a ball in that small of a window lol pic.twitter.com/fylAY7mhEQ — BaddogSports (@MrBaddog7676) July 30, 2026 Some members of the media are saying that cornerback Christian Gonzalez is having the best camp of his career as he continues to assert his claim as one of the best corners in the league. Not bad for someone who is rumored to have been offered the largest contract in Patriots’ history. Switching things over to the New York Jets, who are trying to find their direction heading into the season. They have some intriguing pieces led by wide receiver Garrett Wilson and running back Breece Hall but, like seemingly always, the quarterback is the question mark. The anticipated starter under center seems to be Geno Smith, where the veteran hopes his second tenure with the Jets is a whole lot better than the first. Geno Smith ➡ Garrett Wilson 🎯 #Jets | 🎥 @nyjets pic.twitter.com/f8KjhUoU2N — Harrison Glaser (@NYJetsTFMedia) July 30, 2026 There’s a lot of buzz surround rookie first-round defensive end David Bailey who had a three-sack (unofficial) performance in Thursday’s practice, disrupting a lot of what the offense was trying to do. One of the main questions will be if head coach Aaron Glenn is up to the challenge of being the Jets’ leader into the future. There were moments last season where it appeared the players weren’t giving it their all for Glenn. So… will he be able to pull out 100% effort from this year’s football team? The Miami Dolphins may be one of the most mysterious teams heading into the season. That’s because no one knows what to expect from quarterback Malik Willis who got a sizeable contract from the Dolphins with little film to go off of from his stint with the Green Bay Packers in 2025. One of the characteristics to love about Willis is that he has a big arm, which he likes to show off. Miami Dolphins QB Malik Willis hits Tutu Atwell for the BOMB TD ‼️ pic.twitter.com/EG6mq931ff — Young Slime (@FinsOrDie) July 29, 2026 Second-year defensive end Chop Robinson’s stock is rising, with him becoming a force in practice and making plays all over the place. Offensive lineman Austin Jackson mentioned that Robinson looks like he packed on some muscle but that he’s also a lot quicker coming off the snap. Miami is entering a critical year in their future as some may consider this a rebuilding season. If it is, then the Dolphins will have a huge decision to make regarding the quarterback position if they find themselves in possession of a high first-round draft pick next April.

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting reports: P Mitch Wishnowsky
summary: The Buffalo Bills had some punter problems early on in the 2025 season. After releasing one due to ineffectiveness just one week into the season, the Bills thought they had found a suitable replacement. However, an injury derailed that plan, leading them to sign a third punter just one month into the schedule. That third […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OH - DECEMBER 21: Buffalo Bills punter Mitch Wishnowsky (19) punts out of his end zone during the second quarter of the National Football League game between the Buffalo Bills and Cleveland Browns on December 21, 2025, at Huntington Bank Field in Cleveland, OH. (Photo by Frank Jansky/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Buffalo Bills had some punter problems early on in the 2025 season. After releasing one due to ineffectiveness just one week into the season, the Bills thought they had found a suitable replacement. However, an injury derailed that plan, leading them to sign a third punter just one month into the schedule. That third punter not only stuck around for the rest of the year, but he performed quite well throughout it. In fact, he performed well enough that the team decided to bring him back on a one-year contract for this season. That didn’t stop the Bills from adding competition, though, as they also drafted a punter late in the 2026 NFL Draft. In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss the veteran half of Buffalo’s sure-to-be-epic Great Punter Battle of 2026. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Mitch Wishnowsky Number: 19 Position: P Height/Weight: 6’2”, 220 pounds Age: 34 (35 on 3/2/2027) Experience/Draft: 8; selected by the San Francisco 49ers in the fourth round (No. 110 overall) of the 2019 NFL Draft College: Utah Acquired: Signed with Buffalo on 9/30/2025 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Wishnowsky re-signed with Buffalo this offseason, inking a one-year deal worth $1.475 million overall. Thanks to the veteran’s salary benefit, his cap hit will be a bit less if he makes the club, coming in at $1.25 million for the season. If Buffalo releases him before Week 1, they will carry a dead-cap charge of $150,000. If Wishnowsky is on the roster for the first game, his whole base salary — $1.3 million — is guaranteed thanks to his status as a vested veteran. 2025 Recap: Wishnowsky was released by the 49ers at the end of May, and he was without a team throughout the entire offseason, training camp, and preseason from that point onward. He signed with the Washington Commanders’ practice squad on September 10, but when punter Tress Way was able to suit up in Washington’s next game, they released Wishnowsky just three days later. Buffalo signed Wishnowsky on September 30 after punter Cameron Johnston, who had replaced Brad Robbins after the first game of the season, suffered a knee injury against the New Orleans Saints. Wishnowsky remained Buffalo’s punter for the rest of the season, totaling 38 punts at an average of 45.3 yards per punt. 18 of those punts landed inside the opposing 20-yard line , and 15 of them forced a fair catch. He allowed 11 returns for just 69 yards while netting 41.9 yards per punt. Positional outlook: Wishnowsky and Tommy Doman Jr. are set to do battle for the right to be Buffalo’s punter this season. 2026 Offseason: Wishnowsky is healthy, having participated in all offseason work as of publishing. 2026 Season outlook: Given how little Wishnowsky is set to count against the salary cap, it’s unlikely that finances will play a role in which punter makes the team this season. The best man, whether it’s Wishnowsky or Doman, is going to win. If the Bills cut Wishnowsky and keep Doman, their financial obligations at punter will add up to around $1.07 million between Wishnowsky’s $150,000 dead-cap number and Doman‘s $918,043 cap hit. The difference between just keeping Wishnowsky and moving on is so slight that the finances should not, and likely will not, factor into the decision. Wishnowsky was very good last season, so if Doman is going to unseat him, he’ll have to be excellent in his own right this summer. Part of the way he can do it is by showing that he’s not only a consistent punter, but that he’s also very good at holding on field goals and extra point attempts. With Tyler Bass set to return this season, working closely with the kicker to ensure that holds are done at the proper angle is essential to ensuring maximum success and comfort. Buffalo might not want to put that responsibility in the hands of a rookie, so it could be another way for Wishnowsky to separate himself this season. There might be some sexier battles at more prized positions this offseason, but the punter battle is one that we’ll have to watch closely. Wishnowsky has a great shot at sticking on the roster this year, especially if he can perform at the level he did last season.

full_text: HOUSTON, TX - FEBRUARY 1: Running back DeShaun Foster #20 of the Carolina Panthers scores on a 33 yard touchdown run against the New England Patriots during Super Bowl XXXVIII at Reliant Stadium on February 1, 2004 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Brian Bahr/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #43. DeShaun Foster On Friday, running back Stephen Davis was our player of honor in the countdown of top 100 Panthers. One day later, it’s his former partner in crime, DeShaun Foster. Serendipity. People forget that DeShaun Foster was actually born in Charlotte, coincidentally enough, but he grew up in California and went to college at UCLA. After a standout career there, the Panthers brought him home by making him the 32nd overall pick in the 2002 NFL Draft. Unfortunately, his rookie season ended before it even got started, as a preseason injury took him out for the season. He returned to back up Stephen Davis for his second year, and while his contributions over the course of the season were modest, he was responsible for two of the most memorable plays in Panthers history during their playoff run. First, he broke free from six different Eagles defenders for a two yard touchdown in the NFC Championship game. Then, in the Super Bowl, he broke free for a 35 yard touchdown run that ended with an iconic dive over the goal line that spurred a comeback in a truly unhinged fourth quarter. The injury issues that popped up upon Foster’s entry to the league returned to plague him for much of the rest of his career. He missed the majority of his third season with a broken collarbone. He made it through his fourth season largely in good health, and even supplanted Stephen Davis as the team’s starter by season’s end, but he broke his ankle in the playoffs. His effectiveness began to wane after that, and he gradually ceded more of his workload to the newly drafted DeAngelo Williams over his final two seasons in Carolina. He got a cup of coffee in San Francisco to wrap up his career. When all was said and done, Foster amassed 3,336 rushing yards and 10 touchdowns across five seasons in Carolina. He never topped 1,000 yards in a season, but he amassed just under 900 yards in each of his last three seasons as a Panther, and he chipped in here and there as a receiver out of the backfield. The 3,336 yards are good for sixth in Panthers history. Between the stat compilation and the iconic moments in the playoffs, Foster earns himself spot number 43 on the top 100 Panthers of all time.

title: Brian Answers: Injuries, Hall of Fame Game, Haynes King, and more!
summary: Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! We’ve had a ton of news on the injury front this early cycle of training camp, and all of the reporting has fans buzzing. Let’s dive right in to all your questions! @WTMealey: Given the injuries would you adjust […]
full_text: Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! We’ve had a ton of news on the injury front this early cycle of training camp, and all of the reporting has fans buzzing. Let’s dive right in to all your questions! @WTMealey: Given the injuries would you adjust your win prediction or do we have enough depth and talent at other positions to sustain whatever your win prediction was prior to Training Camp? I had Carolina somewhere between 8-10 wins prior to the start of the preseason. I’m leaning closer to 8 wins with the loss of Nic Scourton. WR Chris Brazzel’s knee injury certainly sucks since he’s also out for the season, but I think if a 3rd round pick from this season screws up their entire offensive gameplan, the team was in trouble to begin with. Hopefully the injury bug doesn’t claim anyone else for an extended period. Godspeed. brake23: Do you see the team picking up another seasoned veteran pass rusher or going after a young guy that is cut in training camp? I could see them potentially grabbing a VERY cheap veteran pass rusher, as in; not one that would excite the fan base. However, I think its more likely they grab someone during the final round of cuts. This current iteration of the Panthers loves to grab a depth piece along the trenches as their 52/53rd roster spot during the final round of cuts. SmoothC: Can we expect to see anyone who makes the roster to see much playjng time at the HOF game? I dont think we will I think its more likely we’ll see that on defense in the secondary, among the likes of Corey Thornton and Will Lee at CB, and probably Lathan Ransom and Zakee Wheatley at safety. I’d imagine it’ll be the Haynes King and Kyle Trask show at QB, and we probably won’t see much of Jonathon Brooks or really any of the top 4 WRs (possibly Xavier Legette) during the game. Revshawn: So who are we betting for in the Hall of Fame game? I’m pretty sure that the game will be decided at the 2nd screen and I think the Panthers have more talent across the board then the Cardinals. It will be a hard match with both of the teams having something to play for: The sacred honor of Luke Kuechly and Larry Fitzgerald. I linked your comment for those who want to see commentary on potentially betting the game. I am not betting on a preseason game. I don’t want to and nobody can make me. SmoothC: If Panthers wasnt in the HOF game, they wouldn’t have been in training camp a week early. If they wasn’t in training camp a week early Scourton injury wouldn’t have happened. Who do we blame? I’m sure this question is half in jest, but I don’t really blame anyone for the Nic Scourton injury. Its just a part of football. positivebob: I know starters usually don’t play much, if at all, in the preseason, but do you think Freeling and Brooks might be exceptions? Freeling is a rookie learning a new position and Brooks hasn’t had but a handful of snaps since November of 2023. Do they need as many live snaps as they can get? They probably both will get a handful of snaps in 2 of the 4 games. Jonathon Brooks might get a little more snaps in one of them, but I think the Panthers actually see him as a big time contributor this season, so I don’t see him playing longer than a quarter (collectively) in any one game. With Monroe Freeling, I could see him getting a lot of work in whichever game the Panthers trot their 1s out for, but they need to be very careful with their tackle depth being so thin. So I’m guessing he won’t get thrown out there when we see the offense playing musical chairs with the offensive line during the 2nd and 3rd team showings too much. Brazilian Panther: With no Ickie, Moton and Scourton against the Bears week 1 (for now anyway) – knock on wood – give us your level of confidence on the team and Bryce especially. I want a W against Williams so bad man… I’m not optimistic on that one. The Bears offense is loaded with passing weapons, and the Panthers offense typically starts out slow. If there’s ever a game for this offense to come out fast, its this one. But I am not very confident in a win. I know, it sucks, I’m sorry. Bull123: should we be concerned about Hunt or Lewis injuries? or it is just 100 degrees in July and just being careful? From what I’ve seen, this is just standard veteran load management for those two. And I’m fine with that. Both aren’t new faces to Carolina and both have been in the league for a long time. Giving them time off when they are feeling things like back tightness are the right way to go. Bruce Guild: Once Haynes Kings takes over the QB1 position, can you see him also going both ways and filling in at OLB for Nic Scourton I think its more likely he fills in for Scourton than he does take over the starting QB position. joecats: Are all of these lower leg injuries we have been seeing due to the turf? Any chance we can fuss at the owner about this issue yet again? The Panthers practice on grass. And the lower leg injury issue is actually a league wide problem. Of course, its hitting the Panthers harder all at once than usual, but this isn’t a new thing, its been going on since the new CBA that lightened the schedule for players in preseason/training camp. I’m not suggesting that is ENTIRELY the problem, as I think the fact that athletes are just bigger and faster than ever before and training to become so has also progressed over the last decade or two factors in, but I do think players having to go full speed from an extended break can certainly be a factor. But I am by no means an expert on the human muscle anatomy or athletes by that matter. Just my personal opinions to try and make sense of it all. dayneb12: What advantages and/or disadvantages do the Panthers get from being in the Hall of Fame game? I think the competitive advantage is getting the extra game of tape on their 3rd and 4th team units, specifically along the offensive line and defensive front seven. They are going to need to rely on some potential unknowns as depth along those units so the extra look at the guys who could shape out the back of the depth chart is helpful. Along the negatives, injuries are always a concern with another preseason game, so they may be very cautious to put anyone out there that could be relied upon in the regular season. Advantage in general; its going to be nice to see Luke Kuechly get some extended praise for the NFL fans base’s first real taste of football that always gets people tuning in just to see something resembling the sport they love. That’s all for this week, Panthers fans. Join us next week for another edition of this week’s fan mailbag.

(Photo by David Allio/Icon Sportswire) (Photo by David Allio/Icon Sportswire/Corbis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #44. Stephen Davis Running back is probably the most well represented position on this list except for maybe linebacker. Today’s running back of note is Stephen Davis, the first ever Carolina Panthers running back to start in a Super Bowl. Davis, a native of Spartanburg, South Carolina, entered the NFL as a fourth round pick by Washington. He played as a fullback and backup running back for the first three years of his career before getting a chance at the lead back role in 1999. He took the position and ran with it, literally. He rushed for over 1,400 yards and scored a league high 17 touchdowns. He followed that with two more stellar seasons before injury troubles messed up his 2002 season. Following that 2002 season, Davis signed with the Panthers to be the team’s starting running back ahead of DeShaun Foster, who was coming off a season ending injury prior to his rookie season. He was able to rediscover the magic that he found in Washington, rushing for 1,444 yards and eight touchdowns as the Panthers made an improbable run to the Super Bowl. He ran for 315 yards during the playoff run, though just 49 came in the Super Bowl as the Panthers went to the air in a game that got wildly out of control. Unfortunately, Davis would end up being a one hit wonder of sorts for the Panthers. Injuries robbed him of all but two games in his second season in Carolina, and he struggled to bounce back for his third. He started ceding work to Foster as he limped to just 3.1 yards per carry in his third and final season in Carolina. Davis spent one last season with the Rams before hanging up the cleats. When that time came, he signed a one day contract to retire as a Panther. Davis only had one standout season in Carolina, but it feels like more than that given the timing. He was a central figure in the Cardiac Cats’ run to the Super Bowl, and that run perfectly coincided with his arrival. While it’s a shame that we didn’t get to see more of Davis at his best, we at least got that one season. And that’s enough to earn him spot number 44 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

(Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images A recap of Chicago Bears training camp practice number 3. The Chicago Bears beat reporters noted the defense got on the board today with Caleb Williams registering his first interception in the 7-7 drill, picked by Jaylon Johnson, and the defense gave trouble to the offense in the red zone. But the Williams-Loveland connection was on display all day. Dan Wiederer of The Athletic remarked, “Jaylon Johnson proof of life. Instinctive, athletic pick at the goal line in red zone 7-on-7.” “Defense had the upper hand in the first red zone period. Both Austin Booker and Montez Sweat with ‘sacks’ on back-to-back plays,” noted ESPN’s Courtney Cronin. Still, it was a pretty good day for the offense and Caleb Williams on the whole. Josh Buckhalter of ClockerSports remarked that the interception to Jaylon Johnson was “Caleb Williams’ only mistake.” He also noted Tyson Bagent had a solid performance running the offense. “It was the Caleb Williams, Colston Loveland show on Friday at Halas Hall in practice number three,” said Nicholas Moreano of Bears REKAP, “when Caleb Williams expected #84 to be in a spot, Loveland was there to make plays…Caleb Williams connected with Loveland on three of his last four passes, including a 14-yard seam route touchdown.” The left tackle situation for the Bears seems very much in flux. Kevin Fishbain of The Athletic noted that the Bears opened team drills with Kiran Amegadjie, followed by Braxton Jones. As Adam Jahns of the Hoge & Jahns podcast remarked, “the LT competition is very, very real.” Kiran did get most of the reps with the 1s today, with Braxton Jones working with the second team and Wills with the 3s. However, while the Bears clearly have an open competition at left tackle, one shouldn’t jump to conclusions based on which player is running with the 1s in a given practice. Because the competition is open, Bears coaches clearly want to see each candidate with different linemates in practice. So as far as the full day of practice goes, the defense made more plays today. The offense had some struggles in the red zone. But it was still a winning day for the Bears offense. As we’ve noted in these writeups before, we shouldn’t get too high or too low from shorts-and-shells practice, but I think we all prefer this kind of news to some of the worrying signs we’ve seen in early practices in past seasons. A few other nuggets from the day. Ben Johnson had an answer in response to Liam Coen’s comments that his players are under the radar because he sees “40 pictures of Caleb Williams” when he scrolls through his feed. He’s used to handling a lot of attention, so I’m not worried about that.” Running back Salvon Ahmed got substantial practice reps as Kyle Monangai missed practice for the second day in a row, and there is still no word as to why (don’t panic…yet). title: Darnell Wright on his future, ‘I’ll be on the Bears for a long time’
summary: Earlier this week, Chicago Bears general manager Ryan Poles was asked about a possible contract extension for right tackle Darnell Wright. “I think there’s a window to get a deal done. and then at some point we got to go play football, Poles said at his press conference. “So we’ll figure that part out, but […]
full_text: Jul 31, 2026; Lake Forest, IL, USA; Chicago Bears offensive tackle Darnell Wright (58) walks on he field during Training Camp at Halas Hall. Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Earlier this week, Chicago Bears general manager Ryan Poles was asked about a possible contract extension for right tackle Darnell Wright. “I think there’s a window to get a deal done. and then at some point we got to go play football, Poles said at his press conference. “So we’ll figure that part out, but obviously, I think I’ve said it before, Darnell’s a guy we want here long term. It takes two sides to get things done, but at the end of the day, I don’t want any distractions or anything like that, so when it’s time to go play football, we’ll go play football and keep it moving.” His comments worried some, especially the “takes two sides to get things done” remark, but I just took it as canned GM-speak. That’s one of those cliches said during a negotiation. Poles capped his answer with a, “But yeah, he’s a guy we would like here for a while,” which is what he’s said before, too, and coupled with today’s comments from Wright, it appears it’s just a matter of time. At his post-practice presser today, Wright was asked how he’s handling the contract talk, and he said , “My main focus really is just football, being as best I can be for the team. Obviously, I know I’ll be here for a long time, hopefully my whole career. So those things kind of handle themselves.” When asked if he’d prefer an extension to get done sooner rather than later, Wright said, “I mean, I’ll be on the Bears for a long time. So it doesn’t really matter to me.” He went on to say his representation is handling the business, and it’s his job to play football. Wright, who turns 25 in August, isn’t going anywhere.

title: Cash, Stash, or Slash: TJ Edwards
summary: The Chicago Bears will have several contract decisions to make over the next 13 months. The Bears have several veterans from the Matt Eberflus era that will have contracts expiring, and the Bears will have to decide if they want to keep them. There are plenty of younger players from the 2023 and 2024 draft […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - JANUARY 10: T.J. Edwards #53 of the Chicago Bears runs out of the tunnel prior to an NFC Wild Card Playoff game against the Green Bay Packers at Soldier Field on January 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears will have several contract decisions to make over the next 13 months. The Bears have several veterans from the Matt Eberflus era that will have contracts expiring, and the Bears will have to decide if they want to keep them. There are plenty of younger players from the 2023 and 2024 draft that will have to decide about extensions as their rookie contracts get close to finishing. We’ve already looked at Darnell Wright’s potential contract; now let’s look at TJ Edwards. Edwards was signed in 2023 and had a great season in Chicago. His 2024 season was solid but a step back from 2023. 2025 also went in the wrong direction and included a significant injury. It’s 2026, and Edwards is under contract with the Bears through the 2027 season. What should the Bears do with their linebacker? TJ Edwards: Slash The Bears need to move on from Edwards as soon as possible. When Edwards was extended after the 2024 season, it was largely met with applause from Bears fans and media. Some had concerns with Edwards’ age and that his production headed in the wrong direction in 2024, and that this might have been done prematurely. Those concerns certainly played out in 2025, where Edwards was nowhere near the same player he was in 2023. We’ve now reached 2026; the Bears have signed Devin Bush, brought back D’Marco Jackson, and have drafted linebackers in each of the last two drafts. The Bears are poised to move on from Edwards sooner rather than later. If Edwards were cut this season, it would do nothing in terms of creating cap space. Cutting him this year would leave the Bears with $10.5 million dead in 2026 and $2.3 million dead in 2027. That certainly doesn’t seem like a sensible plan with their salary cap moving forward. But if the Bears cut Edwards after the 2026 season, he leaves just $2.3 million in dead cap behind. If the Bears can find a trade partner who wants Edwards before the season, that would get him off the books and get his contract largely off the books as well, however, there’s no reason to think a team would give up any draft compensation for a linebacker on the wrong side of 30 with declining production coming off a major injury and pay himn $8.5 million for the season. Edwards will almost certainly be on the Bears for the 2026 season, but the odds he’s on the roster when the new league year hits in March of 2027 are about as close to 0% as it can be.

title: Dan Pitcher is feeling good about the Bengals offensive line
summary: Cincinnati Bengals offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher is very high on his offensive line heading into the 2026 football season. Speaking with Dan Hoard, Pitcher said this is the best he’s felt about the Bengals offensive line. “I sit here in front of you feeling as good about that as I ever felt. You’ve got five […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher takes questions from the press during the annual season kickoff media day event at Paycor Stadium in downtown Cincinnati on Monday, July 27, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Cincinnati Bengals offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher is very high on his offensive line heading into the 2026 football season. Speaking with Dan Hoard , Pitcher said this is the best he’s felt about the Bengals offensive line. “I sit here in front of you feeling as good about that as I ever felt. You’ve got five guys that played together for the bulk of last season, who played their best football as the season went on, and there are a lot of measures that demonstrate that they got better and better and better.” The Bengals return all five starters from an offensive line that played its best football during the last 7 weeks of the football season. According to PFF, the Bengals had a top-five pass-blocking grade during those final 7 weeks of the season, once Dalton Risner took over as the starting right guard. The addition of Dalton Risner helped stabilize the Bengals offensive line. He will be one of the five returning starters in 2026. pic.twitter.com/IM5w1Y8K1m — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) July 20, 2026 Chemistry on the offensive line is such an underrated aspect for an offense. It is refreshing that the Bengals will return five capable starters to begin the 2026 season. If this unit could end up finishing in the top 10 during the season, the Bengals could set several offensive records this year.

title: Ted Karras is ready to guide the best offensive line of the Joe Burrow era
summary: When the Cincinnati Bengals signed center Ted Karras to be the center of Joe Burrow’s offensive line, it immediately became one of the better signings of the Zac Taylor era. Karras has pretty much been an Ironman for the Bengals, missing only one regular-season start, and will enter the 2026 season as the starting center, […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - JANUARY 4: Ted Karras #64 of the Cincinnati Bengals stands for the national anthem prior to the game against the Cleveland Browns at Paycor Stadium on January 4, 2026 in Cincinnati, United States. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the Cincinnati Bengals signed center Ted Karras to be the center of Joe Burrow’s offensive line, it immediately became one of the better signings of the Zac Taylor era. Karras has pretty much been an Ironman for the Bengals, missing only one regular-season start, and will enter the 2026 season as the starting center, possibly for the last time. Ted Karras Height: 6-4 Weight: 310 lbs. Age: 33 (turns 34 next March) College: Illinois Hometown: Chicago, Illinois Experience: 11 years Cap Status Karras signed a one-year extension in June of 2024 that would keep him in Cincinnati through the 2026 season. That extension was worth $6 million and included $3 million fully guaranteed. His base salary in 2026 is set to be $3.4 million with a workout bonus of $100,000. The overall cap hit of $4.5 million represents 1.49% of the team’s total cap space. Background Karras primarily played right guard at Illinois and was the Patriots’ sixth-round pick in the 2016 NFL Draft. He played both guard and center, but he wasn’t a consistent starter at either position until the 2019 season, when he started 15 games at center. The Dolphins signed Karras as a free agent to a one-year deal, and he started 16 games for Miami that season before returning to the Patriots on another one-year deal in 2021, where Karras started multiple games at left guard. The Bengals signed Karras in 2022 to a three-year, $18 million deal, and he has since become one of the most beloved players in the city. Not only is he one of the NFL’s better centers, but he’s also a strong vocal leader who knows how to bring out the best in his teammates. “I love him. He’s probably the most competitive guy I’ve ever been against in practice,” Dexter Lawrence said of Karras following a recent training camp practice . “It’s a joy. In practice it’s easy to lose that edge, but he helps you keep it with how much of a pro he is.” Of course, you have to actually be good for teammates to listen, and Karras is about as good as it gets when it comes to protecting his quarterback at the center position. Ted Karras just finished 2nd amongst Centers in True Pass Sets grade from PFF. This is after he was ranked 3rd in 2024. He gave up 1 sack all year and had his highest Pass Block Efficiency since 2020. https://t.co/JkhU4JPRhb — Goodberry (@JoeGoodberry) February 16, 2026 Outlook for 202 6 Karras has been a consistent force at center for the Bengals since he’s been here, despite consistency issues at both guard positions at times on either side of him. Now, though, the Bengals are entering the 2026 season with the same core five starting offensive linemen as they did the year before, which is a first in Burrow’s career. With Orlando Brown Jr. and Amarius Mims at tackle, and Dylan Fairchild and Dalton Risner at guard, Karras, a team captain, will hopefully lead an offensive line that keeps Burrow clean and opens holes in the running game. If everyone can stay healthy, the sky’s the limit for this offense. Considering Karras is entering a contract year, and Connor Lew, drafted in 2026, is now on the roster, it’s possible that the end of the Karras era will come when the 2026 season comes to a close. Hopefully Karras, who has won two Super Bowls, helps the Bengals win their first, and then he can ride off into the sunset. If this is the last ride for Karras, remember him at his best: #WPMOYChallenge Ted Karras pic.twitter.com/zVhrwBoqI7 — Bengals Graphics (@bengalsgraphic5) December 13, 2023

full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - JULY 29: Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals talks to the media during Cincinnati Bengals Training Camp at Kettering Health Practice Fields on July 29, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images Quarterback Joe Burrow has always had that one thing you need from a quarterback that can never quite be defined with a number you’ll find in the box score. The way he carries himself is just on the next level. The last player we saw similar to that was Tom Brady. Brady is widely viewed as the best quarterback in NFL history between winning championships and statistical accomplishments. Burrow is obviously still searching for his first ring, but just from the way he completely turned this team around upon arrival. From one of the worst teams in the NFL to playing in a Super Bowl. Burrow played a massive role in that. Burrow may never reach the heights of Brady himself, but he is going to be fun to watch for a while either way. Bengals’ rival player revives the rare comparison that seems to only find Joe Burrow in the NFL Since even before he was drafted by the Cincinnati Bengals, quarterback Joe Burrow has been the subject of a truly unfair comparison. An enemy from the AFC North was the latest to compare Burrow’s game to that of the greatest QB of all time during the NFL’s Top 100 Players of 2026. Quick Hits | Knight and Day at LB; Stewart Avoids Major Injury Off their tough rookie seasons, linebackers Demetrius Knight Jr. and Barrett Carter have shown the Bengals a snap-crackle-and-pop confidence in their demeanors, and they teamed up for the rarity of rarities Thursday morning for an interception of quarterback Joe Burrow in a training camp practice. It is good to see signs of life from this linebacker duo. How much this defense can improve may depend on how these two develop. Training Camp Report | ROH Member James Brooks And Chase Brown’s Summit Of Little Big Men “It looks like he can still play,” Brown said of the 67-year-old Brooks. “He was talking about how being physical is a mentality, and he carried that chip on his shoulder. And it was funny because I couldn’t agree with him more. I mean, I carry the same thing on my shoulder. Brooks passing on anything to Chase Brown is just an incredible thing. It is funny how Brooks is today’s standard to be a dual-threat running back. He was a do-it-all back, and now Brown takes up that latest mantle for the Bengals. Bengals DE Stewart out multiple weeks with hyperextended knee The team’s 2025 first-round pick went down Wednesday during team drills on the opening day of training camp. Stewart had to be carted off the field and had imaging done later in the day to see the extent of the damage. From all accounts, this seems like the best case scenario. The way he had to be carted off the field after giving walking a go could easily have signaled a potential season-ending injury. It is still unfortunate that he will be missing some valuable reps after missing so many last year, but at least Stewart avoided the worst-case scenario.
