title: Sean Payton sees a little Drew Brees in Bo Nix
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! People always try to find comparisons and make connections. That is especially true in the wide world of sports. And it’s even truer when you have Sean Payton. As one of the best head coaches in the NFL and for one of the best quarterbacks in NFL history, Payton brings a […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - JANUARY 17: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos warms up before kickoff against the Buffalo Bills in the AFC Divisional Playoff game at Empower Field At Mile High on January 17, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! People always try to find comparisons and make connections. That is especially true in the wide world of sports. And it’s even truer when you have Sean Payton. As one of the best head coaches in the NFL and for one of the best quarterbacks in NFL history, Payton brings a unique perspective. Payton will present Drew Brees for his induction into the Pro Football Hall of Fame next week. Of course, Payton was asked about his years coaching Brees with the New Orleans Saints on Thursday. It makes sense given the success the two had and the relationship they built over their time together. One day at a time. 😤 pic.twitter.com/Wu7BnICusZ — Denver Broncos (@Broncos) July 30, 2026 Regarding the Denver Broncos, Payton was asked about Brees and Bo Nix. Hence, the comparison and connection referenced earlier. Payton said about Brees and Nix: “I think that No. 1, they were high-volume college players. He (Brees) played a lot of snaps at Purdue. I would say the immediate, just analytical statistical number would be the accuracy numbers. From an NFL perspective, he’ll go down as the most accurate passer in the history of the league, and, collegiately, he was at Purdue. I think historically speaking, Bo was the most accurate college passer when you look at a lot of numbers, so that would be the first. “(It’s) a tough comparison for anybody in their (third) year, but that would just be the beginning. Their personalities are different, of course, but their accuracy and their positioning of the ball is certainly noticed.” Nix has a long way to go before he’s in the discussion with Brees. However, Nix is on the right path after his first two seasons in the league. Coming off an ankle injury after one of the best wins in franchise history is an interesting element to the coming season. We’ll see what the future holds, but it’s going to be fun to see Nix’s continued development and growth this season and going forward.

title: Detroit Lions training camp observations: Jameson Williams is getting even better
summary: By Dan Campbell’s own admission, Detroit Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams took his biggest jump last year. His route tree developed, his cuts were sharper, and his hands became more reliable. In short, he became a trusted receiver by Jared Goff and the entire offense. But through the spring program and three training camp practices, […]
full_text: Detroit Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams (1) practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Friday, July 31, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co By Dan Campbell’s own admission, Detroit Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams took his biggest jump last year. His route tree developed, his cuts were sharper, and his hands became more reliable. In short, he became a trusted receiver by Jared Goff and the entire offense. But through the spring program and three training camp practices, Williams has taken his game to another level. And the next step in his development appears to be coming down with contested catches. On the first day of camp, he elevated between Ennis Rakestraw and Chuck Clark to come down with a bomb. On Day 2, he made a couple catches in traffic. And on Friday morning, he was as impressive as ever. It started with a one-on-one rep against Rakestraw. He initially blasted by the third-year corner, but when the pass came up short, he was forced to hit the breaks and elevate over the 5-foot-11 defensive back. Despite Rakestraw being all over him, Williams came down with the grab—as he has done for nearly every contested target this summer. More importantly, these strides have carried over into the team activities. On the final session of the day—an end-of-half drill with 1:10 left—Williams caught two passes in traffic: a short 7-yard catch with Rock Ya-Sin in close pursuit, and a 20-ish yard deep shot with Ya-Sin all over him again that put Detroit’s offense in field-goal position for the simulated win. “He’s doing all the little things right. That’s where he’s made the most growth, man,” Campbell said before practice. “Watch his route definition. Watch the details to it. Him dropping his weight. Him pulling out, playing strong, catching the ball, reaching out, plucking. And, so with his ability, man, the sky’s the limit.” Here’s more from Friday’s practice: The left guard competition is on With Christian Mahogany off of the NFI list after a non-injury related absence, it appears the left guard competition is on. In his first day back, Mahogany split first-team reps with Juice Scruggs and got plenty of work with the second team offense as well. I didn’t get a ton of looks on how he played, but I did see him lock down Tyler Lacy during a one-on-one rep. While Mahogany is already on his way to reclaiming the top spot on the depth chart at guard, his biggest competition—Ben Bartch—should be coming soon. As of now, the Lions have kept Bartch out of team drills as a precautionary measure from the foot injury that ended his 2025 season early. But he has been getting some first-team reps during walkthroughs. Campbell expects Bartch to be out there next week. “We’re being smart with Bartch. We hope we start to get some team reps next week with him, that’s the plan,” Campbell said. As for Scruggs, Campbell says they really like him at center, and some of the reason he’s been getting so much play at guard is because of the absences from Mahogany and Bartch. His play at guard as been up and down, but Campbell noted that playing against Alim McNeill will do that to you. Speaking of McNeill, he left practice early, along with rookie linebacker Jimmy Rolder. We have a full training camp Day 3 injury report here. First taste of 1-on-1s For the first time in camp, we got a look at some highly entertaining 1-on-1 drills. I’ll bullet point my observations from each. OL/DL Detroit clearly didn’t want to overwhelm rookie tackle Blake Miller, so they had Aidan Hutchinson go up against Penei Sewell. It was a pretty clean win for Sewell in both reps between the two, although Hutchinson’s relentlessness had him fighting to the whistle. As for Miller, I had him with a stalemate against DJ Wonnum on the first rep, and on the second rep between them, Miller took the veteran edge defender to the ground when he tried an inside move. Ahmed Hassanein showed off some serious explosiveness in his first rep against Devin Cochran, beating him decisively with an inside move. However, Cochran got the best of him on rep 2, with the frisky Hassanein unable to get out from Cochran’s clutches. The two best collective reps from the pass rushers belonged to rookie Derrick Moore. On the first against Larry Borom, he swam inside for an immediate pressure. On the second, he flashed his speed to get around Colby Sorsdal in a hurry. Tyleik Williams and Cade Mays split their series of two reps. On the first, Williams used his strength to execute a rip move past Mays. On the second, Mays had him locked up. CB/WR Admittedly, I was paying a little less attention to this, as it was taking place at the far end of the field, but I do have a few notes: Isaac TeSlaa made a nice back shoulder grab while shielding his body away from Rock Ya-Sin, who was in relatively good position. Later, Nick Whiteside continued his strong camp with a great pass breakup against TeSlaa. Earlier in the practice, Whiteside logged an interception on a pass over the middle that was intended (but overthrown) to Tom Kennedy (via Teddy Bridgewater). D.J. Reed has been quietly impressive to start camp. He had a very strong jam against Jameson Williams, forcing the young receiver to get a little off balance and mess up the timing of the play. While Williams eventually got by him, the target was way over both players’ head because of the disruption. Greg Dortch cleanly beat Roger McCreary on one rep, but Khalil Dorsey got the best of Dortch later with a pass breakup. Other notes: When McNeill left due to injury, it was Mekhi Wingo who stepped in with the first-team defense at the three tech. Levi Onwuzurike, who picked up another tackle for loss on Friday, continues to rep between the first and second team. McCreary did a great job staying with a play on an attempt to Cedrick Wilson Jr. The veteran receiver bobbled the catch attempt, and McCreary attacked the ball as both players went to the ground. Initially, it looked like Wilson still came down with it, but the ball was jarred loose for the fumble/incompletion. Former UFL WR Lawrence Keys made an improbable toe-tapping catch on an impressive ball from Luke Altmyer. In terms of overall arm talent, I like what I’m seeing from Altmyer so far. Rookie Keith Abney made a nice pass breakup during 7-on-7 drills Detroit worked on a lot of third down on Friday, and unsurpringly, that meant a lot of passes to Amon-Ra St. Brown. Running back Jabari Small made the juke of training camp on linebacker Joe Bachie, who looked like he was left doing splits trying to change direction. The juke drew a large roar from the players. It’s hard to tell without full contact, but I remain optimistic about Isiah Pacheco’s explosiveness. There’s been some warranted concern that he’s lost it after a few injuries, but on one catch during Friday’s practice, he turn upfield and accelerated into the next gear in a hurry. Player who impressed the most Friday: Derrick Moore (multiple pressures in 1-on-1s and team drills), Ahmed Hassanein (another TFL during teams), Jameson Williams, Nick Whiteside (again) End of half drill ends with some hijinx To close out practice, the Lions worked on an end-of-half drill. The scenario: starting on their own 25-yard line with 1:10 left with a couple timeouts. Here’s how it went down (yardage is estimated) : 9-yard pass to St. Brown (in bounds) 7-yard pass to Williams (in bounds) — timeout, 40 seconds left 5-yard pass to Sam LaPorta (in bounds) 8-yard pass to Sione Vaki (in bounds) — timeout, 20 seconds left 20-yard pass to Williams (in bounds) Spike With the offense in somewhat comfortable field goal position, they celebrated the win and it appeared practice was over. But then Campbell got the group together, and the team lined up for a 48-yard field goal to really seal the win. The kick was good. But here’s the twist: it wasn’t Jake Bates kicking the field goal, it was Jack Fox (and Isaac TeSlaa holding). Fox didn’t clear the…

title: Detroit Lions training camp injury update: Alim McNeill leaves early
summary: The Detroit Lions suffered what appears to be their first in-practice injuries of training camp on Thursday. Veteran defensive tackle Alim McNeill and rookie linebacker Jimmy Rolder left early and did not return. But it wasn’t all bad news for Detroit. They did get one player back from an injury list, and it appears others […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive tackle Alim McNeill (54) practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions suffered what appears to be their first in-practice injuries of training camp on Thursday. Veteran defensive tackle Alim McNeill and rookie linebacker Jimmy Rolder left early and did not return. But it wasn’t all bad news for Detroit. They did get one player back from an injury list, and it appears others are making progress. Let’s break down all of the Day 3 injury news below. Returned to practice: G Christian Mahogany ( NFI ) Mahogany was officially taken off the Non-Football Injury list on Friday and immediately got some first-team reps, splitting time with Juice Scruggs. Mahogany told a small group of reporters that his absence was not injury related, and he’s ready to improve upon last year’s perforance. Not practicing: RB Jahmyr Gibbs ( not-injury related ) TE Tyler Conklin (PUP, calf) OT Giovanni Manu (NFI) EDGE Payton Turner (back) S Kerby Joseph (PUP, knee) S Brian Branch (PUP, Achilles) S Christian Izien (NFI, flu) The only updates we got from this group is that Izien’s return got pushed back a practice. “One more day. That’s the hope,” coach Dan Campbell said. “We were hopeful today. We just—hey, let’s back this up one more day.’ So, hopefully after this day off and on Sunday, he’s able to go. He had the flu. He’s just still a little weak.” Kerby Joseph continues to get some strenuous work on the hill outside for practice, but nothing about his status appears to have changed. Gibbs’ hold-in continues. Left practice early DT Alim McNeill (neck) LB Jimmy Rolder (leg) About halfway through practice, both McNeill and Rolder left practice under their own power. McNeill was in good spirits and talking with some of the friends and family in the stands nearby, while Rolder was getting a little more assistance from a trainer that was escorting him inside the facility. At this point, the Lions have only offered the following update: The following players left practice early today to be evaluated for potential injuries. LB Jimmy Rolder (leg) DT Alim McNeill (neck) Earlier in the day, Campbell spoke about just how important McNeill is to the defense this year. “Mac is very important. It is going to be huge,” Campbell said. “Particularly when, look, on all of it, it’s big, right because you’re part of the other 10 that are on that field. But, when you’re talking about transitioning to rush off a play pass from the offense or even just, here we go, man, it’s a known pass down. Somebody’s going to get a one-on-one. […] There’s these times where either he’s not doubled or (Aidan Hutchinson) Hutch—they have got to win. Mac’s got to win. And, he has the ability to win a one-on-one.” Last year, McNeill missed the first half of the season as he recovered from a torn ACL suffered in 2024. Campbell admitted that going back on the film, it was clear McNeill was still favoring that leg when he initially returned. Thankfully, this injury appears unrelated. The Lions next take the field on Sunday, but coach Dan Campbell isn’t expected to speak with the media until Monday. So we may have to wait until then to get an update on both players—if they’re not back in the lineup by Sunday.

title: Christian Mahogany removed from NFI, gets some 1st team reps
summary: It didn’t take long for third-year offensive guard Christian Mahogany to work his way back into the starting lineup. After missing the first two days of training camp while on the Non-Football Injury list, Mahogany was on the field for the Detroit Lions’ Friday practice, and immediately started splitting first-team reps with veteran Juice Scruggs […]
full_text: ALLEN PARK, MI - AUGUST 21: Detroit Lions Guard Christian Mahogany (73) after the joint practice between Houston Texans and Detroit Lions on August 21, 2025 at Detroit Lions Training Facility in Allen Park, MI (Photo by Allan Dranberg/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It didn’t take long for third-year offensive guard Christian Mahogany to work his way back into the starting lineup. After missing the first two days of training camp while on the Non-Football Injury list, Mahogany was on the field for the Detroit Lions’ Friday practice, and immediately started splitting first-team reps with veteran Juice Scruggs at left guard. Mahogany said what he was dealing with was not injury related, just referring to the absence as something internal. Mahogany will look to keep a hold on his starting job from last year, but the Lions brought in some serious competition for the former sixth-round pick. This offseason, the Lions traded for Scruggs as some competition and depth both at center and guard, and they signed veteran guard Ben Bartch to join the room, as well. “Love Juice, man, he’s a pro,” coach Dan Campbell said Friday. “He’s a pro. Same guy every day, very consistent. We know he can play center. And, some of the guard stuff is, ‘Hey, Mahogany’s out right now.’” Bartch hasn’t truly joined the competition yet, as he’s been only working in walkthroughs and individual drills, but coach Dan Campbell said he will start adding some team reps as early as next week. Mahogany says he’s not bothered at all by the broken leg that shortened his 2025 season. He’s also hoping to build on what was a disappointing season last year—although he made sure to point out that he’ll never be fully satisfied with his play. “I can never say I’ll feel pleased (with my play),” Mahogany said. “I’ve probably said this repetitively: Once I feel pleased, like I said, I won’t be here anymore. There won’t be a Christian Mahogany in the building. I won’t be here once I’m pleased. So I’m never pleased. I definitely didn’t play up to who I want to be and the player I want to be.”

title: What was the best part of the 2026 Lions draft episode of ‘Inside the Den?’
summary: With training camp now officially underway, the Detroit Lions gave their fans a surprise Thursday night when they dropped episode two of, “Inside the Den.” The latest episode of the Emmy-award winning series dove into the 2026 NFL Draft, and how Lions general manager Brad Holmes, coach Dan Campbell, and the rest of their staff […]
full_text: With training camp now officially underway, the Detroit Lions gave their fans a surprise Thursday night when they dropped episode two of, “Inside the Den.” The latest episode of the Emmy-award winning series dove into the 2026 NFL Draft, and how Lions general manager Brad Holmes, coach Dan Campbell, and the rest of their staff operated in what was their sixth draft since taking the reigns in Detroit. As always, the Lions’ media department did an excellent job when putting the episode together. From documenting the approach the team took in the first-round when they had their eyes fixed on right tackle Blake Miller, to their decision to move up to draft Michigan defensive end Derrick Moore. “Derrick Moore was our No. 1 guy, we have multiple fours,” Holmes said of his thought process to move up to draft Moore. “That’s why I felt like let’s not lose out on our top guy. That’s why we went ahead and just made the move up just to make sure that we secured them.” We even got a Michigan-Ohio State joke from Principal Owner and Chair, Sheila Hamp, when the Lions drafted another Michigan defender in Jimmy Rolder. That brings us to today’s question of the day—what was your favorite moment from last night’s episode of “Inside the Den?” My answer: I am going with the footage that we got from Lions offensive line coach Hank Fraley’s initial pre-draft meeting with Blake Miller. It was awesome to see Miller breeze through what is essentially the pop quiz section of the interview where he is asked to explain certain looks or checks to Fraley in real time. You could tell the rookie was really prepared, as he rattled off answers to his soon-to-be position coach. Fraley would go on to tell Miller that he really loved his tape and how he plays the game, and that hopefully he would be speaking with him again in the near-future. What about you? What was your favorite moment from last night’s episode? Let us know why in the comments below.
author: Morgan Cannon

title: 4 takeaways from Detroit Lions’ ‘Inside the Den’ for 2026 NFL Draft
summary: Thursday evening brought on a surprise drop of “Inside the Den,” the Detroit Lions Emmy-award winning documentary series. The latest installment was a look back at the 2026 NFL Draft, and it provided for a lot of insight into the things that happened—and nearly happened—for the Lions. Here are a few of the biggest takeaways […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - APRIL 24: Former Detroit Lions Calvin Johnson waves during Round Two of the 2026 NFL Draft at Acrisure Stadium on April 24, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images Thursday evening brought on a surprise drop of “Inside the Den,” the Detroit Lions Emmy-award winning documentary series. The latest installment was a look back at the 2026 NFL Draft , and it provided for a lot of insight into the things that happened—and nearly happened—for the Lions. Here are a few of the biggest takeaways from this newest episode. The Lions feelings on Blake Miller changed their approach to Day 1 Every team’s media department has what very well could be their most difficult job of the year when it comes to producing a behind-the-scenes look of draft day. They comb through hours upon hours of footage, making sure not to unveil sensitive intel— like flashing a draft board directly to the media to make your point —while also looking to cut and edit things in a way that makes it appear as everything happened just the way your team had wanted it to happen. Franchise propaganda provides for a lot of hope, but even so, there’s a lot of footage here that shows the Lions were actually pretty high on their eventual first-round pick, Clemson’s Blake Miller. Brad Holmes and Dan Campbell were shown having a discussion about how—and when—the run on tackles would happen, with Holmes wondering if one would potentially go before the sixth overall pick. “Well, the good news is we got hot on Miller,” Campbell said just a few minutes into the time for Las Vegas to make their pick at No. 1. “You know, that [liking Miller] helped big time.” The Lions appeared to be content with a few names coming off the board at offensive tackle, but by pick No. 12, Detroit started to get active on the phone to ensure they’d come away with Miller. Holmes’ first call was to Eric DeCosta, the general manager for the Baltimore Ravens, who held the No. 14 pick. Baltimore’s asking price was No. 17, 118, 128, and a third-round pick in 2027. The Los Angeles Rams, sitting at No. 13, wanted No. 17, 50, and 118 for No. 13 and 93. Even the Tampa Bay Buccaneers had their price for Detroit to move up to No. 15: No. 17, 118, and 128 for No. 15 and 195. But once the Rams went with Ty Simpson, and the Buccaneers took Rueben Bain, Detroit felt confident that Miller would be there at No. 17. Who Detroit preferred to Miller remains to be revealed, but what’s clear is Miller was the player among the tackles they seemed willing to move up and make sure they left with on Day 1. “We do all the rankings, and when we started to dive into those tackle rankings, it really just kind of came very very clear that we’d love have this guy as a Lion,” Holmes said about Miller. “I can’t believe it worked out that way,” Campbell told to Holmes in the Lions draft room. “I mean, that was crazy. I thought all those tackles were gonna be gone. Got our guy and didn’t have to give up anything to do it.” “Not a damn thing,” Holmes added. No fourth round picks would come in between Holmes and Derrick Moore Much like Detroit’s first day of the draft, the Lions identified a player they wanted to come away with, but weren’t sure if he’d be available at their selection (No. 50). “You always reset and you have that stack, cluster of players that you would really like to have,” Holmes described about the process for Day 2 of the draft, “but Derrick [Moore] was at the top of that stack.” Prior to Day 2 of the NFL Draft, we see both Holmes and Campbell share their interest with Sheila Ford Hamp about Michigan’s Derrick Moore, identifying him as an intriguing player for tomorrow. But then when the day arrives, we hear Campbell spell out his interest more plainly. “We’d love to get the rusher from Michigan. He’s kind of our top target right now. There’s a lot of guys in there that are really good players we like, but that’s kinda because he can play d-end, able to rush, but you know, bring something we can use.” Initially, Holmes felt Moore would stick around until the Lions pick at No. 50, but once Kansas City took R Mason Thomas with the pick at No. 40, Holmes grew concerned with the number of teams after the Chiefs and before the Lions’ pick that had a need at defensive end. So much so that the video footage of Holmes and Campbell learning about the Thomas pick caused Holmes to shift in his chair and grab his phone—and Campbell to bite at his fingernail. “Derrick Moore was our No. 1 guy, we have multiple fours,” Holmes recalled of his thought process in moving up for Moore. “That’s why I felt like let’s not lose out on our top guy. That’s why we went ahead and just made the move up just to make sure that we secured them.” Detroit had their sights set on an undersized defensive tackle heading into Day 3 As the second day of the NFL Draft winded down, a few of the Lions staff gathered to discuss players still available for Detroit’s final selections on Day 3. Holmes throws out a hypothetical: “Would you take [Keith] Abney over [Kendrick] Law?” The Lions director of scouting, Dwayne Joseph prefers Law while Brian Hudspeth, the Lions director of college scouting, would be in favor of Abney. Senior advisory Don Corzine throws out his favorite player: Jimmy Rolder. While these three players would all end up getting selected by the Detroit Lions, Holmes asks everyone in the room to give him their “Halton, Rolder, Abney, and Law rankings.” As in Gracen Halton, the defensive tackle from Oklahoma. The San Francisco 49ers would end up taking Halton with the No. 107 pick, 11 spots ahead of Jimmy Rolder going at No. 118. If Detroit’s guy wasn’t at 118, Holmes was ready to move back “If our guy’s not there, then I’ll let you know,” Holmes told a member of the Los Angeles Chargers. The Chargers were willing to part with No. 123 and a pick in the sixth round according to the footage from “Inside the Den,” and Holmes reiterates to his staff that if the Lions’ top guy isn’t available at 118, he’s willing to move back because there were “five guys” that Detroit considered to be their top targets at this point in the draft. The Chargers would instead make that same trade offered to Detroit with Houston, sending No. 123 and No. 204 to the Texans for No. 117 to select Travis Burke, an offensive tackle from Memphis. That left the Lions with the prospect they’d been hoping to grab in Jimmy Rolder.
author: Ryan Mathews

title: Trey Smack is going to be the kicker this year
summary: If this week hasn’t made it clear enough, let’s go ahead and say it loud and clear: Trey Smack is going to be the Packers’ kicker this year. Despite roster machinations that might have initially appeared to suggest otherwise, that seems to have been the case from the second the Packers traded up to snag […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JUNE 09: Rookie Trey Smack #28 of the Green Bay Packers participates in drills during the Green Bay Packers mandatory minicamp at Don Hutson Center on June 09, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images If this week hasn’t made it clear enough, let’s go ahead and say it loud and clear: Trey Smack is going to be the Packers’ kicker this year. Despite roster machinations that might have initially appeared to suggest otherwise, that seems to have been the case from the second the Packers traded up to snag him in the sixth round of this spring’s draft. The plan was always for Trey Smack to be the kicker, and nothing has changed on that front. Smack has the job, and barring injury or a truly insane collapse in camp, he’s going to keep it through the regular season. The Packers have been sending that message with practically every move they’ve made not just since Smack was drafted, but dating back to last season. Lucas Havrisik, Smack’s recently departed competition, was around and kicking for the Packers while Brandon McManus recovered from an injury. But despite his record-setting performance in Arizona , Havrisik couldn’t hang onto the job when McManus came back — apparently because when called upon to kick in practice, he couldn’t reliably deliver. Unless he’d dramatically changed in the intervening few months, that’s pretty strong evidence that he was never a real source of competition for Smack. He couldn’t take the job from an injured and poorly performing Brandon McManus. What shot did he really have against Smack the draft pick? Then, enter Lenny Krieg. A potential International Player Pathway (IPP) option because of his German roots, Krieg had a solid performance at the 2025 NFL Combine and has been kicking around (pun very much intended) the Falcons and Jets organizations over the past season plus. After Havrisik departed earlier this week, the Packers signed Krieg just to cut him less than two full days later. Did he actually attempt a kick in Green Bay? If he did, it wasn’t noteworthy enough to keep him around. It seems like there’s a pretty obvious plan in the works here. Smack is going to be the kicker, but the Packers are either trying to avoid overworking him or developing their ready sheet in the event that they have to make a call at some point this season. And they want to be up to date on potential alternate kickers not because they don’t believe in Smack, but because even kickers need a break in training camp from time to time — and you can’t just go into a season blind, either. The past few years, the Packers have almost always had a couple of kickers around. In the preseason, there can be up to 91 players on the roster, counting an IPP option. It makes sense to devote one of those spots to a kicker, and the IPP exemption opens the door to have an international prospect around without taking up a roster spot for a more important developmental position. When the regular season rolls around, that IPP designation stays, meaning the Packers can keep an international kicker on their practice squad if they so choose without it affecting the number of players they really want to keep. And for that matter, with 16 spots available on the practice squad, keeping a second kicker just to have one really not that big of an inconvenience. Just don’t expect any kicker they do keep to be a serious threat to Trey Smack. He’s all but locked in, and barring something truly unexpected, he’ll be the Packers’ kicker this year.

title: Packers Cap: Devonte Wyatt’s contract details drop
summary: Green Bay Packers defensive lineman Devonte Wyatt officially signed a new three-year extension with the team earlier this week, and we finally have the hard numbers of what the team looks like. On paper, it’s a three-year, $57 million deal, but the accounting gets more complicated than that, considering Wyatt was set to play on […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-DECEMBER 5: Defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt (95) of the Green Bay Packers walks off the field at halftime during a game between the Detroit Lions and the Green Bay Packers in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Thursday, December 5, 2024. (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Green Bay Packers defensive lineman Devonte Wyatt officially signed a new three-year extension with the team earlier this week, and we finally have the hard numbers of what the team looks like. On paper, it’s a three-year, $57 million deal, but the accounting gets more complicated than that, considering Wyatt was set to play on a fifth-year option worth $12.9 million in 2026 already. Functionally, Packers fans should treat this as a four-year contract, since Wyatt’s base salary (game checks) dropped from $12.9 million to just $1.2 million with this deal. It’s three years and $57 million in new money on top of the one year and $12.9 million already on the books, but the money has been moved around structurally. Here’s the year-by-year breakdown of the cash Wyatt will receive: 2026 $1.2 million salary $20 million signing bonus $2.2 million roster bonus Total: $23.4 million 2027 $1.5 million salary $7.3 million roster bonus $1.7 million active per game roster bonus $500,000 workout bonus Total: $11 million 2028 $9.3 million salary $7 million roster bonus $1.7 million active per game roster bonus $500,000 workout bonus Total: $18.5 million 2029 $14.8 million salary $1.7 million active per game roster bonus $500,000 workout bonus Total: $17 million None of this money is guaranteed at signing other than Wyatt’s signing bonus and his 2026 roster bonus. Here’s what it looks like from a cap perspective for the Packers: Devonte Wyatt cap hits 2026: $8.4 million ($22.2 million dead cap) 2027: $16 million ($15 million dead cap) 2028: $23.5 million ($10 million dead cap) 2029: $22 million ($5 million dead cap) Unsurprisingly, the Packers backloaded the cap hits but frontloaded the payment with a big signing bonus (and low guarantees otherwise). This is pretty standard procedure for Green Bay. On paper, this should be treated like a two-year, $34.4 million contract (from a cash perspective) with two team options. With that being said, that’s only one year and $21.9 million in new money for Wyatt, as his fifth-year option was already on the books. In 2028, the Packers have the option to pay Wyatt $18.5 million in cash for his services or save $13.5 million in immediate cap space (as a pre-June 1st release). In 2029, Green Bay’s options are to pay Wyatt $17 million or save that same $17 million on the cap. Functionally, Wyatt got $21.9 million to be on the team in 2027 and gave the Packers the option to keep him at $18.5 million in 2028 and $17 million in 2029.

title: Packers Training Camp Recap: Dani Dennis-Sutton starting to find a role
summary: Training camp can be fickle. Earlier this week, the Green Bay Packers signed kicker Lenny Krieg. Just yesterday, receiver Brendan Rice missed his first practice with a hamstring injury. On Friday, both of those players were released to make room for the additions of receiver Kaden Prather and long snapper Cal Adomitis. The old adage […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JUNE 09: Kingsley Enagbare #55 and Dani Dennis-Sutton #51 of the Green Bay Packers participates in drills during the Green Bay Packers mandatory minicamp at Don Hutson Center on June 09, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images) | Getty Images Training camp can be fickle. Earlier this week, the Green Bay Packers signed kicker Lenny Krieg. Just yesterday, receiver Brendan Rice missed his first practice with a hamstring injury. On Friday, both of those players were released to make room for the additions of receiver Kaden Prather and long snapper Cal Adomitis . The old adage is that you can’t make the club in the tub, and that’s truer the further you go down the depth chart. This is your reminder of how thin the margins are for the bottom 20-ish players on the Packers’ 91-man offseason roster to keep their jobs on a day-to-day basis. Beyond the transactions, here’s what you missed on Friday if you weren’t able to attend today’s training camp practice. Injuries A big ovation for Tucker Kraft who took a lap around Nitschke before practice. pic.twitter.com/OE2MNTxd0a — weston hodkiewicz (@WesHod) July 31, 2026 TUCKER KRAFT IS BACK . The tight end isn’t participating in team drills just yet, but he is off the physically unable to perform list and did do individual drills on Friday. For those keeping track at home, he did return to practice earlier than receiver Christian Watson did off his ACL tear. If edge rusher Micah Parsons follows the same timeline as Kraft, his return to practice would be somewhere in mid-September (which is now allowed for players on the PUP list due to an offseason rule change). Linebacker Edgerrin Cooper’s injury on Thursday was not serious and be practiced on Friday. In his pre-practice press conference, head coach Matt LaFleur stated that cornerback Kamal Hadden is close to returning to the field and that the hope is that tight end Luke Musgrave’s neck issue will “work itself out, but it’s not gonna be in the short term.” The Musgrave injury is likely why the Packers continue to work out tight ends, including three on Thursday . The only player not on Green Bay’s reserve lists who didn’t practice today was offensive lineman Jager Burton, who is dealing with a short-term hamstring issue. If you need a refresher, this is what the Packers’ reserve lists look like currently: RB Chris Brooks (hamstring, NFI) TE Luke Musgrave (neck, PUP) OL Brant Banks (hamstring, PUP) DL Javon Hargrave (knee, PUP) DL Jordon Riley (Achilles, PUP) EDGE Micah Parsons (knee, PUP) CB Kamal Hadden (ankle, PUP) LS Matt Orzech (calf, PUP) Offense Starting lineup: Love Jacobs Watson – Golden Whyle – Dabney Morgan – Monk – Rhyan – Benton – Kinnard Sorrell – Stackhouse – Brooks – LVN Coop – Zaire Nixon – Bullard – Valentine Williams – X — Andy Herman (@AndyHermanNFL) July 31, 2026 The Packers continue to slow-play their players who are coming off injury, which on the starting offense includes Kraft, right tackle Zach Tom and left guard Aaron Banks. Consistently, Jacob Monk (left guard) and Darian Kinnard (right tackle) have been the “starters” in camp as injury replacements. Worth noting: It doesn’t seem like the Jayden Reed slot-only role is changing. Christian Watson and Matthew Golden are getting priority looks over Reed when the team is running two-receiver sets with the starting offense. Matthew Golden just skied to catch a Jordan Love pass between Xavier McKinney and Zaire Franklin in middle of the field for 18 yards. Best catch of camp so far. Golden got ups. — Ryan Wood (@ByRyanWood) July 31, 2026 Speaking of Golden, he made a couple of splash plays in today’s practice, including a jump ball in double coverage and a 50-plus-yard touchdown. Maybe there’s a good reason why he’s getting reps over Reed at outside receiver, despite Reed’s production. Undrafted rookie receiver J. Michael Sturdivant, who was the highest-rated signing the Packers made in the UDFA period, is starting to generate some buzz, too. While he’s had a couple of drops, the 6’3”, 207-pounder with 4.40 speed is making some plays in camp. Ultimately, the sixth receiver job could come down to Skyy Moore, Sturdivant and Isaiah Neyor. It’s going to be fun to watch that battle in the preseason. Defense Don’t make too much about the defensive line rotation right now, because Devonte Wyatt and Javon Hargrave still aren’t participating in team drills. The starting job battle we can pay attention to, though, is outside cornerback, and it’s starting to be the same story every day. While Brandon Cisse got looks with the first-team “starters” when Kesiean Nixon was outside of the lineup, Carrington Valentine has consistently been a starter throughout camp. With Nixon back, it was Nixon and Valentine at outside cornerback with the 1s to open the day, the same as Thursday. It sure looks like the Packers’ cornerback pecking order right now (and this is obviously subject to change) is: Nixon, Valentine, Cisse and then Benjamin St-Juste. With that being said, St-Juste did make a nice play today, hauling in a pick-six from backup quarterback Tyrod Taylor. Fun DL with the 2’s rn: Sorrell – McClellan – DDS – Oliver — Andy Herman (@AndyHermanNFL) July 31, 2026 Barryn Sorrell is pretty consistently getting the “start” opposite of Lukas Van Ness on the edge right now, but the group is rotating heavily. One interesting trend is that rookie fourth-round pick Dani Dennis-Sutton is pretty consistently kicking into the interior line when the team is presumably working on obvious passing downs. You’d have to think that this role will eventually go to Parsons when he’s healthy, but maybe that’s where we see DDS’ biggest contribution until Parsons returns to the field. Two minute drill. 1:00 left. Tie game. 1 timeouts Ball on own 35. First and 10. 1. Reed from Love for a really nice gain along the sidelines and out of bounds. Ball on opposing 42. Great ball from 10. 2. Love to Golden over the middle. First down. Clock ticks. Opposing 28… — Andy Herman (@AndyHermanNFL) July 31, 2026 The first-team defense won the two-minute drill today, which usually ends practice, on the back of two Nixon pass breakups. Start the hype train now? For what it’s worth, practice actually ended on a competitive red zone period on Friday, where Christian Watson caught a three-yard slant for a touchdown against Valentine. Special Teams New #Packers long snapper Cal Adomitis warming up, providing some relief while Matt Orzech remains on PUP. Matt LaFleur said Trey Smack’s first live field goals of camp won’t come until Sunday. pic.twitter.com/GsBTCsSGUs — Ryan Wood (@ByRyanWood) July 31, 2026 No kicking today, if you were interested in that. You’ll have to wait until Sunday, as the Packers’ players have a rest day tomorrow.

title: Packers activate Tucker Kraft off Physically Unable to Perform list
summary: One of the Green Bay Packers’ biggest injury questions to start the 2026 season is now answered. That question revolved around when tight end Tucker Kraft would be cleared to return to practice coming off his torn ACL, and we now have our answer: that day is today. On Friday morning ahead of the Packers’ […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers tight end Tucker Kraft rides a bicycle to practice during the first day of training camp on Wednesday, July 29, 2026, at Lambeau Field in Green Bay Wis. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co One of the Green Bay Packers’ biggest injury questions to start the 2026 season is now answered. That question revolved around when tight end Tucker Kraft would be cleared to return to practice coming off his torn ACL, and we now have our answer: that day is today. On Friday morning ahead of the Packers’ third practice of training camp, head coach Matt LaFleur told the media that Kraft has officially been activated off the Physically Unable to Perform list and will participate in the day’s practice session. LaFleur did note that Kraft will not participate in team drills, only doing individual work to get him up to speed. The Packers are scheduled to have a day off from practice on Saturday, which will give Kraft one more day before potentially stepping in as part of the team portion of practice on Sunday. Kraft’s return aligns closely with the expectations he has been communicating all offseason, as he had indicated that he expected to be ready to start practicing early on in training camp. It comes at a critical time as well, with the Packers suddenly facing questions about the availability of Luke Musgrave. Musgrave, who like Kraft was a day-two draft pick in 2023, is on the PUP list himself with a neck injury that gives him an uncertain timeline on a return. LaFleur said on Friday that Musgrave’s injury would “work itself out,” but added that it “will not be in the short term.” That’s a discouraging sign for the fourth-year tight end, who dealt with significant injuries in each of his first two NFL seasons before finally playing all 17 games in 2025, and it causes an unfortunate depth concern at tight end, a position where Kraft, Musgrave, and Josh Whyle are the only players on the roster who have taken NFL snaps at the position. It was Musgrave’s lacerated kidney as a rookie that brought Kraft into the starting lineup in 2023, allowing him to grab hold of that job. Kraft started every game from the following week until suffering his torn ACL during the Packers’ week 9 loss to the Carolina Panthers last November 2nd. His activation from the PUP list comes almost nine months to the day after that injury, which closely follows the timeline that Christian Watson followed last season — Watson tore his ACL on January 5, 2025, then returned to practice nine months and one day later, on October 6 of that year, though his first game action came about three weeks later on October 26. That timeline also is important to monitor for Micah Parsons, the Packers’ other star player coming off a torn ACL this year. His injury took place in Denver last season on December 14. Nine months from that date would be September 14th, one day after the Packers’ season opener against the Minnesota Vikings. If Parsons starts the regular season on the PUP list, he would not be able to begin practicing until a week later, following the Packers’ week two contest, but he would be eligible to return as early as week five against the Chicago Bears. Kraft returning to the practice field early in camp should ensure that he is in game shape in time for the season opener, which is just over six weeks away. With the team’s tight end depth already slim, the Packers will need their star player back for a full season in 2026.
author: Evan "Tex" Western

title: Green Bay Packers News: Super Bowl heroes from different eras get their due
summary: Thursday was a big day for two former Green Bay Packers. Earl Dotson and Tramon Williams may have inscribed their names into franchise lore 15 years apart, but they’re now inextricably linked after they were inducted together into the Packers Hall of Fame. On their face, it’s tough to compare these two players. Dotson was […]
full_text: Former Green Bay Packers cornerback Tramon Williams speaks during a press conference before the 2026 Packers Hall of Fame induction banquet on Thursday, July 30, 2026, at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wisconsin. Williams and former offensive lineman Earl Dotson are the 2026 inductees. Tork Mason/USA TODAY NETWORK-Wisconsin | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Thursday was a big day for two former Green Bay Packers. Earl Dotson and Tramon Williams may have inscribed their names into franchise lore 15 years apart, but they’re now inextricably linked after they were inducted together into the Packers Hall of Fame. On their face, it’s tough to compare these two players. Dotson was a big, physical offensive tackle who quietly went about his business and locked down the right side of the line in front of Brett Favre. Offensive linemen rarely make the highlight reel, and Dotson was even quieter than most, with no Pro Bowl recognition. But he simply got the job done, play after play and game after game and year after year. Williams, on the other hand, was an athletic, playmaking cornerback who went from a practice squad journeyman to a Super Bowl starter. He has the highlights — his pick-six of Matt Ryan in the 2010 Divisional Playoffs being his single biggest play — and he got a Pro Bowl nod that same season as he helped lead the Packers’ Super Bowl-winning defense. Still, these two players shared some similarities; for example, neither one was an instant contributor. Dotson was a two-year backup after being drafted in the third round, while Williams spent his first year bouncing around on practice squads and was mostly a special teams contributor in his second professional season. But both were critical pieces of Super Bowl champion teams, and now they both are in the Packers Hall of Fame together. Let’s look at those two players and some current Packers who could follow in their footsteps moving forward. Earl Dotson, Tramon Williams join elite in Packers Hall of Fame | Green Bay Press Gazette Congratulations to these two players for their induction. ‘Underrated’ Earl Dotson finally gets long-awaited recognition | Packers.com Dotson didn’t start a game until his third year, but he became a steady presence at right tackle for the 1990s Packers and was a key component of the team that won Super Bowl XXXI. Green Bay Packers hope they have another Earl Dotson in Travis Glover | Packersnews.com ($) That’s a high bar for a player whose only extended game action was a disastrous stint in a playoff game. Still, the Packers seem to love Glover, who is back in action after missing all of last season with an injury. Keisean Nixon focused on growth after first full season at outside CB | Packers Wire Nixon, who went undrafted and started his career as a special teams stalwart like Williams, seemed to acknowledge that he was a little too focused on his pass breakup stats last season and that helped lead to a huge number of penalties. In 2026, he says he’s locked in on being a more complete corner. Surprise Player Turning Heads at Packers Training Camp | SI.com Jonathan Baldwin spent most of his time on the practice squad last year as a safety, but he has been running as the Packers’ second-string nickel in camp and has impressed early on, culminating in a big interception on Thursday. U.S. FCC approves giant space mirror to deliver ‘sunlight on demand,’ but what are the legal implications? | CBC They’re worried about the legal implications? What about when a tiny space rock shifts the mirror’s axis and turns it into an uncontrollable death laser?

title: The Packers Will Be Asking for Public Money Soon
summary: In anticipation of the annual Green Bay Packers stockholders’ meeting, the Packers released their financials for the world to see. The fact that the Packers are a publicly-owned company subject to disclosure rules gives us an insight into the league’s financials that the rest of the NFL would rather we not see, and it’s frankly […]
full_text: In anticipation of the annual Green Bay Packers stockholders’ meeting, the Packers released their financials for the world to see. The fact that the Packers are a publicly-owned company subject to disclosure rules gives us an insight into the league’s financials that the rest of the NFL would rather we not see, and it’s frankly fantastic that this exists. As always, every team should be organized like the Packers. The Packers also provided additional information via a post by Packers.com editor Mike Spofford , in which Team President Ed Policy laments that the Packers can’t tap into private equity money like everyone else. Some pundits, like Mike Florio , read this as an indictment of the Packers’ organizational structure, and wrote unhinged screeds about the Packers potentially dissolving as a result. This nonsense really spread quickly: I think we’re less than five years away, and it may be more like five months, from the Packers adopting a far more traditional ownership structure. — Matt Lombardo (@mattlombardo.bsky.social) 2026-07-25T13:25:36.762Z There’s nothing to worry about on this front . The Packers are extremely profitable and extremely solvent, and in any case, Mike Florio is wrong about Ed Policy having the power to dissolve the team. He does not. But there is something important in Spofford’s narrative, and a reason the Packers are leaning into the “poor” narrative. Midway through the post, Spofford writes: Other teams also have significant public money invested in their redeveloped or new stadiums, which allows them to spend more money on non-capped football operations. From the Packers’ perspective, Lambeau Field – which will soon be the league’s oldest stadium – will need considerable investment for continued maintenance, as well as future improvements to remain a cutting-edge facility. “It’s critical to have a long-term plan in conjunction with the city, county, state, and stadium district board to keep Lambeau Field both iconic and state-of-the-art,” said Policy. Certainty is needed with the city and stadium district with respect to Lambeau’s lease, and a collaborative approach will be required with the county and state for additional future plans. The emphasis is mine, because what is crystal clear is that the Packers will be going to the local and state governments at some point for money for upgrades to Lambeau Field. The Packer stock sales are great for raising what is essentially free money, but there are limits to how often you can tap that option. And while the Packers do have almost three-quarters of a billion dollars in their rainy-day fund, and objectively do not need public assistance for anything, this is how the NFL does business. Lambeau is fine as is. It’s a great place to see a game; bathrooms are plentiful, and adding more video boards would make it worse, not better. None of that will stop the team from asking for public money in the not-too-distant future. Gotta keep up with the Jerry Joneses.

full_text: BLOOMINGTON, INDIANA - APRIL 23: Josh Hoover #10 of the Indiana Hoosiers throws the ball during the 2026 Indiana Spring Football Game at Memorial Stadium on April 23, 2026 in Bloomington, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images for ONIT) | Getty Images for ONIT How is Quarterback a need? To be determined how Daniel Jones looks post-Achilles tear at the start of the season. Could take time if ever to regain confidence in his ankle. Can Daniel Jones stay healthy? Struggled to finish a full season every year he’s been in the league. Anthony Richardson Sr. is on an expiring deal. He is unlikely to be retained. Chris Ballard is on last year of deal and with new ownership who didn’t hire him in charge. Should 2026 be another disappointing year, the Irsays could look to hire a new General Manager after a decade of Ballard at the helm. Unclear if Shane Steichen would be fired as well too. New leadership could want to bring in their own QB, either via 2027 or 2028 Draft. Top 10 Quarterbacks In Summer Scouting Dante Moore, Oregon*: Round 1 Grade Arch Manning, Texas*: Round 1 Grade Drew Mestemaker, Oklahoma State*: Round 1-2 Grade CJ Carr, Notre Dame*: Round 1-2 Grade Julian Sayin, Ohio State*: Round 1-2 Grade Darian Mensah, Miami*: Round 1-2 Grade Jayden Maiava, USC: Round 2 Grade Drake Lindsey, Minnesota*: Round 2 Grade Trinidad Chambliss, Ole Miss: Round 2-3 Grade LaNorris Sellers, South Carolina*: Round 3 Grade Honorable Mentions Josh Hoover, Indiana Sam Leavitt, LSU* Brenden Sorsby, n/a Katin Houser, Illinois John Mateer, Oklahoma *Has remaining eligibility post-2026 collegiate season. All we've heard for the last year is how legendary the 2027 quarterback class is. Today it's time to find out SUMMER SCOUTING IS BACK @ConnorJRogers & I are live on @NFLSEshow right now giving you our top 12 QBs for the 2027 NFL Draft Come hangout! https://t.co/NrbppfLBgu — Trevor Sikkema (@TampaBayTre) June 22, 2026 Tier 1: Definitely Outside Colts Pick Range Dante Moore really impressed me throughout the 2025 season, raising his stock significantly as the year went on. He will be missing his top target Kenyon Sadiq from last year, but the Ducks have a strong successor in Jamari Johnson who could be another Round 1 Tight End in the 2027 Draft. The WR2 of 2024 behind Tez Johnson returns with Evan Stewart coming back from injury that cost him all of 2025. They also added a speedy slot Iverson Hooks out of UAB to the room. Dante Moore | QB | Oregon | 6-3, 215 Natural in every way of playing the position. Smooth release that distributes in a timely and efficient manner. Plays with his eyes, feet, and motion all connected. pic.twitter.com/oCTwZdcAZ3 — Jordan Reid (@Jordan_Reid) June 26, 2026 Can Moore build off of his impressive 2025 season? Can he step up after draft losses to his offensive line and top target? Was the issues against the Hoosiers’ pressure a sign of his limits as a passer or just a rare off game or two? Can he show off more dynamism as a mobile QB and increase his decent but nothing special ball velocity? Arch Manning is the continuation of the Manning Quarterback dynasty. The nephew of both Peyton and Eli and grandson of Archie, he inherited his dad Cooper’s athleticism as the only Manning who didn’t play QB: he was a highly recruited wideout. So unlike his uncles and grandfather, Arch can run like a dual threat QB with 399 yards and 10 Rush TDs in his first year as a starter at Texas. Quick scouting reports on some of the top QBs that could be in the 2027 NFL draft: • Arch Manning, Texas • Dante Moore, Oregon • CJ Carr, Notre Dame • Drew Mestemaker, Oklahoma State • Darian Mensah, Miami pic.twitter.com/jeuxKUcHm7 — Jordan Reid (@Jordan_Reid) July 15, 2026 He still had his inconsistencies on tape, especially early on in 2025. But there were flashes of true dominance and high end QB talent worthy of his family’s legacy. He knows what to do in terms of processing, field reading, passing technique, and touch. Manning just needs to show it more consistently and be more disciplined. With Arch’s tantalizing upside and resources to at least 1 Hall of Fame QB (and 2 Hall of Very Good QBs at worst on top of that), there is a strong chance he continues the family legacy of being a top draft pick. After all, the lowest draft pick in the Manning family is his grandfather Archie at 2nd Overall. Arch could very well be the QB1 on my board once the season begins, but based off of 2025 tape I got Dante Moore just ahead of him due to more consistent tape of Moore being a very polished QB. Deep Class…maybe Much has been said about the depth of the 2027 QB draft class. This class has a lot of hype behind it, but plenty of questions remain for all these QBs. 2026 will be a big opportunity for each of these passers to show development and vie for positioning on the QB totem pole. Only two currently have Round 1 Grades for me, but that can change and QBflation in draft big boards vs draft slot is a major thing. There could be a lot of jostling and changes in rankings by end of season. One under-reported factor that dilutes the hype of this QB class: 8 of the Top 10 QBs in the class has remaining eligibility left. With NIL contracts getting more and more lucrative, plenty of QBs have opted to stay longer in college in recent years to continue to develop/try to improve their draft stock rather than enter the NFL Draft immediately. Dante Moore most notably could have competed with Fernando Mendoza for the top QB in the 2026 Draft and was a lock to go in the top 5 of the draft, but opted to return to Oregon. ✍️ Why is Dante Moore still here? Instead of being a New York Jet with $50 million guaranteed, he's still Oregon's QB. Why he came back and why he says it wasn't about the Jets. "He didn’t want to let $50 million get in the way of $600 million." Story: https://t.co/AV2oDXv5Tc pic.twitter.com/9jW5u00UIr — Chris Vannini (@ChrisVannini) July 28, 2026 There is hardly a guarantee even half of the QBs listed in the top 10 enter the 2027 Draft, and even then the 5 that do could very well get taken before the Colts Round 2 pick. The Colts will be hoping for a large amount of declares if they decide they need to address QB in 2027, as otherwise their options may be amongst the honorable mention QBs. Or they could hope for a lot of QBs to return to college and potentially boost the 2028 Draft class when the Colts have their own Round 1 pick back again. The Best Last Year Eligibility QBs Of the QBs with no eligibility left after 2026, Jayden Maiava from USC and Trinidad Chambliss out of Ole Miss stand out as the top 2, with Indiana’s Josh Hoover and Illinois Katin Houser up transferring to the BIG10 and having opportunities to really raise their stock against one of the toughest conferences in college after previous starting experiences at TCU for Hoover and Michigan State (freshman year) and East Carolina for Houser. Maiava is a prototypical size QB at 6’4 230 lbs and has showcased a ton of toughness, escapability as an improviser, high end velocity, and touch passes into tight windows at every depth. He had some spectacular throws on tape to Makai Lemon and Ja’Kobi Lane, helping both of them be very productive and well drafted in 2026. Jayden Maiava 2025 pic.twitter.com/j4QRubE70F — James Foster (@NoFlagsFilm) July 16, 2026 The native Hawaiian also has shown strong presnap adjustments and identification, able to find soft spots in coverage and mismatches consistently. His problems predominantly lie with his gunslinger mentality, which has gotten him in trouble (26 INTs in 34 games) with picks. Paired with some questionable field reading post snap and inconsistent mechanics in his throwing platform that cause inaccuracy at times, Maiava still has work to do to reach his potential. Jayden Maiava in 2025: ⚔️ 3,711 passing yards (5th) ⚔️ 92.3 grade from clean (9th) ⚔️ 6.2% BTT rate ⚔️ 4.6% TWP rate pic.twitter.com/VeNkkvmDnU — PFF College (@PFF_College) May 12, 2026 Still, Maiava’s…

title: Colts Training Camp Day 3: ‘Find a way’ when opportunity knocks
summary: WESTFIELD, Ind. — I never thought that it would be so simple, but, I found a way. I found a way.  When Indianapolis Colts principal owner Carly Irsay-Gordon stood before the team early in training camp, her message wasn’t complicated. Find a way.  The phrase couldn’t escape her mind as she was speaking to the […]
full_text: WESTFIELD, Ind. — I never thought that it would be so simple, but, I found a way. I found a way. When Indianapolis Colts principal owner Carly Irsay-Gordon stood before the team early in training camp, her message wasn’t complicated. Find a way. #Colts owner & CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon spoke to the team this week and she shared this very important message regarding the upcoming season: pic.twitter.com/lapJ9Syira — WISH-TV News (@WISHNews8) July 31, 2026 The phrase couldn’t escape her mind as she was speaking to the team. Find a way to make the roster. Find a way to make the play when it matters most. Find a way to fly through the turbulence, through adversity. Ultimately, the goal is to find a way back to the playoffs. Three practices into training camp at Grand Park, that mantra continues to echo across the practice field as players try to climb their way up the depth chart. For some veterans, finding a way means stepping into a larger role. For young players and rookies, it means simply proving they belong. Friday’s practice featured prime examples of both. Wide receiver Nick Westbrook-Ikhine is looking to carve out a significant role after signing with Indianapolis in March. With the Colts trading away Michael Pittman Jr. this offseason, the veteran receiver has been presented with an opportunity to earn the third starting spot. On Friday, Westbrook-Ikhine spent extensive time working with both the first- and second-team offense and rewarded all three quarterbacks who looked in his direction. Westbrook’s moment came during the opening 11-on-11 team period as quarterback Daniel Jones held onto the ball a tad too long, but still trusted his new receiver and let it fly anyway. Westbrook noticed he was about to overrun where the throw was heading, so he rose up to elevate over the back of standout cornerback Justin Walley, made the catch, stuck the landing and took off racing to the end zone. Nice highlight catch from longtime Colt killer Nick Westbrook-Ikine 👀 pic.twitter.com/2jkLPmVwTk — Logan Hancock (@ProFanLogan) July 31, 2026 It was exactly the kind of contested play that reflects Irsay-Gordon’s message. Find a way. Jones later connected with Westbrook-Ikhine on a comeback route and shorter completions throughout practice, while the veteran Hoosier also hauled in routes from Anthony Richardson Sr. and Riley Leonard during work with the second unit. The competition to make their presence felt on the field extends beyond the receiver room. First-round draft pick C.J. Allen returned to practice after being activated from the physically unable to perform (PUP) list, instantly stepping into the starting defensive unit alongside fellow rookie Bryce Boettcher. Rookie safety A.J. Haulcy continued earning snaps with the second-team defense while also receiving opportunities with the starters. Defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo mentioned the plan is to roll with certain guys on certain days, which is another indication that opportunities will continue to be given as camp progresses. Richardson is trying to find his own path entering his fourth NFL season, now competing for the backup quarterback job with Leonard. The 24-year-old delivered arguably the highlight of training camp on Friday, while leading the third-team offense. Richardson sold the play-action fake before he unleashed a missile down the far right sideline and receiver Sahmir Hagans never broke stride, collecting the pass in full sprint for a 50-yard touchdown that brought perhaps the largest roar of the week from the crowd gathered at Grand Park. The one thing Richardson is still able to showcase is his rocket of arm talent that has always made him dangerous. Richardson did struggle with ball security, however, dropping two snaps and bobbling at least three others throughout practice. Two consecutive mishandled snaps ended the final team period, illustrating a lousy finish just moments after his electrifying play. Running back Seth McGowan also continued turning heads in the first week of camp. All you hear from fans is discussing how shifty the rookie looks in practice. McGowan found daylight with the starting offense, showcasing quick feet in the backfield and sharp cuts that repeatedly created space. It should be noted that without pads, defenders naturally ease up before full contact, but McGowan’s burst and ability to make defenders miss have remained difficult to ignore through the first three practices. Every repetition offers another opportunity to earn trust of your teammates, your coaches, and another chance to make a way on the field. The Colts wrap up the first week of training camp on Saturday, with practice starting at 4 p.m.

title: Jaguars draft class: 5 things to know about Parker Hughes
summary: Not every NFL Draft pick follows the same route. Some are five-star recruits destined for the league from the moment they leave high school. Parker Hughes’ journey couldn’t have been more different. The former Middle Tennessee State linebacker had to battle uncertainty, setbacks and even thoughts of giving up football altogether before hearing his name […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - MAY 09: Parker Hughes #53 of the Jacksonville Jaguars practices during rookie minicamp at Miller Electric Center on May 09, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images Not every NFL Draft pick follows the same route. Some are five-star recruits destined for the league from the moment they leave high school. Parker Hughes’ journey couldn’t have been more different. The former Middle Tennessee State linebacker had to battle uncertainty, setbacks and even thoughts of giving up football altogether before hearing his name called by the Jacksonville Jaguars. Along the way, he quietly built one of the most remarkable stories in college football. Here are five things you probably didn’t know about Parker Hughes. He was ready to walk away from football for good We have selected MTSU LB Parker Hughes with the No. 240 overall pick! @Dream_Finders | #NFLDraft pic.twitter.com/rVQ35ZZR8V — Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) April 25, 2026 Parker Hughes came dangerously close to never becoming an NFL player. After beginning his college career at Middle Tennessee, Hughes transferred to Samford in search of a fresh start. Instead, he found himself in a scheme that simply didn’t suit him. The Bulldogs wanted him to play as a stand-up edge defender, a role he never truly felt comfortable in, and football quickly stopped being fun. When he decided to leave Samford, another transfer wasn’t even part of the plan. In Hughes’ own words, he intended to quit football altogether. That changed when former Middle Tennessee assistants Dustin Royston and Scott Shafer reached out and invited him back to Murfreesboro. There was no guarantee of playing time, no scholarship waiting for him and no promises about the future. Hughes returned as a walk-on simply because he wanted to be part of the program again. “I literally just want to be here,” Hughes said at the time. “It doesn’t even matter if I play.” It’s an astonishing quote when you consider what happened next. The player who almost walked away from the sport became the heartbeat of the Blue Raiders’ defense, recording over 100 tackles in his final season before completing one of college football’s most unlikely journeys to the NFL. He was recruited as an offensive star, not a linebacker With the 240th pick, the Jacksonville #Jaguars select Parker Hughes (LB, Mid Tennessee) – 6’1”, 220 LBs (7.59 RAS) – 4.39 40-Yard Dash‼️ – 25 Bench Reps – Low missed tackle % (6.5%) – 74.3 NFL Rating Allowed in ‘25 – 586 Special Teams snaps – Team Captain pic.twitter.com/P8Ix23OmLA — Daniel Griffis (@DanDGriffis) April 25, 2026 If you only watched Hughes at Middle Tennessee, you’d assume he’d always been a linebacker. The reality couldn’t be more different. At Elizabethton High School in Tennessee, Hughes was one of the state’s most explosive offensive weapons. During his senior season alone, he caught 62 passes for 1,326 yards, rushed for another 539 yards and scored an astonishing 28 total touchdowns. As if that wasn’t enough, he also intercepted six passes while playing in the secondary. He finished his high school career with more than 4,200 all-purpose yards, starring at receiver, running back, defensive back and as a return specialist. Most colleges looked at those numbers and saw an offensive playmaker. Middle Tennessee saw something else entirely. The Blue Raiders believed Hughes’ instincts, toughness and football IQ would translate better on the defensive side of the ball, making them one of the few programs to recruit him primarily as a linebacker. That decision proved inspired. Rather than becoming another athlete trying to find touches on offense, Hughes developed into one of Conference USA’s most productive tacklers and eventually an NFL Draft selection. Sometimes the best talent evaluations aren’t about seeing what a player is—they’re about recognising what they could become. He achieved something even Jason Witten never did LB Parker Hughes has been nominated for the @BurlsworthTrust Trophy! #BoroBuiltMiddleMade pic.twitter.com/sCID93wIjF — Middle Tennessee Football (@MT_FB) November 5, 2024 Elizabethton High School has produced its fair share of football talent. Its most famous graduate is undoubtedly future Pro Football Hall of Famer Jason Witten, whose legendary NFL career made him one of the school’s greatest-ever athletes. Yet Hughes managed something that even Witten never accomplished. He became the first player from Elizabethton to win the prestigious Tennessee Titans Mr. Football award. For Hughes, that honour carried enormous significance. Growing up in a town that had already produced NFL stars, setting a brand-new benchmark for his school meant more than the individual trophy itself. It represented years of hard work and showed younger athletes from Elizabethton that they could continue raising the standard. It’s easy to overlook awards won in high school once an NFL career begins, but this one remains a defining moment in Hughes’ journey. Being mentioned alongside Jason Witten is impressive. Creating a piece of school history that even Witten never achieved is something altogether different. His return to MTSU wasn’t nearly as straightforward as it sounds Jaguars finish their draft with MTSU linebacker Parker Hughes at pick #240. His 4.40 40-yard dash at his pro day ranks 1st among LBs at the NFL combine 💨 pic.twitter.com/RO4i8gGAO7 — Nash Henry (@NashJagsNats22) April 25, 2026 Returning to Middle Tennessee should have been the easy part. Instead, Hughes found himself caught in an NCAA eligibility process that delayed his comeback and left him waiting on the sidelines while paperwork was resolved. After transferring back from Samford, he wasn’t immediately cleared to play, forcing him to watch the opening weeks of the season while the situation played out. For many players, that sort of delay would have been frustrating enough to derail their momentum. Hughes responded differently. When he finally became eligible, he wasted absolutely no time announcing that he was back. In his first career start for the Blue Raiders, Hughes recorded five tackles, a sack and blocked a punt in a performance that showcased exactly why the coaching staff had fought to bring him back. From there, his role only continued to grow. The linebacker who had once wondered whether he’d ever play football again quickly established himself as one of the leaders of Middle Tennessee’s defense. Sometimes careers turn on huge moments. Sometimes they turn on simply refusing to let bureaucracy become the end of the story. He quietly became one of college football’s cleanest defenders From Middle Tennessee to an NFL draft pick! This MTSU linebacker proves dreams really do come true if you persevere. An incredible journey for Parker Hughes. #MTSU #NFLDraft #CollegeFootball #BoroBuiltMiddleMade @MT_FB @BlueRaiderPod @ParkerHughes_7 pic.twitter.com/Y2Am3vMY95 — The G5 Hive 🎙️ (@G5Hive) July 2, 2026 There’s a statistic that rarely makes headlines but means everything to coaches. title: Andy Reid says Mansoor Delane playing ‘one-handed’ early in camp
summary: Early on, most vibes coming out of the Kansas City Chiefs’ training camp at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph have been positive through three full-squad workouts. One unfortunate exception has been the status of rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane, the sixth overall selection in April’s draft. Delane suffered a shoulder injury earlier this summer […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Mansoor Delane #5 during during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Early on, most vibes coming out of the Kansas City Chiefs ’ training camp at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph have been positive through three full-squad workouts. One unfortunate exception has been the status of rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane, the sixth overall selection in April’s draft. Delane suffered a shoulder injury earlier this summer in organized team activities (OTAs). He was reportedly just cleared for practice as rookies arrived to St. Joseph last week. Delane has participated in every practice dating to the rookie portion last weekend. He has worn a yellow, non-contact jersey each time. Speaking after Friday’s session, head coach Andy Reid described Delane as in an unusual position of practicing while still recovering from injury. “He’s a tough kid,” the coach remarked. “He was a state wrestling champ and all that stuff. Tough kid. He wants to be out there. He wants to do everything. We’re not allowing him to use that arm. He’s out there playing kind of one-handed. Until he’s completely clear, we’re going to keep an eye on him.” Rookie CB Mansoor Delane breaks up the pass to Cyrus Allen #Chiefs l #ChiefsKingdom pic.twitter.com/1F7bp2e0ZJ — Sports Radio 810 WHB (@SportsRadio810) July 31, 2026 As such, Delane’s focus in camp so far has been on what his feet can do, as opposed to arm placement while covering receivers. While Reid stressed the importance of time, fans may see his work lessened in the coming days as the team transitions to padded practices. Still, the rookie is getting valuable work in during his first camp working with Chiefs’ defensive backs coach Dave Merritt. “When we get into the contact stuff,” Reid predicted, “we’ll back off a little bit on him there. But he’s working his tail off and doing what he can do with that. It’s great for him because he has to work his feet, his techniques, his level, how high are you rising up as guys are making moves on you, are you pedaling, what are you doing there. It actually works to his benefit in the long run.” Ultimately, the Chiefs hope for Delane to join with second-year cornerback Nohl Williams for a pair of young starters at an increasingly expensive position. Williams has been one of the stars of camp so far. Reid is happy with the work Williams has put in with Merritt ahead of Year Two. “Up to this point, he’s done a nice job,” Reid observed of Williams. “He had a good offseason program…Out here, he’s been strong where he can bend, maintain that bend and still move with his feet. Dave overemphasizes all of that: use your feet [and] then be able to build cushions from there and angles. He’s done a nice job of that. He’s really worked hard at that.”
