title: Chiefs training camp notebook Day 3: Two rookies are stealing the show
summary: It was another nice, cool day in St. Joe for Kansas City Chiefs training camp on Friday. It was another ramp-up practice before the pads come on Monday. The session lasted roughly two hours. Here’s everything to know from Arrowhead Pride’s in-person observations of practice: Attendance report Check out our coverage of the information head […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Cyrus Allen #13 runs with the ball during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images It was another nice, cool day in St. Joe for Kansas City Chiefs training camp on Friday. It was another ramp-up practice before the pads come on Monday. The session lasted roughly two hours. Here’s everything to know from Arrowhead Pride’s in-person observations of practice: Attendance report Check out our coverage of the information head coach Andy Reid shared with local media after practice on Friday . It includes clarification on the only injury of Friday’s practice: defensive end Ashton Gillotte straining his hamstring. Kahlil Benson starts for a second consecutive day To open training camp, veteran offensive tackle Jaylon Moore manned the starting right tackle position. On Thursday and Friday, rookie Kahlil Benson was the starter on the right side while Moore went from playing left tackle with the second-team unit on Thursday to playing the right side more on Friday. Andy Reid shared his thoughts on Benson’s performance in camp so far. “He and Moore kind of rotated through that, but he’s done a nice job,” Reid said of Benson. “He’s learning, but very strong, powerful, good feet, good athletic ability, and is working the consistency part scheme-wise. Physically, he’s got all the tools there, so he’ll just keep working at it, and we’ll see where it goes.” With full pads set to come on Monday, Reid is being cautious in talking up the undrafted, rookie-minicamp tryout signing from Indiana. “He’s got talent,” Reid reiterated. “We’re early… I want to see how he does as we go. Can you pound through those two-and-a-half-hour practices, in the heat, with pads on? And so on… then you got the preseason games, how do you handle that? It’s a long road… but to this point, my hat goes off to him; he’s doing a good job.” Cyrus Allen refuses to go quietly into the Chiefs’ rookie-receiver narrative Through two days of full-team practices, with the context that starting receiver Rashee Rice has been leaving practice for rehabilitation, rookie wideout Cyrus Allen has been the most consistent option for quarterback Patrick Mahomes during seven-on-seven and team periods. After contributing in standard ways out of the slot during Wednesday and Thursday’s practices, Allen took another step in showcasing what he can do on Friday. This guy is unreal pic.twitter.com/8HjzcPupRb — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) July 31, 2026 After hauling in a one-handed pass down the field, between three defenders, during a full-team period, Allen made another catch on a tight-window throw from Mahomes in a seven-on-seven period. After Mahomes scanned the front side of the route progression, he turned to the backside route being run by Allen on the sideline versus cornerback Nohl Williams. Allen secured the catch in bounds and through the ground, proven by the crowd roar that came with it. On Wednesday, Reid alluded to the belief that Allen has gained Mahomes’s trust. He doubled down on that point after practice on Friday. “He’s done a nice job; the quarterback trusts him,” Reid said. “He’s got to clean some things up, but he’s willing to work at it and do that. He’s had a productive two days; you have to keep stacking those as you go, then you have to get the pads on, and we’ll see from there.” Third-year wide receiver Xavier Worthy, who is working to strengthen his chemistry on downfield throws with Mahomes, reminded local media after practice that he warned them . “This isn’t even surprising,” Worthy described Allen’s performance through three practices. “I told y’all in the offseason that Cyrus is doing this. He’s going to continue to show out in camp.” Our first ‘chippy’ play of camp comes before the pads During a seven-on-seven period featuring the starting offense and the starting defense, running back Kenneth Walker caught a pass going towards the sideline and advanced upfield as the play wrapped up. In pursuit, linebacker Drue Tranquill came over and wasn’t able to slow up before Walker cut back in. The two collided. Walker went to the ground, but quickly bounced up and threw the football directly at Tranquill, pairing the gesture with a quick staredown. Tranquill stood at the podium after practice and addressed one of the first “fiery” plays of camp. “Small moment,” Tranquill said. “We’re just competing at the end of the down, trying to get the ball out, punch, and then Kenneth’s fired up, throws the ball, and it’s all love. We’re smiling at each other after the play, but we’re just making each other better rep by rep. “[We’re] trying to make an emphasis this year on getting the ball out; we need to get the ball out more on defense,” Tranquill emphasized to finish his description of the play. Other notes from practice Backup quarterback Justin Fields was impressively accurate throwing deep passes for the second consecutive day. During a team period, he perfectly placed a fade pass on the pylon for wide receiver Nikko Remigio to secure between a trailing corner and a safety coming over. The tough catch produced one of the loudest crowd roars of the day. In the backfield, it appears rookie running back Emmett Johnson has work to do to contribute to the first-team offense. Second-year back Brashard Smith has been featured with the starters much more often; on Friday, Johnson seemed to run exclusively with the second- or third-team units. It’s hard to take too much away from the Chiefs’ usage of under-center plays during camp so far, but there has been a clear focus on working from those types of formations when running through plays or pass routes in seven-on-seven periods. During a team period on air in the early stages of Friday’s practice, the starting offense ran six of seven plays; most were under-center formations with play action. With Gillotte out, fourth-year defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah seemed to be a formidable fill-in. Reid pointed him out after practice. “Felix is actually doing a nice job; it looks like his get-off, his explosion, is better,” Reid shared. “We’ll see when the pads get on… he’s shown us some things here.”

JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: R Mason Thomas #51, Ashton Gillotte #97 and Omarr Norman-Lott #55 walk to the field before practice during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After Friday’s training camp practice, the third full-team session of the preseason for the Kansas City Chiefs , head coach Andy Reid spoke to the local media and provided an injury update to open his time at the podium. Defensive end Ashton Gillotte was the only player with a status to share. “We had one injury with Gillotte; he had a strained hamstring,” Reid told reporters. “So we’re just checking that out, got him out of there, and he’ll start his rehab and MRI and all that stuff. [I] don’t think it’s too bad.” While observing practice, Arrowhead Pride noticed undrafted rookie wideout Omari Evans staying down after attempting to catch a pass on the sideline from third-team quarterback Garrett Nussmeier. Evans was attended to, but got up quickly; he might’ve gotten the wind knocked out of him. Reid did not comment on Evans. Wide receiver Rashee Rice and cornerback L’Jarius Sneed continued the same routine the two have had for the first week of full-team practices: start off on the field, then leave for planned rehabilitation during the team’s work in team periods. “We’re just building them up,” Reid said. “We know it’s going to take a little bit of time, they haven’t much on the conditioning part of it and rehab part of it. We know they can play; we want to be smart getting them there and how we go about that.” Rashee Rice running a Post on air pic.twitter.com/CKAEEy65kI — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) July 31, 2026 This clip of Rice running a downfield route on air shows he has work to do before he is 100% physically recovered and can play the full-time role the Chiefs’ offense is accustomed to. Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott continued to work off to the side during the Chiefs’ practice as he stays on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list. Another note from Reid’s opening statement: the Chiefs are still in a ramp-up or “acclimation” period of training camp through Saturday’s practice. The full pads won’t be donned until Monday, after the team gets a rest day on Sunday. Saturday’s practice will begin at 9:15 a.m. Arrowhead time and will run roughly two hours, according to Reid.

Mandatory Credit: Denny Medley-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The latest On Monday, we covered wide receiver Andrew Armstong’s meandering journey from small school Texas A&M – Commerce to Chiefs training camp. Armstrong’s work so far at the team’s training camp at Missouri Western State University has also caught the eye of The Athletic ’s Jesse Newell. Newell compared Armstrong’s longshot bid to that a year ago of one-time draft bust Tyquan Thornton a year ago. Armstrong’s height offers a profile observers have long wished the Chiefs would add to the wideout rotation. That said, Armstrong has never played a regular season NFL snap is will turn 26 during the coming season. New Chiefs wideout is following Tyquan Thornton-like path. Will he make the roster? | The Athletic The 6-foot-4 Armstrong added to his strong offseason Thursday, pulling down a deep contested catch from quarterback Justin Fields during seven-on-sevens as one of the team’s top highlights of a rainy practice session. Chiefs coaches also seem to be taking notice of Armstrong. With receiver Rashee Rice still sitting out live drills as he ramps up after offseason knee surgery, Armstrong received numerous reps with Mahomes and the first-team offense Thursday. History of Super Bowl in Los Angeles: The birthplace of the big game | ESPN Super Bowl I: The start of it all The game wasn’t even called the Super Bowl yet; it was known as the first AFL-NFL World Championship. It wasn’t anywhere close to a sellout either. The official attendance of 61,946 is a bit generous, as there were plenty of seats to be had at the massive Coliseum. And the Packers didn’t think it would be much of a game. To hear Hall of Fame guard Jerry Kramer tell it years later, they viewed the Chiefs as somewhat of a joke. Fantasy Football’s Biggest Boom or Bust Players in 2026 | Bleacher Report WR Rashee Rice, Kansas City Chiefs ADP: WR11 There isn’t a more polarizing wide receiver in fantasy football in 2026 than Rashee Rice of the Kansas City Chiefs. In terms of per-game production, he has flashed elite fantasy upside—he averaged almost 10 targets, over 70 receiving yards and 18.5 PPR points per game in 2025. That last number was fifth among wide receivers. These five 2026 opponents are still searching for their first win over Patrick Mahomes | Arrowhead Addict Mahomes against the 49ers The Chiefs and Mahomes will host the 49ers in Week 16 this season, two days after Christmas. By then, both teams expect to be in the thick of the playoff race once again. Of course, we had to look back at Mahomes’ outings against the 49ers first. Two of his three Super Bowl wins have come over San Francisco. Court delays for son of Chiefs coach accused of shooting his mom delayed pending mental health check | Associated Press Bieniemy remained in the Loudoun County Adult Detention Center on Thursday. He had a court date to hear motions scheduled for later in the day, and a preliminary hearing date had been set for Aug. 31. But both appearances have been continued pending a mental health evalation, according to records available from the Virginia judiciary system. Around the NFL ‘Disrespected’ Baker Mayfield voices displeasure over lack of new Bucs contract: ‘Very disappointing’ | NFL.com Mayfield is relishing the opportunity, which he knows could lead to a lucrative opportunity elsewhere as a free agent in 2027. “If you’ve waited this long to take care of your franchise quarterback, that’s too bad because it’s only going to get worse from here,” Mayfield said. “I’m going to have a really good year.” A great year could command entry into the $50 million-per-year club, a desire Mayfield made known Thursday when speaking with ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler. He spent six seasons in San Francisco before playing last year with the Washington Commanders. Receiver is a position of need for the 49ers, who are dealing with injuries to Ricky Pearsall and Christian Kirk early in training camp. Police say Tony Romo had open alcoholic beverage in car during OWI arrest | The Athletic Romo received three citations, according to the police documents obtained by The Athletic , including for operating while intoxicated after he was arrested on suspicion of that offense on July 23. Romo was given a second citation after a deputy observed an open alcoholic beverage “on the passenger side of a vehicle when an inventory of the vehicle was conducted” because it was being towed. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride Chiefs training camp: Excitement for revamped screen game is brewing As camp moves forward, the use of Walker in the screen game should continue to be monitored; he has the explosiveness in the open field that makes screen plays worth calling, to a much higher degree than Kansas City’s backfield was able to offer before. “He’s a dynamic player,” Humphrey said about Walker. “Freak athlete, great with his reads, everything like that.” After Wednesday’s practice, Walker talked about learning the balance between patience and explosiveness as a runner from doing it over and over in football from an early age, working with his father. title: Los Angeles Chargers Roster: Kimani Vidal, RB, scheme fit, 2026 outlook
summary: Next up in our 90-in-90 series is third-year running back Kimani Vidal! Let’s get to know him! The Basics Height: 5’8Weight: 215 poundsCollege: TroyExperience: 2 Vidal was born in Atlanta, Georgia where he attended Marietta High School and was a three-star prospect. Despite having the opportunity to play for powerhouse programs such as LSU and […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - JANUARY 11: Kimani Vidal #30 of the Los Angeles Chargers runs during an NFL wild card playoff game against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on January 11, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Next up in our 90-in-90 series is third-year running back Kimani Vidal! Let’s get to know him! The Basics Height: 5’8 Weight: 215 pounds College: Troy Experience: 2 Vidal was born in Atlanta, Georgia where he attended Marietta High School and was a three-star prospect. Despite having the opportunity to play for powerhouse programs such as LSU and South Carolina, he chose to continue his athletic career at Troy University. As a true freshman, Vidal saw 101 carries which he turned into 516 yards and four touchdowns. He was named Honorable Mention All-Sun Belt and became the first true freshman running back in program history to rush for 100+ yards in consecutive games. Vidal’s workload increased in his second year, going from 101 carries to 152 which he turned into 701 yards and five scores. He also pitched in 22 catches for 134 receiving yards and was once again named a Honorable Mention All-Sun Belt selection. The stocky runner officially broke out in his third season with a new career highs of 231 carries, 1,132 rushing yards, and 10 touchdowns. With another 140 receiving yards thrown in, Vidal went on to earn Second-Team All-Sun Belt honors. With a pair of performances that topped 200 yards on the ground, Vidal also became just the second player in program history to rush for 200+ yards in multiple games during a season. Vidal saved his best season for last, rushing for 1,661 yards on a whopping 297 carries to go with 15 total touchdowns (14 rushing, one receiving). He would go on to be named a First-Team All-Sun Belt selection, the Sun Belt’s Offensive Player of the Year, and a Third-Team All-American. In the Sun Belt Conference Championship Game, Vidal was named the MVP after rushing for five touchdowns in the Trojans’ win, becoming the first player to ever rush for five scores in a conference’s title game. Following his collegiate career, Vidal was selected in the sixth round of the 2024 NFL Draft by the Chargers. His first NFL touchdown came on a nifty catch over the head of a Broncos defender for a touchdown. His rookie campaign saw him tote the rock 43 times for 155 yards while recording 62 receiving yards and the aforementioned score. Vidal saw an increase in usage during the 2025 season after injuries hit both Najee Harris and rookie Omarion Hampton. He earned 10 starts while playing in 13 total games, rushing for a career-high 643 yards and three touchdowns. He also score once more through the air and recorded 136 receiving yards on 16 receptions. In the team’s playoff loss to the Texans, Vidal rushed for 31 yards on 11 carries and caught two passes for 20 yards. The Good Vidal went from a sixth-round pick to impact player for the Chargers by his second year. He stepped in for two talented backs and helped keep the offense afloat with several strong rushing performances. Several of Vidal’s biggest runs from 2025 were outside the tackles which may have proved to the coaching staff that he can play and succeed in Mike McDaniel’s outside zone scheme. The Bad Vidal may have been a better fit for Greg Roman’s gap run system over McDaniel’s outside zone scheme on paper and there’s a chance McDaniel feels the same way given the team’s signing of speedster Keaton Mitchell. The production from Vidal during his stretch of starts was extremely inconsistent. In between three games with over 100 rushing yards, Vidal recording single-game rushing totals of 11, 13, 20, 30, and 33. The line obviously did him no favors, but he was more down than up when given the chance to lead the backfield. 2026 Outlook Vidal showed he was a valuable member of the backfield last season and he’s rightfully in the mix as one of the team’s top three running backs. There are no real threats to his position on the depth chart behind him and I would be shocked to see him not make the active roster as RB3, at the minimum. As far as his production goes, he’ll likely fall between his rookie and sophomore production numbers as he jockeys his way into snaps behind Hampton and alongside Mitchell.

Per ESPN’s Kris Rhim, veteran Trey Pipkins was the starting left guard for the Chargers when the team broke for 11-on-11 drills. Kayode Awosika was the frontrunner through OTAs and […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - NOVEMBER 02: Trey Pipkins #79 of the Los Angeles Chargers looks on during the third quarter against the Tennessee Titans at Nissan Stadium on November 02, 2025 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s the third day of training camp and we’ve now got a third new face to receive snaps at left guard with the first team. Per ESPN’s Kris Rhim, veteran Trey Pipkins was the starting left guard for the Chargers when the team broke for 11-on-11 drills. Kayode Awosika was the frontrunner through OTAs and minicamp, along with earning the majority of snaps on day one of camp with rookie Jake Slaughter rotating in. On Thursday, Awosika saw more snaps but rotated in and out with Trevor Penning. Now on day three, it’s Pipkins seeing snaps with the first team while Awosika remained within the rotation. Line blocking for Justin Herbert to start 11v11 right now LT: Rashawn Slater LG: Trey Pipkins C: Tyler Biadasz RG: Cole Strange RT: Joe Alt — Kris Rhim (@krisrhim1) July 31, 2026 Pipkins has a year of experience playing guard in the NFL, but that came on the right side during the 2024 season when he started 15 games there. He was subsequently moved back to tackle in 2025 after the team signed Mehki Becton to fill that role. I think it’s the consensus opinion across the fan base that the way the Chargers are not going about solving the left guard spot in the best way possible. They had all the money, but signed just Awosika and Strange, re-signed Penning, and drafted a full-time center in Slaughter. Now, just three days into training camp, we’ve seen four different players spend time with the first team line. Look, as long as they arrive at the right place, they can take whatever journey they want. Just don’t ask the fans to “chill and let it play out” because they spent the better part of 19 weeks during the 2025 season doing just that. Their reward? The gutting image of Justin Herbert being peeled off the turf at Gilette Stadium by Bradley Bozeman and Zion Johnson. Until the season has begun and the Chargers interior offensive line looks like a strong unit, the skepticism will unfortunately and unsurprisingly remain.

title: McVay implies Aaron Donald leaning towards return
summary: The possibility of Aaron Donald returning to the Los Angeles Rams has never gone backwards, but only inched closer to the three-time Defensive Player of the Year coming out of retirement since the rumors first started. The likelihood that the Rams will add another future Hall of Famer after trading for Myles Garrett took another […]
full_text: Inglewood, CA - February 08: Los Angeles Rams defensive end Aaron Donald (99) hugs head coach Sean McVay after defeating the Cincinnati Bengals 23-20 in Super Bowl LVI at SoFi Stadium on Monday, Feb. 8, 2016 in Inglewood, CA. (Wally Skalij / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) The possibility of Aaron Donald returning to the Los Angeles Rams has never gone backwards, but only inched closer to the three-time Defensive Player of the Year coming out of retirement since the rumors first started . The likelihood that the Rams will add another future Hall of Famer after trading for Myles Garrett took another step forward on Friday, as Sean McVay told the media that “If there’s an arrow, it’s trending upward.” McVay is finding it harder and harder to keep the worst-kept secret in the NFL . That ever since L.A. traded for Garrett , Donald has wanted to return to the Rams. HC McVay on a potential Aaron Donald return, via @michaeljduarte : "Things are going in the right direction. If there’s an arrow, it’s trending upward." — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) August 1, 2026 “Things are going in the right direction,” said McVay on Friday. But he’s continuing to preach patience as it pertains to when Donald will return, not necessarily “if” anymore. McVay doesn’t expect until a final decision for at least another week, as the head coach said he doesn’t expect an update until the Rams return to Woodland Hills, which will happen after their final Loyola Marymount practice on August 7 . “There’s some conversations that we’ve had,” McVay said after Friday’s practice at Rams Training Camp presented by CommunityAmerica Credit Union at LMU. “We’ve loosely had some different timelines that are kind of temporary. I want to keep those between us, just if something unforeseen happens, out of respect for him and the situation. But I know this, things are going in the right direction, and if there’s an arrow, it’s trending upwards.” The Rams still have to settle the $30 million question : How much of Donald’s original salary want to be paid in order to come back? Sean McVay said he doesn’t expect there to be an update on Aaron Donald’s return until the Rams get to Woodland Hills. McVay did say that if there’s an arrow, “it’s trending upward.” — Sarah Barshop (@sarahbarshop) August 1, 2026 It’s not a question of whether the Rams want to pay Donald $30 million, it’s what his contract stipulates he’s owed if he returns to the team. Donald can work out a different contract to the return to the team, but he can always demand $30 million if the team wants him that bad. However, given that it would be Donald coming out of retirement for this opportunity to play on L.A.’s defense this year, we can assume money is not his motivation. If it was, why did he retire in the first place? By most accounts, Aaron Donald is trending towards a Rams return.
author: Kenneth Arthur

title: Terron Armstead thinks the Rams could have a perfect season
summary: Terron Armstead was on some great teams during his 12-year NFL career with the Saints and Dolphins, but the retired tackle thinks the 2026 Los Angeles Rams could be the best team in NFL history. “If this roster is healthy, I see no reason why they don’t go undefeated,” Armstead said in a recent sit-down […]
full_text: UNITED STATES - DECEMBER 16: Football: Hall of Famer and former Miami Dolphins coach Don Shula at ceremony for 1972 undefeated team during halftime of game vs Baltimore Ravens, Miami, FL 12/16/2007 (Photo by Bob Rosato/Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) (SetNumber: X79280 TK1 R3 F22) Terron Armstead was on some great teams during his 12-year NFL career with the Saints and Dolphins, but the retired tackle thinks the 2026 Los Angeles Rams could be the best team in NFL history. “If this roster is healthy, I see no reason why they don’t go undefeated,” Armstead said in a recent sit-down with Rich Eisen. They were discussing the implications of the trade that brought Myles Garrett to the Rams. Is it possible for the Rams to go undefeated? Of course it is; it’s been done before by the 1972 Miami Dolphins, but only in a 14-game season. Could it be done today? The 1972 Dolphins Don Shula was hired by the Dolphins in 1970 to replace George Wilson, who apparently had a real eye for talent but lacked the coaching skills to capitalize on it. Wilson was bitter after being fired and suggested Shula had inherited a ready-made team. In 1970, the Dolphins went 10-4 and reached the playoffs for the first time. They returned in ‘71 and defeated the KC Chiefs in the longest game in NFL history, 82 minutes and 40 seconds of game clock. Then, after shutting out Shula’s former team, the Colts, in the AFC Championship game, they were humbled by the Dallas Cowboys, 24-3, in the Super Bowl. In 1972, the Dolphins were superb on both sides of the ball, leading the league in both points scored and points against. The running back tandem of Larry Csonka and Mercury Morris became the first teammates to both run for over 1,000 yards in a season. They were definitely a run first offense. The Dolphin’s defense that year was nicknamed the “No Name’ defense by Cowboys’ head coach Tom Landry due to their lack of high-profile players, but they gave a masterclass in cohesive defensive play. 2026 Rams Is Armstead right? Can the Rams do the unthinkable and have a perfect season? Has GM Les Snead assembled such a good squad? I don’t see why not; all the pieces are in place. On offense, the 2025 Rams led the league in scoring last year with 518 points , and, with the exception of Tutu Atwell, all of the relevant starters have returned for this season. Those would include: MVP Matthew Stafford Receptions leader Puka Nacua Touchdown leader Davante Adams Perennial 1,000-yard rusher Kyren Williams With the exciting prospect of the potential of head coach Sean McVay’s new twists with ‘13’ personnel offensive schemes, this offense could improve. On defense , the Rams did a terrific job of self-scouting, recognizing their greatest weaknesses and making moves to improve. And boy, did they ever. The Rams acquired All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie from the Kansas City Chiefs via trade. They gave up the No. 29 overall first-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, a 2026 fifth-round pick, a 2026 sixth-round pick, and a 2027 third-rounder, then promptly turned around and redid his contract, making him the highest-paid corner in the league. The Rams then signed former Kansas City Chiefs cornerback Jaylen Watson to a three-year, $51 million contract with $34 million guaranteed. The icing on the cake, of course, was the Rams trading for Myles Garrett. They gave up Jared Verse, a 2027 first-round pick, a 2028 second-round pick, and a 2029 third-round pick. While the Rams were 10th in PPG allowed last year, these changes could improve that standing; in my opinion, they are at minimum a top-three defense this season. Can it be done? Looking at the Rams’ opponents this season, I’d be hard-pressed to pick one, in any individual game, to beat the Rams. On paper, they should be favored in every game this year—on paper. But as we all know, the football is not round; it takes funny bounces that can drastically change a game, and most importantly, the injury gods have to be smiling for the whole season. The 2007 New England Patriots went 16-0 and then reached the Super Bowl at 18-0, but found out that even the New York Giants could beat them. The 1972 Dolphins led the league in both offense and defense. This Rams team could do the same thing, but they’ll have to do it over three more games. The Rams would need an almost perfect record with bounces and injuries to have a perfect season. Do I think it will happen? No, but there’s at least one person out there who believes it’s in the realm of possibility.
author: John Newman

title: How Rams have fared during every Spider-Man release year
summary: With training camp beginning this week, it starts a new day for the Los Angeles Rams. Speaking of brand new days, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” also opens this weekend, which is great timing. Let’s do something fun and look at how the Rams have fared whenever a new Spider-Man movie is released. For this exercise, […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 13: Matthew Stafford #9 of the Los Angeles Rams looks on as Andrew Whitworth #77 of the Los Angeles Rams hoists the Vince Lombardi Trophy after defeating the Cincinnati Bengals in the NFL Super Bowl LVI football game at SoFi Stadium on February 13, 2022 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images With training camp beginning this week, it starts a new day for the Los Angeles Rams. Speaking of brand new days, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” also opens this weekend, which is great timing. Let’s do something fun and look at how the Rams have fared whenever a new Spider-Man movie is released. For this exercise, only live-action Spider-Man movies will be considered. So, the Spider-Verse movies, as utterly fantastic as they are, will be excluded. The last time a live-action Spidey movie came out, the Rams won the Super Bowl at SoFi Stadium, so given the loaded roster, there’s a strong chance we might see a sequel this February. But let’s not get ahead of ourselves web-slingers, so let’s get into it! “Spider-Man” (2002) – Rams (7-9) “Spider-Man” marked the dawn of a new era and paved the way for the abundance of superhero films that we see today. Tobey Maguire proved a perfect fit for the role and remains a fan-favorite Spider-Man all these years later. The 2002 Rams didn’t experience the same highs as Maguire’s first Spidey appearance. Fresh off a Super Bowl loss to the Patriots — the franchise’s Green Goblin — the team fell apart and missed the playoffs for the first time since 1998. “Spider-Man 2” (2004) – Rams (8-8) “Spider-Man 2” marked the last of truly great live-action Spider-Man films until the Marvel Cinematic Universe oversaw the series. For the Rams, 2004 marked the final time they made the playoffs until the 2017 campaign. It marked the end of an era, but success eventually found its way back to the team and the Spider-Man series. “Spider-Man 3” (2007) – Rams (3-13) Maguire’s third and final outing as Spider-Man was a jam-packed mess, while the Rams’ season was a mess period. St. Louis began the year 0-8, the worst mark in franchise history, and finished 1-7 at home. Additionally, their defense allowed the second-most points in the league with 438, or 27.4 per game. Big yikes all around. It was a season as ugly as Peter Parker’s infamous dance moves . “The Amazing Spider-Man” (2012) – Rams (7-8-1) In the first live-action reboot of the Spider-Man series, Andrew Garfield took on the role and did an admirable job. He was no Tobey Maguire, yet he made the character his own, so it was a welcome addition. St. Louis had a reboot of their own with Jeff Fisher taking over as head coach. The Rams improved on their 2-14 record from the previous year. Like Garfield, Fisher did fairly well in his position given all he had to work with. Mediocrity ensued from then on, but it was seemingly a step in the right direction at the time. “The Amazing Spider-Man 2” (2014) – Rams (6-10) The first “Amazing Spider-Man” was a solid start for Garfield’s iteration of the character. However, the sequel was all over the place, similar to the Rams’ 2014 season. St. Louis finished last in the NFC West, but managed to defeat the reigning conference champion Broncos and Seahawks, along with shutting out the Raiders and Washington in back-to-back weeks. It was a season about as weird as how Electro looked. Seriously, what were they thinking?! “Spider-Man: Homecoming” (2017) – Rams (11-5) In the third major live-action reboot of the series (to date), Tom Holland took over as the web-slinging hero. The Rams had another reboot of their own in 2017, as the season marked the beginning of the Sean McVay era in Los Angeles. This season marked L.A.’s first playoff appearance since 2004. Oddly enough, both the Rams and Spidey took on bird foes in the end. While Spider-Man managed to take down Vulture, McVay’s squad was unable to vanquish the Falcons in the Wild Card Round, ending their most successful season in quite some time. “Spider-Man: Far From Home” (2019) – Rams (9-7) Holland’s second go-around as Spider-Man wasn’t nearly as good as his first, but it was still an entertaining ride. The same could not be said about the 2019 Rams, who went from a Super Bowl appearance to missing the playoffs entirely in McVay’s third season. There were some fun moments here and there. However, between Jared Goff’s decline and Todd Gurley’s effectiveness waning, the season didn’t have as satisfying an ending as it could’ve had. “Spider-Man: No Way Home” (2021) – Rams (12-5) Judging from the title, Spider-Man had a difficult time finding his way home, but the same could not be said for the Rams. Los Angeles became the second team in a row to win a Super Bowl in their home stadium, despite being the visitors. Technically, they won the title in 2022, yet it was part of the 2021 campaign, so I’ll count it. Victory is mine (insert evil Green Goblin laugh).
author: Evan Craig

title: Joe Buck’s flimsy reason to question Rams hype
summary: Arguably the best part of training camp starting, outside the obvious sight of an oasis in the all-too-long football desert of summertime, is that we finally start to get real stories and storylines to discuss. We largely get to move on from the never-ending narratives of the true offseason. Which is what makes Joe Buck’s […]
full_text: GLENDALE, AZ - JANUARY 13: ESPN TV announcer Joe Buck looks on before the NFL Wild Card Playoff football game between the Minnesota Vikings and the Los Angeles Rams on January 13, 2025, at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, AZ. (Photo by Kevin Abele/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Arguably the best part of training camp starting, outside the obvious sight of an oasis in the all-too-long football desert of summertime, is that we finally start to get real stories and storylines to discuss. We largely get to move on from the never-ending narratives of the true offseason. Which is what makes Joe Buck’s recent comments on ESPN’s Get Up that much funnier. We know all about the hype the Los Angeles Rams are getting this offseason. They’re the Super Bowl favorites according to all the major sportsbooks, reigning MVP Matthew Stafford is being placed near the top of nearly every preseason quarterback ranking, they improved their weaker side of the ball by adding the best defensive player in the league and a multi-time All-Pro at cornerback. The good news has almost been overwhelming, and the Rams are justly being placed on a pedestal for all of it. L.A. Rams News: Myles Garrett will let the Aaron Donald rumors play out So, after a spring and summer lauding the franchise, it was at least eyebrow-raising to see a video at ESPN.com this week titled “Why Joe Buck questions the hype around the Rams.” Opinions on Buck are split, to say the least. He’s been a part of the NFL ecosystem for over three decades, first as the long-time No. 1 play-by-play broadcaster on Fox for both the NFL and MLB, and since 2022 as the voice of Monday Night Football on ESPN. To add a personal thought, as someone who does play-by-play professionally, I think Buck is quite good at what he does and have been a fan for years. You ask others and they’ll tell you, often graphically, how much they despise him and wish he’d be disappeared from society. Needless to say, it’s a mixed bag. But there’s no denying the guy knows football, he’s been calling games plenty long to have learned at least something. So, what does Joe Buck think about the Rams and why we should pump the breaks on the hype train? “As we all know, it’s why the schedule feels a lot different in November than it does when it comes out in May, you’ve got to stay healthy,” Buck said. “The Rams have an MVP quarterback who is not a young guy and still has that bad back, I assume, so they just have to, and we as fans have to hope he stays healthy.” That’s it. That’s all. They have to stay healthy, and that’s why Buck “questions” the Rams’ hype. I implore you to watch the video itself (linked above), because it only helps you realize how absurd this exercise is. And it doesn’t appear to be Buck’s fault either. He joins in a discussion about the impact of possibly adding Aaron Donald, and he also shares that he thought the defense was already good before adding Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie. Then, at the 54-second mark of the clip, he awkwardly stares into the camera, passes for an unnatural half beat and adds in the bit about why they have to stay healthy. It’s impossible to say without having an IFB in your ear on the day of the show, but that sure looks like a producer telling him to say something to stir the pot or to disagree instead of just continuing to build the hype. Rams Players Under the Most Pressure in Training Camp More than anything, this is just funny. The Rams aren’t perfect on paper, by any means, but they deserve the hype they’re getting and with so much positive news all offseason (from L.A.’s perspective, anyway), the Worldwide Leader In Sports is grasping at the flimsiest straws to create some kind of back and forth about it. Thankfully, there will be real football to talk about and debate soon enough. By the way, the Rams will play two Monday night games this year: Week 2 against the New York Giants and Week 5 against the Buffalo Bills.

Maybe the offensive lineman would dread practice a bit more, but seemingly everyone on the Rams would welcome AD back with open arms. However, Garrett says more or less whatever will […]
full_text: Westchester, - July 26: Defensive End Myles Garrett #95 of the Los Angeles Rams during the first day of the Los Angeles Rams Rams training camp on the campus of Loyola Marymount University in Westchester on Sunday, July 26, 2026. (Photo by Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images Myles Garrett has expressed that he’d be excited to have Aaron Donald back with the Los Angeles Rams. Who on the Rams wouldn’t be? Maybe the offensive lineman would dread practice a bit more, but seemingly everyone on the Rams would welcome AD back with open arms. However, Garrett says more or less whatever will be will be with Donald coming back. It’s up to AD. That seems like a good approach. Dont get too high, don’t get too low. Easier said then done, but a good approach. If Donald comes back, one assumes the Rams will be in an even better position than they already are, and they are seemingly already in a very sstrong position to compete for a Super Bowl. If this team can stay healthy, sky seems the limit, but it won’t be easy. Whether Donald is back or not. I have some good news, it’s Friday! Please comment on whatevery you want. Be safe, be well. Thank you for checking out Turf Show Times! MYLES GARRETT WON’T PUSH AARON DONALD’S ‘DIFFICULT’ COMEBACK DECISION WITH RAMS (nfl.com) ““If he’s here, I’m going to be excited to be his teammate, his partner in crime,” Garrett said Wednesday, via the Associated Press . ”I think we’re going to do great things. But it’s a difficult thing, coming back.” Donald began a workout program following the blockbuster Garrett trade , but has yet to decide whether he’s in a place to return. The Rams have no desire or reason to force the 35-year-old to make a decision. “I think there’s a lot we can learn from each other,” Garrett said. “I’d love to pick his brain on the kind of things he does to attack his matchups, and I think the same could be said vice versa. … I’ve told him I’d love to learn from him. I’ve watched his tape. Obviously, I think everyone who’s been a rusher from anywhere across the line, they have a lot of respect for him. But I don’t want to push him one way or another.” Myles Garrett describes differences between Rams and Browns training camps (ramswire) “I would just say it’s a team that has a culture that’s a little bit more set in stone with leaders all across the board and I think Cleveland has some leaders that are continuing to develop,” Garrett said. “Some great teammates that I had and some great young talent that they continue to draft or pick up. You see a lot of older veterans here who’ve had a lot of years here or a lot of years in the league and been able to learn things and develop who they are as a person, as a teammate, as a leader and they’ve helped instill a great culture here. I think that’s something that’s already ingrained and I can help to nurture, but it’ll take time.” Sean McVay respectfully blocks out media expectations for the Rams | ‘The Insiders’ (nfl.com) “Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay addresses the media at 2026 NFL Training Camp.”

Masses was a playmaker for the Bears last season […]

title: Las Vegas Raiders Summer Scouting: EDGE Rankings
summary: I broke down the 2027 scouting classes in my early summer scouting series, and the room has a ton of potential with a long list of potential standout players. I broke down the offense and defense in articles and I suggest reading those for a broad aspect of the room. The Raiders do have some […]
full_text: Aug 31, 2024; Columbia, South Carolina, USA; South Carolina Gamecocks edge Dylan Stewart (6) celebrates after a sack against the Old Dominion Monarchs in the second quarter at Williams-Brice Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jeff Blake-Imagn Images I broke down the 2027 scouting classes in my early summer scouting series, and the room has a ton of potential with a long list of potential standout players. I broke down the offense and defense in articles and I suggest reading those for a broad aspect of the room. The Raiders do have some talent on the interior OL, and I’d expect Las Vegas to add more in 2027 as John Spytek does. These rankings are extremely early, and they will evolve over not only the summer but the next 8-10 months throughout the season, and into draft season. Some lists will feature 10, 15, 20, or more ranked prospects but I’ll include others on the list below to note. Colin Simmons, Texas – 6’3/245, Jr Simmons is twitched up, and he’ll have a race to be the first EDGE off the board with Dylan Stewart. He’s posted a career 29.5 TFL and 21 sacks in two seasons and he’s extremely athletic, strong, and shows a ton of pass rush moves. Simmons converts his speed to power, uses his full body, and plays with extreme violence. While slightly undersized, Simmons does have elite length, he is extremely quick off the ball, and moves exceptionally well when working laterally. Simmons has the ability to anchor vs the run, shows great lower body flexibility, and his biggest goal in 2026 is to continue developing and stay healthy. Simmons reminds me a lot of Jared Verse, and should be a perennial Pro Bowler in the NFL. Dylan Stewart, South Carolina – 6’5/250, Jr If you want to know what a scouting report means when they say twitch, speed to power, and explosiveness watch Stewart. The 20 year old flys off the line of scrimage, has exceptional length, and he appears to teleport at times. Stewart is extremely athletic, has a ton of lower body agility, and his ability to bend is exceptional with an innate ability to basically play lateral to the ground. I’d like to see Stewart add a bit more strength and not rely solely on the speed to power conversion. He has great lateral movement, is able to plant and drive, and his hand combat while raw shows a ton of true dominant moves. He’s more raw than Stewart, but he’s longer, more athletic, and likely has a higher ceiling as well. Anthony Smith, Minnesota – 6’6/280, R-Jr Anthony Smith will fly up boards, and he is an impressive player. He broke out in 2025 with 17.5 TFL’s and he’s shown improvements as a pass rusher over time. Smith has awesome length, a good first step, and his ability to play in 2, 3, 4 point stances is impressive. The junior fires off the ball, drives up field, and has good hip/ankle flexibility with decent bend. Smith does a great job converting his second step speed to power, and shows great strength across his full body while driving the core through the rep consistently. Smith is raw, but he’s shown the speed to power, athleticism, and a ton of versatility to thrive in any modern NFL defense. Clev Lubin, Louisville – 6’3/255, R-Jr Lubin was a fan favorite in the 2026 class, and in 2027 he should have a chance to be a quick riser as well. Lubin, a former JUCO standout has never failed to record double digit sacks/TFL in his career across JUCO, Coastal Carolina, and now Louisville. He’s undersized, but does have good length, though he wins off pure speed, speed to power, and lower body agility. Lubin has flashes of elite hand strength, his pass rush moves are violent, and he has a diverse bag with an NFL ready chop/swipe/euro step. Lubin is smart, he knows how to rush the passer, and he does an excellent job setting tackles up to use his athleticism to his advantage. He uses his core, fires off the ball, and shows incredible second/third step pass rush athleticism. Lubin is a weakenss vs the run, he’s needing to add lower body power, and his frame makes him an easier target but there’s no denying the pure elite pass rush ability he has. Matayo Uiagalelei, Oregon – 6’5/275, Sr A true 3-4 end or base big end in a 4-3, Matayo is the brother of former Clemson/Oregon State/Florida State and Chargers QB DJ. He’s a stout physical defensive end with great explosion off the line of scrimmage, a strong second step, and elite speed to power. Uiagalelei does a good job using his full body in the rep, and he can be stiff at times, with a move to DT possible in his future. Uiagalelei has great length, elite core strength, and his overall pass rush arsenal is inconsistent but shows flashes of brilliance. This is a high rank, I think Uiagalelei can get back to his form from 2024 after a disappointing 2025, but he has the blend of athleticism, power, and technique to be a dominant EDGE. Boubacar Traore, Notre Dame – 6’4/250, R-So Traore will rise, and while reading these defensive breakdowns prepare to hear Notre Dame a ton. Traore has just 16 TFL and 10.5 sacks in his career but he’s on pace for a breakout 2026. Traore has elite speed to power, is extremely strong, and also shows a diverse set of pass rush moves. Traore can defend the run at an elite level, and he needs to develop as a pass rusher. Quincy Rhodes Jr, Arkansas – 6’6/275, R-Jr Damon Wilson, Miami – 6’5/255, R-Jr Kenyatta Jackson Jr, Ohio State – 6’6/270, Sr Adam Trick, Texas Tech – 6’4/245, R-Jr Trick was dominant in the MAC at Miami (OH) with 18 TFL, 13 sacks, and 5 FF in the last two seasons. He converted to EDGE from ILB in 2024 and has since been a standout at the position as well, he’s an elite run defender with an ability to breakdown blocks, use his lower body strength, and has elite anchor/stack technique. Trick is a very raw pass rushers, he’s an elite athlete with a ton of moves but nothing flashes as NFL ready yet. Trick will win with strength, he’s able to use his core and lower body to defeat tackles, has great length, and does have good bend ability. Texas Tech has produced defensive lineman, and I’d expect them to develop Trick’s pass rush bag quickly. John Henry Daley, Michigan – 6’4/250, Jr Daley is coming off a serious knee injury but he’s a very similar player to Trick with improved pass rush technique, though he’s an adequate athlete. There’s a huge ceiling for Daley as a third pass rusher, high end run defender. Princewill Umanmielen, Ole Miss – 6’5/250, Sr Teitum Tuioti, Oregon – 6’3/264, R-Jr Yhonzae Pierre, Alabama – 6’3/250, R-So Will Heldt, Clemson – 6’6/270, R-Jr Heldt can rise, and I’d almost expect him too quickly. He’s new to the EDGE position and broke out in 2025 with 7.5 sacks and 16 TFL. He has elite athletic ability, has an elite frame, and does show good strength at the POA as well. Heldt is raw, he doesn’t know how to rush the passers, and he too often can be too aggressive. His ability to rush out of multiple stances and techniques is intriguing, but limited him in terms of development. Heldt also has below expected strength, and that will be crucial to develop this season. The sky is truly the limit with Heldt, and you can’t teach length/athleticism. Other Names To Watch: Taylor Wein, Oklahoma Anto Saka, Texas A&M Jordan Ross, LSU Toby Anene, Colorado Trey White, Texas Tech – Former San Diego state standout, smaller, limited athlete. Ton of production. EDGE 3/4 player Ade Adebawore, Oklahoma – Up/Down career, likely a true 4/5 tech similar to Tonka Hemingway. Elite athlete, struggles vs the run Melkart Abou-Joude, UNC – Elite athelte, struggles to defeat top tackle with average length and inconsistent pass rush plan. Jayden Virgin-Morgan, Boise State Wendell Gregory, Kansas State Bryce Young, Notre Dame – 6’7/270 EDGE with twitchy alien like athleticism. Extremely raw strength and pass rush technique, diverse, versatile pass rusher. Good season can skyrocket him into Round 1. Beau Atkinson, Ohio State Indiana Trio – Three adequate pass rushers/run defenders, no true standout.

title: Aaron Brewer: ‘I’m chasing perfection’
summary: The Miami Dolphins are early in their 2026 training camp, but the differences between the 2025 version of the team and the one hitting the practice field each morning this summer are already obvious. New head coach Jeff Hafley envisions a physical team that brings intensity into everything they do, including how they practice. All-Pro […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FL - NOVEMBER 30: Miami Dolphins guard Aaron Brewer (55) before the game between the New Orleans Saints and the Miami Dolphins on November 30, 2025 at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Miami Dolphins are early in their 2026 training camp, but the differences between the 2025 version of the team and the one hitting the practice field each morning this summer are already obvious. New head coach Jeff Hafley envisions a physical team that brings intensity into everything they do, including how they practice. All-Pro center Aaron Brewer recognizes the changes and appreciates what this year’s Dolphins team is becoming. “You want to make practice as hard as it can be, and that’s our goal, like going to practice this whole year, you want to be aggressive,” Brewer said on Thursday. “You want to be intense. Like you want it to be incomparable to the game. You want the game to be easy. And so when we’re out there, we want to compete. We want to push each other, push it all the way to the edge, as close to the fighting as we can. And yeah, that’s the energy this year.” As for what Hafley is bringing in his first year as a head coach as compared to last year’s experience with Mike McDaniel, Brewer stated, “Yeah, you know, it’s two different coaching styles and so it’s definitely a different culture, and we just lean into whoever we bring into this building. Like they’re coming in as more aggression and so we lean into his identity and what he wants this team to be.” While Miami will look to be more physical under Hafley and the team is expected to run the ball more this year, the offense as a whole may not look drastically different under Bobby Slowik, who served as the team’s senior passing game coordinator last year under McDaniel before taking over as offensive coordinator this year. “I’d say it’s pretty similar,” Brewer said. “You know, him and Mike were working like hand in hand, close together last year. And so they kind of got that same philosophy a little bit, but they all got their own little things that they’re different in and so it’s very similar. That’s just real-life football. We’re not out here playing flag football. Aaron Brewer One major difference between last year’s practices and what the team is doing this year is with the drills being run. Miami has gone away from 7-on-7 lineups on the practice field, preferring to use a full team 11-on-11 matchup, with Hafley wanting to get the offensive and defensive linemen involved in the repetitions. Brewer spoke about the change, saying, “That’s just real-life football. We’re not out here playing flag football. Like when you go to game day, it’s 11-on-11, not 7-on-7. So I feel like it’s more work. It translates from practice to the game, and that’s what we’re trying to do. Agreeing to a contract extension Brewer, entering his seventh year in the league and third with Miami, was a Second-Team All-Pro selection last year, his first time receiving individual recognition. The former undrafted free agent was identified by new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan as one of the core pillars around whom the Dolphins would rebuild their roster, leading to an agreement on a three-year contract extension earlier this summer. “I’m thankful, man,” Brewer said of receiving the extension and being seen as a leader of the team. “It’s a blessing and I’m just grateful that he believed in me on that level. Like that’s the role I wanted to be in. That’s the role I own. And so for him to believe me, to be in that same role, like it’s an honor.” That leadership was on display when Brewer signed his new contract as he brought other members of the offensive line to the team facility to celebrate with him. “Because in my position, I can’t do nothing alone,” he explained. “It was a collective effort and also, they’re young right now and just have them there to see the whole process and just keep them by my side, like they’re my brothers right now. Right now and forever on. So I just felt it was special to have them there with me.” Leading the younger players Brewer understands that he and right tackle Austin Jackson are the veterans of the offensive line group, as both players enter their seventh seasons. On the left side, tackle Patrick Paul is headed into his third campaign, while rookie Kadyn Proctor is expected to start at guard. Between Brewer and Jackson will be second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea, who shifts to tight right after rookie struggles on the left last year. Brewer sees an opportunity to help build the line’s confidence and production. “KP [Proctor], he already, like he’s got a lot of good qualities already,” Brewer said of what he has seen from Miami’s first-round draft pick this year. “He’s big, he’s fast and he’s aggressive. As an offensive lineman, that’s what you want out of him. And so with him, I’m just trying to keep pushing him and just allow him to know like it’s more and just have him, like not competing with what he sees every day out here. Like it’s more to the league, it’s 32 teams and there’s plenty of great defensive linemen out there. So I want him to be prepared for when he’s going against the bottom of the bottle and the best of the best. I want him to be the best player he can be. I want him to be the No. 1 guard in the league. And so that’s my goal. That’s my attitude with him every day.” Brewer has also wrapped his arms around Savaiinaea and helping him rebound this year. “Same thing. I said in the spring, [I] like him on the right side, he looked way more comfortable. I’ve been with him all offseason. We’ve been up here working out together. So I’ve been seeing like how he been coming to work, his intentionality towards everything he’s doing. And so I feel like it’s the same thing with him. Anybody playing along with me, anybody on this team, anybody on offense with me, I want them to be the best in the league. And so that’s what we’re trying to push. We preach. I’m preaching it every day to him and trying to push each other every day to do that.” As for those offseason workouts, it was not limited to just Brewer and Savaiinaea, but the entire offensive line stayed in Miami and continued to work together. Brewer explained the mentality and decision-making for everyone coming together as a unit, “Like we understand Pat’s [Paul] going in year three, Jonah is going into year two, A.J. [Jackson], he’s year seven with me; so we’re trying to merge together. Like we want to be better, we want more. And so just sticking around, just growing that bond with each other. We’re working out every day together, pushing each other, just continuing to grow that connection with each other. So I definitely believe it was definitely intentional.” Personal goals for 2026 Ain’t no such thing as perfect, but I’m chasing perfection. Aaron brewer What does Brewer want to see from himself this year? He would like to turn that Second-Team All-Pro selection into a First-Team tag as he continue to improve his game. “To be better than I was last year,” he said. “There’s always room to growth. I wasn’t perfect. Ain’t no such thing as perfect, but I’m chasing perfection. And so that’s all I got to do. I try to be the No. 1 center in the league. We got to try to be the No. 1 rushing offense in the league. No. 1 passing offense. No. 1 offense as a whole. I’m trying to go first-team All-Pro. I want everybody else to go first-team All-Pro. Pro Bowl, Protector of the Year. Like those are the top of the top and so that’s what we’re striving for.” Jackson’s importance to the line The discussion returned to Jackson’s importance to the line. The 18th overall pick in 2020, Jackson has struggled with injuries throughout his career, including being limited to just 14 games played over the last two seasons. Brewer was asked about Jackson trying to shake the “injury-prone” label and what he has gone through in…

title: Vikings Training Camp 2026: McCarthy vs. Murray QB Battle, Jamal Adams & What We’ve Learned So Far
summary: Minnesota Vikings training camp is two days in, and the J.J. McCarthy vs. Kyler Murray quarterback competition is already generating must-watch storylines. Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano of The Real Forno Show — part of the Vikings 1st & SKOL network on Bleav — broke down the early themes, key roster battles, and what to […]
full_text: EAGAN, MINNESOTA - JUNE 10: J.J. McCarthy #9 of the Minnesota Vikings looks on during minicamp at Twin Cities Orthopedics Performance Center on June 10, 2026 in Eagan, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images Minnesota Vikings training camp is two days in, and the J.J. McCarthy vs. Kyler Murray quarterback competition is already generating must-watch storylines. Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano of The Real Forno Show — part of the Vikings 1st & SKOL network on Bleav — broke down the early themes, key roster battles, and what to watch for as camp progresses. The Quarterback Competition: Context Over Completions Head coach Kevin O’Connell has been clear: this competition will be thorough, but not a rigid 50/50 snap split. As Forness explained, “It’s not a exact science, as O’Connell says. You wanna get the information and you wanna find out how he’s going about things.” The Vikings are scheduling practices in blocks of four, giving coaches a richer sample before drawing conclusions. The early theme for McCarthy? A noticeably higher completion percentage — but a significantly shorter average depth of target. Forness flagged it as a trend worth monitoring: “Over the course of the first two days, some of the themes of J.J. McCarthy have been he has a higher completion percentage, but he’s got a much lower depth of target.” Is McCarthy pressing, playing conservatively to win the job, or simply working within what the defense is giving him? The answer isn’t clear yet — but O’Connell’s offense rewards quarterbacks who take calculated risks. As Forness noted, “O’Connell wants you to make those throws, and he will live with a couple extra interceptions because it’s going to result in touchdowns, hence Sam Darnold in 2024.” Murray, meanwhile, is showing the inconsistency expected of someone who received the Vikings playbook in March. He’s made some impressive downfield throws — including a deep corner to Dontae Fleming and a near-miss to Jordan Addison — but has also dealt with snap-exchange issues with Blake Brandel and Michael Jurgens. “He’s still kind of getting his bearings,” Forness said, calling it entirely normal for a quarterback learning a new system. Key Bullet Points from This Episode: • Quarterback timeline: Forness projects O’Connell will name a starter between August 18–23, around the joint practices window. • Jamal Adams worked with the first-team defense early, but his special-teams role remains a major question vs. Ivan Pace. • Demond Claiborne (RB) draws mixed reviews — elite speed, praise from Matt Daniels as a potential kick returner, but contact balance and pass-protection concerns remain. • Blake Cashman was all over the field and continues to be a critical piece of Brian Flores’ defense. • Brian O’Neill signed a 4-year, $96 million extension and made clear he hated missing even OTA drills — a strong culture sign. • Jordan Addison reportedly looked sharp and is coming off a relatively quiet offseason. • Gavin Bartholomew had a standout Wednesday practice and is emerging as a name to watch at tight end. • Vita Vea trade rumors: Forness doesn’t expect the Vikings to pursue Vea, preferring a younger edge rusher to backup and eventually replace Alex Van Ginkel. • Whoever loses the QB competition is likely headed to the trade block, per Forness — including Kyler Murray if J.J. wins. title: 3-Point Stance: Patriots’ training camp expectations have changed
summary: The 2024 season left the New England Patriots in a bleak spot. New England finished the season with a 4-13 record and moved on from Jerod Mayo as head coach after just one season. The only factors offering the fan base hope were 2024 third overall pick Drake Maye making a potential leap and new […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - July 25: New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel at training camp on July 25, 2026. (Photo by John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The 2024 season left the New England Patriots in a bleak spot. New England finished the season with a 4-13 record and moved on from Jerod Mayo as head coach after just one season. The only factors offering the fan base hope were 2024 third overall pick Drake Maye making a potential leap and new head coach Mike Vrabel building a competitive culture and foundation in year one. But none of that was guaranteed. Still, everything seemed to go right for the Patriots. They made the Super Bowl last season as champions of the AFC, which was a surprise to a majority of NFL fans and media, who had lower expectations. Maye also became an MVP finalist while Vrabel put together one of the most well-rounded coaching staffs in the league, raising the floor of the team and elevating the franchise’s player development pipeline. As a result, expectations entering training camp have changed from a year ago. Eyeing cohesiveness over individual player development In 2025, Vrabel’s goals for his players heading into the summer sessions were built on creating a foundation: building a team, earning a role and preparing to win. “We have to start coming together as a football team,” Vrabel said ahead of last summer’s first practice. “The other thing is [the players] have to earn a role, and that’s a great time for them to personally earn a role through training camp, what they can do for the team, how they can help us and how they can help themselves.” Leading into 2026, however, that approach has changed in Vrabel’s second season with New England, wanting to expand on the team’s season success as starters established themselves. “The expectations always get higher … Our job is to recreate the things that we did really well last year, the culture, the ability to win different ways, to find ways to win, understand how to win and how to prepare,” Vrabel said before practice on July 25. “We’re going to have a more difficult journey.” From an evaluation standpoint, the emphasis last year was centered on tracking the progression of young talent and identifying potential long-term starters. Maye was the focal point, with each practice offering another opportunity to evaluate his development and ability to lead the first-team offense. But through a championship-level lens, the attention has now shifted to how well each unit orchestrates as a collective group; it’s about how Maye is meshing with the new offensive pieces as they get acclimated to a new scheme. One of the biggest storylines of camp, for instance, is his connection with A.J. Brown, which progressed from an out-of-rhythm start to four completions on Thursday and a 50-yard touchdown the following practice. We’re nitpicking the details that could determine whether they can raise banner No. 7, like the tight end room’s needed young talent and Cory Durden’s transition to becoming the starting nose tackle. Schematic expansion and fine-tuning schemes En route to building one cohesive group at each unit, part of the change this summer is conducted within the playbooks. In the spring, quarterbacks coach Ashton Grant mentioned the coaching staff trying to “weaponize” the quarterbacks’ minds. And of course, as the starter, much of that responsibility to improve mental processing falls on Maye. Rather than proving he can lead the offense, training camp is now about determining how much more responsibility Maye can handle making adjustments at the line of scrimmage as offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels expands on his scheme. The same principle applies to Zak Kuhr’s defense as well. Back in February, Vrabel called for his staff at all three units to bring him “fresh ideas” for 2026. Both staffs identified over the offseason what worked last year and what didn’t, correspondingly adding pieces throughout the calendar break to fine-tune areas of the roster they felt needed change. Left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker was signed to bolster the point of attack for both Maye and the ground game. Meanwhile, second-round pick Gabe Jacas and free-agency signing Dre’Mont Jones were brought in on the defensive edge to help turn pressures into sacks — the primary shortcoming of a largely successful defense in 2025. Veterans sustaining the team culture The team culture Vrabel guided his players into cementing last year was a driving variable for why outside talent came to Foxboro in free agency. “I think it comes down to Vrabel coming in and establishing that culture where everybody has real love for each other, wants to play for each other, and wants to do everything they can on that field,” Vera-Tucker said earlier this offseason. “All those factors came into play in the decision to come here.” Vrabel overhauled the Patriots’ roster entering 2025, resetting around 50% of the roster he originally inherited from the season prior. Currently, a large majority of 2025’s active roster is intact as the franchise selectively upgraded. Instead of Vrabel building the culture from scratch, returning players and New England’s veterans are now tasked with establishing that camaraderie with those new additions.
author: Andrew Guindon

title: Efton Chism leaning on mental growth entering second season
summary: Getting ready to enter the NFL as a rookie, the focus for Efton Chism III was preparing for the physicality of the league. After signing with the Patriots as an undrafted free agent, Chism went on to make the 53-man roster following a standout training camp and preseason. Entering Year 2, his offseason focus then […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Efton Chism III (86) makes a catch during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Getting ready to enter the NFL as a rookie, the focus for Efton Chism III was preparing for the physicality of the league. After signing with the Patriots as an undrafted free agent, Chism went on to make the 53-man roster following a standout training camp and preseason. Entering Year 2, his offseason focus then shifted to the mental side of the game. “How can I stay on top of my playbook, stay watching film, keep doing all those little things to where when I get back I can still talk coverages, I can still talk plays and not feel like I’m three months behind or trying to catch up to the veterans how I felt when I first got here. So that I think was probably the biggest thing I did this offseason,” Chism said. “Obviously speed training, always trying to get bigger, faster, stronger. But I think mentally that was a huge thing for me this offseason.” His wide receiver coach quickly noticed the progression. “Understanding the details a little bit better,” Todd Downing said during minicamp. “I think he had some exposure last year when Mack [Hollins] went out of moving around in different spots. That’s accelerating and improving as well this offseason. Being able to walk in and know what a concept is or what the formation is without having to think about it is going to help him play faster when the ball is snapped.” After making the 53-man roster as a rookie, Chism appeared in eight regular season games, catching three passes for 75 yards and a touchdown. He then added a 20-yard reception in the Patriots’ Wild Card victory over the Los Angeles Chargers. The additions of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs have only made the Patriots’ wide receiver room more competitive entering 2026, but Chism has embraced that reality and has continued to make plays this summer. Efton Chism athletic touchdown catch pic.twitter.com/2ajoQUSmKn — Savage (@Savageboston) July 31, 2026 “I think as I’m starting to understand the NFL, I think every year is going to be like that,” Chism said. “That’s kind of a mindset I feel like I’ve adjusted to. It’s like every year, all of us are competing. We all want to play. We all want to make plays, and that’s just the nature of the NFL. “So, I’m excited for it, and I appreciate it and I think competition makes us all better. I think me and Pop competing makes us better. I think Kayshon and A.J. make each other better. Everyone in the whole room, like we’re all trying to make each other better each and every day.”

title: Patriots 2026 scouting report for WR Kyle Dixon
summary: The New England Patriots decided to forgo the wide receiver position in this year’s NFL Draft, but they did sign a bunch of rookie free agents afterwards. Among that group, nobody had as unique a background as Kyle Dixon. A former baseball player in college, he spent his only two football seasons at Culver-Stockton in […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Kyle Dixon (83) runs after making a catch during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New England Patriots decided to forgo the wide receiver position in this year’s NFL Draft, but they did sign a bunch of rookie free agents afterwards. Among that group, nobody had as unique a background as Kyle Dixon. A former baseball player in college, he spent his only two football seasons at Culver-Stockton in the NAIA. Now, he is trying to leave his mark on the Patriots. Hard facts Name: Kyle Dixon Position: Wide receiver Jersey number: 83 Opening day age: 25 (9/14/2000) Measurements : 6’2 1/2”, 220 lbs, 9” hand size, 31 7/8” arm length, 78” wingspan, 4.50s 40-yard dash, 7.05s 3-cone drill, 4.51s short shuttle, 40 1/2” vertical jump, 10’11” broad jump, 15 bench press reps, 9.42 Relative Athletic Score Experience NFL: New England Patriots (2026-) | College: Southern Illinois Carbondale (2019-20), Southern Illinois Edwardsville (2021-22), Georgia Gwinnett (2023), Culver-Stockton (2024-25) Despite being of the most productive wide receivers in Illinois state history as well as an all-state defensive back as a junior, Dixon decided not to continue his football career beyond Carlinville, IL, High School. Instead, he opted for baseball entering college and ended up spending five years as a bullpen pitcher at various schools. In 2024, he made his return to a gridiron. It was a successful one. In just two seasons and 22 games with the NAIA’s Culver-Stockton Wildcats in Canton, MI, he caught 143 passes for 2,394 yards and 24 touchdowns. He also was voted first-team All-HAAC in both seasons. And yet, Dixon received only moderate interest entering the NFL and eventually went undrafted in 2026. He joined the Patriots as a rookie free agent shortly after hitting the market. Scouting report Strengths: Tall, lean, with broad shoulders and long limbs, Dixon very much looks the part of an NFL wide receiver — and not just that. He also offers decent straight-line speed and good leaping ability; he is well-suited to be competitive as a downfield receiver and competitive catch player both inside and on the perimeter. He transitions quickly from a receiver to a runner with the ball in his hands, and has shown the ability to break tackles to gain extra yards. His college production also was nothing short of impressive given his background. Weaknesses: There is no denying that Dixon’s game translating to the NFL is far from a given. Looking at his tape at Culver-Stockton, he mostly was the best athlete on the field and therefore at a clear advantage over his opposition. As far as his actual skillset is concerned, he is unsurprisingly raw throughout his route; his release technique, footwork at his break, and working back to the football are all a work in progress. He also is not the shiftiest receiver and more of a linear streaker but without the top-end speed to begin with. 2025 review Stats : 11 games | 83 catches, 1,282 receiving yards (15.4/catch), 12 TDs, 1 fumble (1 lost) | 1 carry, 5 rushing yards | 1-of-1, 11 passing yards Season recap: Typically in this section of our scouting reports, we provide some extra info that goes beyond the basic stats. However, this being Culver-Stockton we are talking about, there is limited information available about how Dixon fared statistically in 2025. What we do know is that he was once again pretty productive and finished the season as the Wildcats’ most productive pass catcher and one of the top performers in the NAIA. But just to paint the picture here. At Culver-Stockton, Dixon played in front of a crowd typically a fraction of what he is experiencing at your average Patriots training camp practice. The team’s highest recorded home attendance of 2025 was 945 spectators against St. Ambrose (IA). Dixon caught eight passes for 109 yards and a touchdown in that game. That was one of seven 100-yard games he had last season, but far from his top outing. A week later versus Central Methodist (MO), he recorded 11 catches for 236 yards and three scores — breaking a school record in receiving yards that had stood for 36 years and earning Heart Football Player of the Week honors. Unsurprisingly, Dixon was also named first-team All-HAAC for a second straight season. He also was later invited to participate in the Hula Bowl, where he hauled in four passes for 71 yards. 2026 preview Position: X-receiver | Ability: Camp body/Practice squad candidate | Contract: Signed through 2028 (2029 RFA) What will be his role? Dixon was used both outside and in the slot during his brief college football career, but based on his skillset projects mostly as an outside receiver at the next level. That said, the Patriots do like to cross-train their wideouts if they believe they can do so, meaning that a more flexible role could be in the cards as well especially given concerns about his ability to beat press-man coverage. Either way, Dixon is a package and backup player. What is his growth potential? Athletically, Dixon provides a decent ceiling. This, in turn, could help him develop into a usable depth piece on offense. Whether or not he can be anything more than that remains to be seen; the sample size thus far is simply too small and of an entirely different quality than what he will face as a pro. His potential for development is sizable, though. Does he have positional versatility? While not the most versatile of players, Dixon does have some attributes to his game that suggest he can be used as more than a one-trick pony. Training camp so far has already shown that: he has spent time with the returners, something he did not do in college. What is his salary cap situation? The Patriots signed him to a three-year undrafted rookie deal that came with sizable guarantees: a $17,000 signing bonus prorated over the length of the deal, plus $235,000 in salary guarantees for the 2026 season. As far as his cap impact is concerned, it consists of his $885,000 base salary plus that $5,833 signing bonus proration for a combined sum of $890,833. Under the Top 51 rule, only his guaranteed bonus counts against the cap in the offseason. How safe is his roster spot? Minimally. As an undrafted rookie receiver, Dixon was at a disadvantage to begin with; there is a reason he was not selected in the draft. So far this training camp, little has changed: he still remains near the bottom of the depth chart, with second-unit work the height of his success. Summary: Dixon has an intriguing skillset and after playing only two college seasons still has significant room for growth, particularly considering the massive jump in competition he is facing. That might be enough for him to be kept around on the practice squad, if his practice and preseason performance look the part as well. What do you think about Kyle Dixon heading into the 2026 season? Will he emerge from the depths of the roster? Will he maybe factor into the returner mix? Please head down to the comment section to share your thoughts.

summary: New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye described his wide receiver room by two words on Friday: crowded and competitive.
