full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - JUNE 5: Trenton Irwin #83 of the Jacksonville Jaguars works out during a NFL Organized Team Activities (OTAs) offseason practice at Miller Electric Center on June 5, 2025 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Thursday evening, the San Francisco 49ers brought back a very familiar face to their receiving core, signing wide receiver Deebo Samuel to a one-year, $7 million deal, ending his long-lasting free agency. Samuel, 30, had spent the 2025 season with the Washington Commanders after getting traded there last offseason ahead of the final year of his contract. He caught 72 passes for 727 yards and five touchdowns, but did not see much usage as a rusher, taking only 17 carries for 75 yards. Samuel hit free agency this offseason along with many other veteran receivers and went unsigned until Thursday, when the 49ers brought back the former All-Pro wideout on a one-year deal. The news came after Ricky Pearsall dealt with knee swelling and was held out of training camp, with surgery being a potential option for his nagging PCL injury. Well, on Friday morning, the 49ers added even more pass-catching depth, signing tight end Josiah DeGuara and wide receiver Trenton Irwin to one-year deals, according to ESPN’s Adam Schefter. DeGuara, a third-round pick of the Green Bay Packers in the 2020 NFL Draft, has 53 career catches for 471 yards and three touchdowns. He spent the 2025 season with the Arizona Cardinals, bouncing between the practice squad and the active roster, as he played in 12 games. Irwin, on the other hand, went undrafted in the 2019 NFL Draft, and has not played in an NFL game since 2024. He spent the first six years of his career with the Cincinnati Bengals, catching 46 passes for 601 yards, before being waived in December of 2024. He spent last year with the New York Jets on the practice squad.

title: The 49ers are set to become the 4th team in the Super Bowl era to do this if Deebo Samuel starts
summary: If signing Deebo Samuel is a 1-for-1 swap, the San Francisco 49ers are going from 25-year-old Ricky Pearsall to 30-year-old Deebo Samuel. Even if Samuel isn’t the starter and it’s Christian Kirk (turns 30 in November) or Demarcus Robinson (31), the Niners’ offense just got five or six years older. According to Josh Dubow of […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 04: Deebo Samuel #1 of the Washington Commanders walks through the tunnel prior to the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on January 04, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images If signing Deebo Samuel is a 1-for-1 swap, the San Francisco 49ers are going from 25-year-old Ricky Pearsall to 30-year-old Deebo Samuel. Even if Samuel isn’t the starter and it’s Christian Kirk (turns 30 in November) or Demarcus Robinson (31), the Niners’ offense just got five or six years older. According to Josh Dubow of the Associated Press, the 49ers could start five skill-position players age 30 or older: Mike Evans, Christian McCaffrey, George Kittle, Kyle Juszczyk, and the “Z” receiver, between Deebo, Kirk, and Robinson. The only teams in the Super Bowl era to start five non-QB skill position players age 30 or older in the same game were the 2004 Tampa Bay Bucs for one game, the 2003 Denver Broncos for one game, and the 1992 Washington team for two games. The 49ers aren’t entering the season hoping those players start a game or two. Those are the players they’re counting on for the remainder of the season. So, assuming one of the three 30+ year-old wideouts starts, the 49ers will become the fourth team in the Super Bowl era to start five non-QB skill positions. The 49ers will undoubtedly be older without Pearsall. They may lose their ability to stretch the field in some ways without Pearsall. But Deebo can still run. Last September, on a kickoff against the Raiders, Deebo reached a max speed of 19.23 miles per hour. That would have been among the top times among all 49ers last season. For a team that was coming into the year with inexperience at returner, Samuel could solve the kick returner question. Deebo averaged 30.1 yards per return on 15 tries. That was good for fourth in the NFL.

title: Pros and Cons of a Baker Mayfield Extension
summary: Training camp for the 2026 season is officially underway but for the Buccaneers, a lot of the focus is unfortunately off the field right now and the attention has turned to the contracts of quarterback Baker Mayfield as well as defensive tackle Vita Vea. Vea has already requested a trade after not being able to […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - JANUARY 3: Baker Mayfield #6 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Carolina Panthers at Raymond James Stadium on January 3, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Training camp for the 2026 season is officially underway but for the Buccaneers, a lot of the focus is unfortunately off the field right now and the attention has turned to the contracts of quarterback Baker Mayfield as well as defensive tackle Vita Vea. Vea has already requested a trade after not being able to get an extension done with the team and even though it is unlikely he is dealt, this is still not something you want becoming a distraction. On the Mayfield front he has made it very clear that he will not be negotiating with Tampa Bay any further once training camp started a Mayfield was very blunt when talking to the media Thursday afternoon. Mayfield confirmed he addressed the team, saying this won’t be a distraction. Plans to have a huge year, believes he’s in best shape. ‘If you’ve waited this long to pay your franchise quarterback, it’s only going to get worse…I’m going to have a big year.’ https://t.co/DiAmpgw5g2 — Jeremy Fowler (@JFowlerESPN) July 30, 2026 Mayfield isn’t happy, the team isn’t happy but what are the pros and cons of signing Mayfield to an extension right now? Lets dive right into it. Pro: Sign him early to keep him happy This ship probably has already sailed huh? Now if I had to guess, Mayfield was genuine when he set a deadline. That being said though, if the Bucs call his agent with an offer that is much improved in Mayfield’s eyes are they really not even going to hear them out? The agent has to take that call and if they offer the deal, you are looking for, I wonder if Mayfield’s deadline all of the sudden doesn’t appear so set. The team probably has already lost the ability to keep Mayfield completely happy unless they give him an incredible deal but that’s the risk they ran when they didn’t extend him. Had they come to an agreement by this point, Mayfield would have been pretty pleased and it would have avoided a lot of awkward interviews and limit the distractions. Mayfield says he is now focused on football but the contract situation will be looming in the back of everyone’s head. Extending him by this point would have made things a lot more simple. Pro: Bucs could get a bargain Now this obviously is reliant on Mayfield performing at a high level for an entire season but getting an extension done could end up looking good for the team if he is able to play like a top ten quarterback and lead the team back to the playoffs. The salary cap in the NFL is only going to keep rising and with that eventually a contract that may be a lot right now will look a lot better in 2-3 years. Short term pain for long term could happen but again, that relies solely on Mayfield performing well and at times outperforming his potential new deal. Con: Bucs could also be stuck with a bad contract Yes, if Mayfield plays well and the Bucs win a lot of football games then that contract looks really good. If he doesn’t though and it looks a lot like the second half of 2025 for Baker, the Bucs would have one of the worst contracts in the NFL on their hands with no realistic way to get rid of it. Teams can often survive giving out a bad deal or two, but it’s not often a team can survive it when it is at the quarterback position. Look at the Cardinals with Kyler Murray and Dolphins with Tua Tagovailoa, both were signed to massive extensions with their teams, and they just never got to that next level. Both Murray and Tua are now on different teams playing for very little money. You could make the argument that Mayfield is better than both of those guys, but it still doesn’t change the fact that handing out a big contract to a QB that doesn’t perform can sink a team. Bucs would be betting on Mayfield and if they are wrong, it becomes a hole that would take a long time to dig themselves out of. Con: Uncertainty in other areas for Tampa Bay Simply put, this team could look a lot different in just a few months. After missing the playoffs in embarrassing fashion, it is safe to assume Head Coach Todd Bowles enters 2026 on the hot seat and he likely won’t survive a second straight year without a playoff appearance. If Bowles is out, how bad does the season have to be to question General Manager Jason Licht’s job security? I think it would take a lot for Licht to be in trouble but if Tampa Bay only wins a handful of games and find themselves at the bottom of the NFC South, all bets could be off. So, with all the uncertainty surrounding the head coach and potentially general manager, what if they commit to Mayfield right now? Tampa Bay would be stuck with Baker who, if the Bucs played bad enough to get Bowles and Licht fired likely didn’t play well himself. Any new coaching or general manager candidate would now be stuck with Mayfield as their signal caller for 2027 and likely 2028 as well. That is a tough sell when you are trying to pitch to other external candidates. Tampa Bay knows they may look different in 2027 and I’m not sure if they want to strap themselves to Baker Mayfield at this time.
author: Evan Wanish

title: With DQ’s focus on competition, Commanders must gel as a team to win
summary: Competition, competition, competition Dan Quinn has been adamant this will be the Commanders’ most competitive training camp since he took over in 2024. “You’ll find some competition in an everyday sense, and I think that’s one of the very best ways that we’ll get better — just good-on-good situations. Into tomorrow, there’ll be a two-point […]
full_text: Competition, competition, competition Dan Quinn has been adamant this will be the Commanders’ most competitive training camp since he took over in 2024. “You’ll find some competition in an everyday sense, and I think that’s one of the very best ways that we’ll get better — just good-on-good situations. Into tomorrow, there’ll be a two-point play competition — best out of five — and those are the moments I think you’ll find some game scenarios and situations in every practice [like] two minute and four minute [drills], last plays, setting up field goals. “Can we put ourselves in these spots so when we the air gets thin, that we feel like that’s our space, and we’re going to work really hard into that spot? I feel a hunger from the team, so they’re ready to get into that.” Reacts survey This week’s Reacts survey comprised a single question: Outside of quarterback, which position group’s development during this training camp will most dictate the Commanders’ success in the 2026 season? The results were a bit unusual in that four different position groups got double-digit percentages of the overall vote. Visit our partners at FanDuel Two defensive groups (LBs and DBs) and two offensive groups (WR/TEs and OL) comprised those 4 groups of top vote-getters. In my mind, the four groups break out into three sub-groups when it comes to why readers voted for them. Group 1: High confidence The linebacking corps drew the largest percentage of this week’s responses, and I believe that’s because fans feel highly confident that this is a deep and talented position group. In fact, I’ve heard and read many people (myself included) suggest that this is the best overall group of inside linebackers that the Commanders has fielded in recent memory. It may take some time to adjust to thinking about Washington’s edge rushers as primarily aligning as outside linebackers in a 3-man front instead of DEs in a 4-man front, but the work that Adam Peters did this offseason to re-make the edge rushing group was also part of what drove some Hogs Haven readers to vote for this position group. To put a finer point on it, I think these 12 players are the ones that likely are in most people’s minds when they think of Washington’s training camp linebackers: Anchoring the middle, the inside linebackers appear to bring elite instincts, lateral speed, and bone-crushing physicality. While Sonny Styles is a rookie and unproven at the pro level, he is the son of an NFL player, and was drafted 7 th overall for a number of good reasons. Expectations are high that Styles will step right into a high-performance group, and that the rookie will see a lot of play time alongside proven veterans Leo Chenal and Frankie Luvu. Frankie, in 2025, was asked to play out of position for much of the season to make up for a devastating number of injuries to other players. With him back in his natural position and in a scheme that is built to take advantage of his strengths, the group’s sideline-to-sideline pursuit ought to be perfectly complemented by the still-developing high-motor play of Jordan Magee, with Kain Medrano, and Ale Kaho competing for roster spots primarily on the strength of their special teams play. On the perimeter, the outside linebackers have gotten a lot of “wows” from training camp observers in the first two days. With their size and experience, they should provide a terrifying edge presence characterized by raw speed and versatile coverage capabilities. The explosive tandem of Odafe Oweh and Dorance Armstrong will likely have the ability to set a ferocious edge against the run while consistently collapsing the pocket. Complemented by the twitchy athleticism of K’Lavon Chaisson and the length and potential of rookie Joshua Josephs, this group will be counted on the create consistent pressure, made relentless by the expected blitz-heavy scheme of new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. Both Javonte Jean-Baptiste, who played about 26% of defensive snaps over the past two seasons, and Drake Jackson, who appeared in the final 3 games of the ’25 season after being activated from injured reserve, look to be on the roster bubble in 2026 following March and April roster upgrades. Group 2: Shaky confidence The pass catchers and defensive backs each drew about 1 in 5 voters this week, and I think the reason was that many Commanders fans remain unconvinced that Washington’s front office did enough to ensure that the starting talent is good enough or that the depth is sufficient to withstand injuries to starters. Pass catchers For the purposes of the survey, I had to combine the WRs and TEs together. At tight end, I think most fans are sold on Chig Okonkwo being an explosive playmaker in the passing game, but may have more questions about his run game blocking. John Bates would be his mirror image as a skilled blocker, but merely a competent receiver. Questions hover around 2024 second-round pick Ben Sinnott, as well as 2024 UDFA Colson Yankoff. The bigger concerns at WR have been discussed all offseason. Firstly , does Washington have enough skill at the position outside of Terry McLaurin, with the rookie Antonio Williams being added to the group of veterans that all have question marks: Luke McCaffrey, Jaylin Lane, Dyami Brown, Treylon Burks and Van Jefferson? "If Jayden Daniels is sitting back there and nobody's getting open with a decent scheme, that puts him into a position where he's at more risk because he's extending and he's running more." – Kevin Sheehan on the risk of Commanders' lack of WR depth pic.twitter.com/wfu4pGsVXj — The Team 980 (@team980) July 31, 2026 Many argue that, if Jayden Daniels is healthy, he will elevate this group of generally undistinguished receivers to achieve on the field just like he did in 2024. In fact, the argument can be made that: (a) this group is more skilled than the ‘24 group was; (b) Daniels is a more fully developed QB than he was in ‘24; and (c) the new offensive coordinator will be better able to use scheme and motion to create passing opportunities than was true in ‘24. So, maybe, with a healthy JD5, this group will be good enough. That raises the second concern , however, of whether the group can perform at a playoff level if Terry McLaurin misses significant playing time , as he did in 2025. His absence from the field in training camp and most of the regular season last year is seen by many as a central factor in the team’s struggles. His presence throughout the offseason so far in 2026 has been credited as a major factor in a more energetic ‘vibe’ in this year’s camp. It’s hard to overstate the negative impact that another serious injury to Terry would have on the 2026 season, making the lack of a clear playmaking #2 receiver an issue that simply won’t go away. One noticeable difference at #Commanders camp this year is Terry McLaurin The difference? He's there… and practicing! With last year's contract dispute in the rear view, the star WR has his focus on performing, and mentoring. @JPFinlayNBCS has the story #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/V7C5w704bG — NBC4 Sports (@NBC4Sports) July 31, 2026 Defensive backs The concerns about the DBs mirror those that surround the wide receivers. There are no proven stars at safety or cornerback, and question marks are linked to health, size, or performance of nearly every player in the position group. While many people have made strong arguments that Nick Cross, Will Harris, Trey Amos, Mikey Sainristil, Amik Robertson or Rasul Douglas will play very well this year in Daronte Jones’ expected new blitz-heavy, zone-heavy scheme, a different fan, analyst or observer could make an equally strong evidence-backed case against each of those players having a great year in 2026. Clearly, as defined in this week’s question, the development of the secondary during this training camp will probably have a lot to do with the Commanders’ success in the coming season. title: How being ‘multiple’ will help Washington Commanders’ offense, defense
summary: Tyler’ Take: New coordinators, talent give Commanders the ability to be ‘multiple’ With training camp now underway, the guessing game of what Washington’s new offense and defense will look like this season is almost over. Earlier this week I wrote about weapons in this new-look David Blough offense and gave some scenarios as to how […]
full_text: Tyler’ Take: New coordinators, talent give Commanders the ability to be ‘multiple’ With training camp now underway, the guessing game of what Washington’s new offense and defense will look like this season is almost over. Earlier this week I wrote about weapons in this new-look David Blough offense and gave some scenarios as to how those weapons may be deployed. We discussed quite a bit in the comments section, and you saw me use the word “multiple” many times. I want to talk a bit more on this, and how being “multiple” on both sides of the ball will help breed success for both new coordinators. During Tuesday evening’s training camp opening presser , general manager Adam Peters spoke a bit about Washington’s new offense and defense. New offense will be more “multiple”. Many different ways to attack a defense. Quarterback friendly Defense has “multiple” ways to attack you Adam Peters referred to David Blough's #Commanders offense as "multiple" and "more QB-friendly" Defense has "multiple ways to attack you… we have answers… couldn't be happier" #RaiseHail — Full Command (@FullCommandShow) July 28, 2026 Being “multiple” on both sides of the football is a theme that has come up now on, well, MULTIPLE occasions. So, what exactly does it mean to be “multiple?” Being “multiple” on offense Being “multiple” on offense is about different ways to attack a defense using: Same formations, but different plays out of those formations Same play, out of different formations Moving guys around to create favorable mismatches Having versatility on offense, so defenses can’t key in on anything Being unpredictable Over last two years, Washington was too predictable under then-offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury . Opposing defensive players would often say they knew exactly what was coming based on formations, pre-snap calls and personnel. One example of this includes former Commander Zach Ertz in the tight end role. You knew what you were getting with Ertz. He would work the short to intermediate area of the field in a “post-up” fashion. It was infrequent that you get a designed route where he was given the opportunity to run after the catch, such as a shallow crosser or over route. The same could be said with receiver Terry McLaurin. Kingsbury often lined him up on the outside left and didn’t put him in motion much. This allowed defenses to key on him and often have a “bracket” defender shaded to his side. This Davis Blough offense should be much different. In my offensive weapons article, I gave some examples of how Blough could attack opposing defenses out of certain personnel groupings. In my opinion, this ability to be so “multiple” on offense really flows around the players we have and the versatility they possess. I talked a lot about the tight end room — more specifically, Chig Okonkwu and Ben Sinnott — and how defenses couldn’t key on these guys doing any one specific thing in the sets. This is a good example of this new scheme being “multiple.” Being “multiple” on defense With a heavy zone-coverage scheme being implemented by defensive coordinator Daronte Jones this season, head coach Dan Quinn spoke about the ability to be “multiple” on the defensive side: Every good defense that plays zone, you better have a pass rush in order to do that because there is not the leverage, so the quarterback has to feel like he’s getting affected. Quinn emphasized that he wants to see different personnel groups who can do this during camp. The Commanders defense under Joe Whitt was anything but “multiple.” Instead, it turned out to be incredibly predictable. In the NFL world, predictability is the impediment to progress. Under Jones, the defense is said to be “multiple.” What does that mean in this instance? This new look should feature a 3-4 UNDER base look. The UNDER aspect means the nose tackle shifts to the weak side and a SAM linebacker (strong side), is usually in a stand-up position as the EMOLS (end man on the line of scrimmage). The fun part about this defense being “multiple” is that you don’t know exactly where the rush will come from and what player(s) could get home. You may see certain guys coming from different areas of the formation, while others may show a certain look but drop back into coverage. All three levels of this defense have the ability to be “multiple” when it comes to getting after the head of the snake, and the athletes Washington now has will make that job a lot easier. Being “multiple” is just as important on the back end, as disguising coverages is an integral part of a successful scheme. We are expecting to see a lot of three-safety looks, with one of those guys being a hybrid linebacker type. The hybrid player can rush, drop or rob, which can help dictate to an offense instead of having the offense dictate to the defense (which we saw all too often last season). In sets where there is a more traditional slot corner being used, that player can also create confusion with disguised coverages that are meant to look like man, but turn out to be a cloud zone. Having guys with inside/outside versatility certainly help to make this job easier. Commanders Versatility Offense: Jayden Daniels: Can beat you as a passer and runner Rachaad White: RB who can double as a WR out of the backfield Chig Okonkwo: Move TE who plays more like a Jumbo WR Ben Sinnott: More traditional TE who can play as an H-back Antonio Williams: WR with inside/outside versatility who can uncover quickly Luke McCaffrey: Bigger-bodied receiver who has inside/outside versatility Defense: Javon Kinlaw: Multiple techniques along the D-line Daron Payne: Multiple techniques along the D-line Tim Settle: Multiple techniques along the D-line Charles Omenihu: DT/EDGE versatility Deatrich Wise: DT/EDGE versatility Sonny Styles: Versatility to play all three LB spots Leo Chenal: Versatility to play all three LB spots Frankie Luvu: Pass rush versatility from linebacker spot Mike Sainristil: Inside/outside CB versatility Amik Robertson: Inside/outside CB versatility Quan Martin: CB/S versatility Nick Cross: S/Hybrid-LB versatility Tyler Owens: S/Hybrid-LB versatility In today’s NFL, being able to do a variety of different things with a variety of different players from a variety of different sets is instrumental. Washington is now focused on being “multiple” on both sides of the football and it’s because of the scheme and personnel that allow them to do that. As training camp moves forward and the regular season approaches, you are going to hear this word used more and more – so be prepared; its definitely a good thing!

title: Analyzing top storylines from early Commanders training camp practices
summary: The first two days of Washington Commanders training camp are in the books, and fans are reveling in the start of football again. The updates and nuggets have been coming fast and furious with pressers, social media posts, and articles pouring in from on-site analysts and fans. With a one-day break in the action, Hogs […]
full_text: The first two days of Washington Commanders training camp are in the books, and fans are reveling in the start of football again. The updates and nuggets have been coming fast and furious with pressers, social media posts, and articles pouring in from on-site analysts and fans. With a one-day break in the action, Hogs Haven stops to take a closer look at some of the storylines from the first two days of camp. Will Dyami Brown make the most of his second chance with the Commanders? For the most part, receiver Dyami Brown didn’t live up to expectations when Washington drafted him in the third round of the 2021 NFL draft. Things changed with the arrival of Jayden Daniels in 2024 and a new approach to his offseason. While Brown’s regular season numbers were modest, in the wild-card-playoff win over the Buccaneers, he had five catches on five targets for 89 yards and a touchdown. In the divisional-round upset over the Lions, Brown had eight targets with six catches and 98 yards. Another 42 yards came against the Eagles in the NFC Championship Game, giving Brown 229 receiving yards for the three-game postseason run — more than any of his first three full seasons. The Commanders and Brown parted ways in 2025 as general manager Adam Peters opted not to match a one-year, $10 million deal from the Jaguars that was almost fully guaranteed. Things didn’t go according to plan in Jacksonville, and Washington decided to bring him back on a one-year, $1.75 million deal that does not lock him into a roster spot. Brown seems to realize the importance of this second chance, arriving early and staying late the first day of camp. Commanders TC, Day 1 first player to the is … drumroll … Dyami Brown pic.twitter.com/RjUDQ8PqZi — Mitchell Tischler (@Mitch_Tischler) July 29, 2026 Dyami Brown got some extra work in with the DBs after the Commanders’ first day of practice. Brown is determined to make an impact this season pic.twitter.com/yyntPlrLI5 — Zach Selby (@ZachSelbyWC) July 29, 2026 Brown has flashed previously in training camps, then failed to have his performance carry over into the regular season, but he seems determined to change that this go-around. It is interesting to note that he made some plays in red-zone drills, including a toe-tap touchdown grab in the corner of the end zone, which is not something he had been known for in the past. Treylon Burks missed Friday’s session with foot soreness, while Luke McCaffery and Antonio Williams both made plays. The receiver competition is wide open, and Brown will have to fight to make his mark. Is Bill Croskey-Merritt ready to be a complete three-down back this year? There has been a lot of discussion surrounding Bill Croskey-Merritt’s physical conditioning over the offseason, but lost in the mix is how he has looked in receiving drills. Croskey-Merritt has been challenged by head coach Dan Quinn to become a more complete back this offseason and has been working on his receiving skills. In Thursday’s session, Bill caught a ball out of the backfield and beat first-round rookie Sonny Styles in a footrace to the corner of the end zone. Running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt outraced linebacker Sonny Styles to the edge for a catch from quarterback Jayden Daniels ran it in for a touchdown in early red zone team drills. — David Harrison (@DHarrison82) July 29, 2026 Grant Paulsen from 106.7 The Fan also noted that Croskey-Merritt was split out wide at times during Thursday’s session, and commented how the receiving game will need to be a key component of Croskey-Merritt’s game this season. Unfortunately, the second-year back followed up Thursday’s good start with a fumble in Friday’s session, highlighting the concerns around his ball security. As Bill had four fumbles last season, he will have to fix this issue in camp if he wants to have a larger role in the offense. According to Pro Football Reference , Rachaad White typically has three fumbles per year but was perfect in ball security last season. Does the early defensive performance mean the Washington Commanders should add a free agent wide receiver? Several on-site reports noted how strong the defense played the first two days with “ sticky ” coverage and a noticeably faster front seven. Odafe Oweh, in particular, caught the eyes of media in attendance. The defense had four total turnovers on Friday, including a “throw-away” pick for Ahkello Witherspoon and a pick-6 by Rasul Douglas to end the practice session. Mike Sainristil also stripped Croskey-Merritt for his fumble and had a nice pass deflection on Thursday. FR0Z0NE 🚫 @MikeSainristil | #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/yoHitIq8i4 — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) July 29, 2026 This is all occurred without projected top corner Trey Amos on the field, so the secondary has looked good early. The defense is most always ahead of the offense at the start of camp, and some early troubles are to be expected with Jayden Daniels and other quarterbacks learning a new system against a defense designed to generate confusion. Still, the lack of separation and dropped balls by the pass catchers on Friday had many asking if now is the time to add a wide receiver in free agency. The short list of available (or potentially available) receivers from Sharp Football Analysis is listed below. Tyreek Hill Stefon Diggs Brandon Aiyuk Keenan Allen DeAndre Hopkins Brandin Cooks Curtis Samuel Sterling Shepard Noah Brown Tyler Lockett Should Washington add a veteran free agent center? Nick Allegretti was injured early on the first day of camp, with Dan Quinn telling the local media on Friday that the center had a strained calf . While the injury is not expected to be a long-term issue, it sounds like he will be out at least through the weekend. Julian Good-Jones stepped in for first-team reps and reportedly looked rough in Thursday’s session. While Matt Gulbin certainly needs all the reps he can get at the center position, there is not much behind him. In fact, the current options might not be good enough for the back end of the offense to run properly. The group of centers warming up the quarterbacks snapping: Julian Good Jones —> JD5 Matt Gulbin —-> Mariota Tyler Cooper —-> Kaliakmanis Timothy McKay —-> Hartman pic.twitter.com/mlg4cxLsFb — Mitchell Tischler (@Mitch_Tischler) July 30, 2026 If it looks like Allegretti is facing even a slightly protracted absence, the Commanders may decide they need to kick the tires on a veteran addition sooner than later. Another short list from Sharp Football Analysis , this time listing free agent centers. Graham Glasgow Andre James James Daniels Daniel Brunskill Sam Mustipher UDFA Watch Jaden Bradley continued to draw positive attention from observers during the first two days of camp. At 6’3” and 203 pounds, he should thrive in red-zone drills and did with two scores, including one over the top of a defender, and also caught a slant versus Rasul Douglas. Terry McLaurin continues to mentor the young wide receiver, with both working together after practice on the first day. McLaurin also gave a glowing review of the undrafted free agent in his Friday presser: #Commanders veteran Terry McLaurin on UDFA and former @DeMathaCatholic WR Jaden Bradley: "he's a bigger receiver but he moves very smoothly. His releases are very smooth. He's sudden in his releases…he kind of has a pro-like feel…he's a sponge, man" pic.twitter.com/Q4or8fB171 — Commanders on Roundtable (@WSHRoundtable) July 30, 2026 Both players competing for the kicking job were perfect on Wednesday , and then went 6-for-6 on Thursday. Jake Moody went first with a perfect performance, and UDFA Drew Stevens answered with one of his own. On a particularly breezy day in Ashburn, VA., with a new holder, fans have to be excited about the level of competition currently occurring at the kicker position. Stevens appears to have the stronger leg. Malik Spencer was the first defensive UDFA to make his presence felt, recording the initial interception of camp. Malik…

title: Commanders News: Kay Adams at camp with DQ, Jayden Daniels & Sonny Styles
summary: The Daily Slop – 31 July 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. full_text: The Daily Slop – 31 July 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles The Athletic (paywall) The Commanders have remade their roster; they will still rise or fall with Jayden Daniels For Washington to bounce back to the team that earned its way to the NFC title game in 2025, the Commanders need their lodestar to again play light and with joy — and to throw seeds past opposing defenders’ earholes on the way to his receivers’ hands, the way he did in his historic 2024 rookie season, when he was the AP NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year. The dazzle , the swagger, the hope that the franchise can compete again year in and year out in the NFC, the new stadium that will now rise where RFK once stood: It all emanates, first, from Daniels. A new year presents another chance. Daniels got healthy, working out with his longtime trainer and quarterback coach, Taylor Kelly, who works at the development group 3DQB in Huntington Beach, Calif. He organized separate workouts for his offensive skill players in Los Angeles: one in April , and the second just a couple of weeks ago at UCLA . McLaurin, Dyami Brown and other receivers, along with tight ends and running backs , took part in on-field drills and off-field bonding with Daniels and third-string quarterback Sam Hartman. A better defense should also create more than 10 measly turnovers — second-lowest in the league last season — and get Daniels and the offense the ball in plus territory. Blough’s offense should lessen potential risk to Daniels by leaning more on the run. In all ways, now, the Commanders will go as Daniels goes. And says. And acts. And performs. The phrase people in sports use these days is “I’m built for this.” We will soon see how the first two years of Jayden Daniels’ time in Washington have shaped the third and all the years that will follow. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE JP Finlay Training Camp Day 2: Minor (injury) bug bites 1) Quinn says Allegretti will be ok. 2) NFL rosters are currently sitting at 90 men. By the end of August those rosters will be at 53/70, so there will be experienced centers either hitting the wire or available to poach off other practice squads. Maybe this Allegretti calf issue will encourage Adam Peters to add a veteran after roster cuts. It’s also possible that Washington would actually go with Matt Gulbin , the 6th-round rookie out of Michigan State, if Allegretti missed time. But maybe they’re not ready to do that in July. Listen, it’s not good news that Allegretti strained his calf on the first day of camp. Coupled with fan confusion over the offseason release of Tyler Biadasz and not adding another veteran snapper in free agency, it seems worse. It’s something to monitor, for sure, but probably too early to worry. Burks’ injury lands a bit different, mainly because of his lengthy injury history. A 1st-round pick in 2022, Burks has never played more than 11 games in a season. He’s a big, strong receiver with good hands that runs good routes. He’s just never been able to stay healthy, and like Allegretti’s calf issue, foot soreness on the first day of training camp is unnerving. The good news is unlike at the center spot Washington did much more to build WR depth this offseason. The team brought in veterans Dyami Brown and Van Jefferson , so they’re in better shape then last year when the injury bug hit the WR room. Could the Burks foot scare hasten the organization’s desire to sign a veteran free agent wideout? Maybe. And Stef Diggs remains available. Onto the notes: John Bates didn’t get much action (maybe a vet day?), so in his place there was plenty of work for Chig Okonkwo and Ben Sinnott . It was another impressive day for both tight ends, although arguably the catch of the day belonged to Colson Yankoff . Nick Allegretti injury doesn’t seem too serious, but getting injured on the first day of camp is a reminder of just how big of a gamble at Center Washington made settling with Nick. #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/CljCCw0W16 — Jamual (@LetMualTellit) July 30, 2026 To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Last Man Standig Nick Allegretti, Treylon Burks injuries serve as an early reminder of the NFL’s fragile plans The Commanders are banking on center Nick Allegretti enhancing the offensive line communication directly in front of Jayden Daniels. Wide receiver Treylon Burks is a tantalizing talent with overt athletic gifts. Washington made several bold choices in the offseason. Much of its ample free-agent spending occurred on all three levels of the defense that ranked last in yards allowed and 31st in turnovers. Premium draft capital was used on first-round linebacker Sonny Styles. Washington also invested on offense, headlined by the signing of tight end Chig Okonkwo and drafting third-round receiver Antonio Williams. There were more subtle choices on that side of the ball. Perhaps none more than positioning Allegretti as the line’s man in the middle after an unsuccessful pursuit of free-agent center Tyler Lindenbaum. Neither injury is expected to keep the player sidelined for long. Other bumps, bruises, and worse for others on the roster are inevitable, no matter the best-laid plans. Thursday’s news reminded the hopeful that you just never know what the next day will bring. For more from Ben Standig, click here Commanders.com Training camp notebook | Defense has strong Day 2 performance It’s becoming clearer by the day that this year’s defense is much faster than the one that was on the field last season. The Commanders started the day with another competition — a first-and-goal drill — and the defense was the clear victor in the five-minute series. Things started off well with a touchdown from the offense, but a play was later ruled dead as Jayden Daniels scrambled to avoid pressure. Daniels was “sacked” on the following play (the pocket collapsed around Daniels, which forced the coaches to blow their whistles), and his end zone shot to Jaylin Lane fell incomplete. Although there is still plenty of work to be done, it appears that the secondary and pass rush are working well together to create difficult scenarios for the quarterbacks. It’s worth pointing out that most of the snaps taken in team drills have been in the red zone, where it’s more difficult for receivers to find open space downfield, but all the quarterbacks have needed more time than normal to find targets and are working through their progressions thanks to the coverage from the secondary. At the same time, the Commanders’ pass rush is putting pressure on them, which has led to some off-target throws. That should please defensive coordinator Daronte Jones, who wants to emphasize creating turnovers after the unit generated just 10 takeaways in 2025. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE ESPN Latest news from Commanders camp Thursday, July 30 Washington’s tight ends have been far more active as a group than they had been the previous two seasons. Newly-signed Chig Okonkwo can be used all over, with wide receiver Terry McLaurin saying he runs routes like a big receiver. That versatility was evident again Thursday, but it’s also not just Okonkwo — all the tight ends, including 2024 second-round pick Ben Sinnott, have run a wider variety of routes. “It’s not even close,” Sinnott said. “So many different variations. Today we’re lining up at number one [receiver on the outside], we’re running five-step ins, we’re running corners, we’re running options, we’re running flat [routes]. We’re just doing everything. It’s so much fun. It’s a breath of fresh air for this offense and how it uses tight ends.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE NFL.com Top 11 NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year candidates in 2026 Rank 3 – Sonny Styles – Washington Commanders · LB We haven’t seen…

title: Why Jaylin Lane will be better in Year 2 as a Washington Commander
summary: When Jaylin Lane was selected in the fourth round of the 2025 NFL Draft, Adam Peters made it clear the selection was endorsed by everyone in the building. Part of the reason was the Virginia Tech alum was their No. 1 punt returner in the draft. Lane met expectations with two punt return touchdowns, which […]
full_text: When Jaylin Lane was selected in the fourth round of the 2025 NFL Draft, Adam Peters made it clear the selection was endorsed by everyone in the building. Part of the reason was the Virginia Tech alum was their No. 1 punt returner in the draft. Lane met expectations with two punt return touchdowns, which tied for the league lead last season. His 314 punt return yards were good for eighth-most, and his average of 13.7 yards per punt return finished fifth-best. Jaylin Lane got the Commander tag and was the top punt returner on Washington's board pic.twitter.com/7yiBuULfn5 — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) April 26, 2025 Peters also drafted the wide receiver for his speed and versatility in the passing game. Despite his success on special teams, Lane has become something of an afterthought in the receiver room headed into his second season. Analysts are predicting either Treylon Burks, Luke McCaffrey, or Dyami Brown will have a bigger role than the Commanders fourth-round selection. In this article, we will look at why one of the team’s fastest skill players is currently being slotted towards the bottom of the receiver depth chart, and what the reasonable expectations should be for his sophomore season. The first thing to discuss regarding Lane’s rookie season is his drop rate. Fan perception is that it was unusually high but, in fact, Pro Football Reference only credited Lane with one drop for a rate of 3.1%, which is well below the league average of 4.0% in 2025. Jaylin Lane drops the easy catch on 1st down, and the #Commanders are badly missing their top 3 receivers. pic.twitter.com/doKV8XGilx — Chad Ryan (@ChadwikoTWW) October 19, 2025 Jaylin Lane drops what would have been his first NFL Touchdown catch. #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/VpqZMsZp0S — Chad Ryan (@ChadwikoTWW) September 21, 2025 While clearly at least one more drop could be credited to Jaylin, his total on the season still wasn’t excessive. Lane wasn’t known for having an issue with the drops coming out of Virginia Tech, with only 12 dropped passes on 294 targets at Middle Tennessee State and Virginia Tech. The problem is those drops came in key moments that altered the perception of his performance. There is a strong possibility the moment may have been too much for him in his rookie season, and he will be able to resolve this issue with a full offseason and less pressure to carry the offense. The other issue with his receiving ability revolves around a similar, yet different metric, catch rate . Catch rate is simply the number of passes a receiver catches divided by the number of targets in his direction. Targets can be hard to assess — there are some passes that get arbitrarily assigned to a receiver even though they’re not remotely catchable or get batted away before the receiver has a shot at catching the ball. Still, a receiver’s catch rate is a worthwhile measure of efficiency. Lane’s 2025 catch rate was 50%, well below the 62.4% league average, which leads us to the next part of the discussion— route running. While drops certainly play into catch rate, part of the reason his production was down on 32 targets was due to his route running. While going from starter Jayden Daniels to backup Marcus Mariota accounts for some of it, Lane’s lack of timing and refinement on his routes resulted in several missed connections. Coming into the league, Lane was not known as a great route runner, needing to work on being more consistent and fluid while adding separation at the top of his routes. While it was by no means perfect, Jaylin did demonstrate significant improvement over the course of his rookie season. Lane’s All-22 film from the Bengals preseason game showed some early promise, as he gains separation by driving the corners off balance with his speed, but it also highlights how he lacks variation and nuance in the timing of his routes. Most of Lane’s routes are run at 100% speed. Jaylin Lane All-22 (12 routes) vs Bengals #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/y71bFPB66N — brandon (@JayDanielsMVP) August 19, 2025 Over the course of the season, Jaylin started to add to the mix. Below you can see it against Tyrique Stevenson in the Bears game, and then later in the year versus Pat Surtain. The rookie Jaylin Lane with the sweet double move pic.twitter.com/Uu9T3bl5ls — NFL (@NFL) October 14, 2025 Pretty nice route by Jaylin Lane vs Pat Surtain pic.twitter.com/8Zj5QtIKX0 — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) December 3, 2025 While the double move is impressive, I would like to focus more on Lane’s route versus the Broncos. Initially, you can again see how Lane uses his speed to eat up the big cushion Surtain gives him, and then takes a subtle jab step at the 45-yard line to gain some space before breaking his route inside. There isn’t a huge amount of separation as Surtain recovers quickly but, given the cornerback’s talent level, it is impressive. This may have been a completion if Mariota didn’t have quick, direct pressure in his face. While his route skills have improved, Lane still won’t consistently win on press coverage and needs to be schemed open to utilize his speed and yards-after-catch ability. Prior to his rookie season, I detailed ways then offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury could use his play-calling to maximize Lane’s skill set, including switch releases, stick routes, and screens in the short area of the receiving game. Possibly due to Terry McLaurin’s absence, Kingsbury went almost the complete opposite direction with the wide receiver’s utilization, making Lane into more of a vertical threat. His average depth of target was 13.3 yards last season. Instead, Deebo Samuel was the one moved around the formation and heavily targeted in the underneath passing game ( ADOT 5.2 ) with varying levels of success. Below is a route diagram Bobby Peters of Alert The Post drew of one of Kingsbury’s plays last season. Creative Cross / Wave variation from Kingsbury and the 2025 Commanders. Flat and Hook control underneath the Cross with two vertical clear outs. pic.twitter.com/m7veC8DdWj — Bobby Peters (@b_peters12) June 23, 2026 You will note how the diagram demonstrates Kingsbury’s use of the vertical passing game to help clear out the underneath with crossers happening well down the field. Kliff typically had Lane playing on the outside or in a stasis role, instead of using him in motion or underneath. Conversely, new coordinator David Blough’s offense is expected to utilize multiple players with Lane’s type of versatility that can split wide, line up in the slot, and take sweeps off designed runs. The offense is expected to target the short-to-intermediate portions of the field, and there should be opportunities to get multiple players in space where they can use their speed and quickness to create yards after the catch. For a visual reference, here is another diagram from Bobby Peters on how Ben Johnson utilizes stick combinations. A few Ben Johnson Stick combinations pic.twitter.com/AGRivAE0Iy — Bobby Peters (@b_peters12) June 24, 2026 Washington’s prospective offense and Lane’s development both appear to set the receiver up for an improved sophomore campaign. But in order to realize his potential within the offense, Jaylin needs to earn his place within it. Competition for snaps will be greater this season than last, with the addition of TE Chig Okonkwo and WRs Antonio Williams, Brown, and Van Jefferson. UDFAs Jaden Bradley and Chris Hilton Jr. will also push for a spot on the team. So far, Lane has been keeping pace, returning from a December ankle injury for full participation in offseason activities and minicamp. He continues to work on his route running and footwork, and Dan Quinn singled him out during those sessions, saying “You see it, I think [WR Jaylin] Lane is taking that step that you’d hope to see a player take from Year 1 to Year 2 of what it can be.” As training camp gets rolling, Lane will need to make his mark early to win a spot in the rotation.
